paragraphs: Archaeological sites such as Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land have produced stone tools and ground ochre that excavators date to around 65,000 years ago, evidence used to argue for early human arrival in Australia by sea from the Indonesian archipelago. The date remains debated among archaeologists, with some preferring a somewhat later arrival, but it places people on the continent well before comparable settlement of Europe.

What followed was not one culture but hundreds of distinct language groups, each with its own law, ceremony and territory, connected by trade routes and shared song traditions that crossed group boundaries. Many of those languages and the knowledge carried in them continue among Aboriginal communities across Australia today, passed on through kinship rather than written record.

The didgeridoo is made from a eucalyptus branch or trunk that termites have already hollowed out, cut to length and often coated inside with beeswax at the mouthpiece. Rock art in Arnhem Land showing players with the instrument has been dated to roughly 1000 BCE, making it one of the oldest wind instruments still played anywhere, though estimates of exactly how old vary among archaeologists.

In its home region it is played using circular breathing, drawn air stored in the cheeks while inhaling through the nose, to sustain a continuous drone beneath song and dance at ceremonies. Traditionally its use was restricted to men in many communities, a restriction still observed in some areas even as the instrument has since spread into wider popular use across Australia and abroad.

Rock shelters across Australia, from the Kimberley to Arnhem Land, hold layered images built up over thousands of years rather than made at any single moment, including the Gwion Gwion figures and the X-ray style paintings of Kakadu that show internal organs and bones. Painters used ochre, charcoal and white clay, sometimes applied by mouth spray, and some panels have been repainted by later generations maintaining them.

Because the paint sits on rock rather than in a datable layer, archaeologists date most panels indirectly, from mineral crusts over the pigment or from extinct animals some images show, such as the thylacine in mainland sites. Many sites are still maintained by traditional custodians whose lore explains particular figures, kept separate from what archaeological dating can independently confirm.

A songline is a fixed sequence of verses that tracks a creator being's route across country, naming waterholes, ridgelines and other features in the order a traveller would reach them. Sung correctly, it works as a memorised itinerary, letting a singer navigate country on foot without a map, and some documented lines run for hundreds of kilometres, crossing many language groups along the way.

Each group holds custodianship of the verses that pass through its own country, handing off to neighbours at shared boundaries, so no single person knows an entire line end to end. Anthropologists recording these routes since the twentieth century have relied on the custodians themselves, since the words are tied to specific descent groups and cannot be read off a map or transcript.

Uluru is a single sandstone monolith rising about 348 metres above the surrounding plain in Australia's Northern Territory, with most of its bulk lying underground. To the Anangu, its traditional owners, individual features on its surface, caves, fissures and waterholes, mark events from ancestral stories that assign specific sites to specific family groups responsible for their care.

European surveyor William Gosse named it Ayers Rock in 1873 after a colonial official who had never seen it, and that name stood alongside Uluru until 1993, when both were used jointly. Ownership of the surrounding land was handed back to the Anangu in 1985, and in 2019, after years of Anangu requests, the Australian government banned recreational climbing on the rock itself.

No single canvas or manifesto marks a start; the label covers painters, among them Jackson Pollock, Willem de Kooning and Mark Rothko, who had worked through the Depression on federal art projects and emerged after the war painting without a recognisable subject. Pollock began laying canvas on the floor and dripping paint from above around 1947, a method he called action painting.

The critic Harold Rosenberg wrote in 1952 that for these painters the canvas was an arena to act in rather than a space to reproduce. Peggy Guggenheim's Art of This Century gallery, open in New York from 1942, had given several of them their first shows before larger institutions paid attention.

Named for a Ohio estate where an early mound was excavated in 1901, the Adena culture is known mainly through its earthworks rather than any written record, since it left none. People across the Ohio Valley built conical burial mounds, some over 20 metres tall, and larger earthen enclosures whose exact use, ceremonial or defensive, is still argued over.

Grave goods recovered from Adena mounds include copper from the Great Lakes and marine shell from the Gulf coast, showing exchange networks reaching far beyond the valley itself. Adena people also grew squash and sunflower, among the earliest cultivated plants in eastern North America, alongside continued hunting and gathering.

Adena communities across the Ohio Valley built conical earthen mounds over log-lined burial chambers, adding layer upon layer of soil over generations so that some grew to more than twenty metres high through repeated use rather than a single act of construction. Grave goods placed with the dead included copper ornaments, engraved stone tablets and platform pipes carved into animal and human forms.

The people who built these mounds left no writing, so their name comes from Adena, the Ohio estate on which the first major mound was excavated in the early nineteenth century, not from any word they used for themselves. Grave Creek Mound in West Virginia, one of the largest Adena mounds to survive, still stands roughly 19 metres tall in the middle of the modern town built around it.

Before Aeschylus, Greek tragedy is said to have relied on a single actor speaking against a chorus. His surviving play The Persians, staged in 472 BC, adds a second actor so that two characters could address each other directly on stage rather than each only addressing the chorus, letting a scene hold argument and reply instead of report.

The Persians dramatises a Greek naval victory, at Salamis, that Aeschylus himself is thought to have fought in only eight years earlier, told from the losing Persian court's point of view rather than the winning Athenian one. Aristotle later credited Aeschylus, in the Poetics, with introducing the second actor and reducing the chorus's role to make room for it.

Almost everything told about Aesop comes from later legend rather than record: a Greek slave from Thrace or Phrygia, freed for his wit, put to death at Delphi on a false charge of temple theft. Herodotus, writing a century after the fables were supposedly told, is the earliest source to mention him at all.

None of the fables were written by Aesop himself; they were passed along orally and only collected and versified generations later, first by Demetrius of Phalerum and then, more durably, by the Roman poet Phaedrus. The talking foxes and crows carried a moral pointed enough to survive the name attached to it being unprovable.

Activist Cleve Jones conceived the memorial after a 1985 candlelight march in San Francisco, when he asked marchers to write the names of friends who had died on placards taped to a federal building, forming a pattern that reminded him of a patchwork quilt. The NAMES Project Foundation began sewing individual fabric panels the following year, each roughly the size of a grave, submitted by families and partners of people who had died of AIDS.

The quilt was laid out on the National Mall in Washington for the first time on 11 October 1987, made up of 1,920 panels covering an area larger than a football field, timed to coincide with a national march for lesbian and gay rights. Volunteers read the names aloud as it was unfurled; it has since grown to tens of thousands of panels.

Monks cut thirty rock chambers into a horseshoe-shaped cliff above the Waghora river in the Deccan, working the sandstone into halls for prayer and small cells for living, then plastering the walls to paint over them. The later phase of work, largely from the fifth century under patrons connected to the Vakataka dynasty, added most of the surviving murals and carved images of the Buddha.

The paintings show scenes from the Buddha's past lives, the Jataka tales, alongside court processions and figures whose modelled bodies and shading owe something to earlier Gandharan and Gupta sculpture. The site was abandoned and overgrown by jungle for centuries until a British officer, John Smith, came across the entrance while hunting tigers in 1819.

Akbar had spent years holding debates at Fatehpur Sikri between Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, Christian and Jesuit scholars before announcing his own faith around 1582, built from pieces of several traditions and centred on loyalty to the emperor himself as a kind of spiritual guide. He took the sun as a central symbol and asked initiates to greet him with a set phrase, Allahu Akbar, that echoed his own name.

Din-i Ilahi never reached a wide following outside a small circle of courtiers close to Akbar, and no organised structure of temples or clergy grew around it. It was suppressed by force after Akbar's death in 1605, though later histories argued over whether it had ever been a genuine third religion or mainly a device for binding the loyalty of Akbar's court.

Amenhotep IV took the throne around 1353 BC and within a few years changed his name to Akhenaten, closed temples to Egypt's traditional gods and diverted their funding to worship of the Aten, the sun disc. He abandoned Thebes for a new capital built from scratch at Akhetaten, modern Amarna, on land he claimed no god had previously owned.

Art from his reign shows him and his queen Nefertiti in unusually informal, elongated poses, kissing their daughters in scenes earlier pharaohs never allowed on temple walls. After his death the old priesthoods were restored, his capital was abandoned, and his name was struck from king lists, so the episode survived mainly through the ruins his successors tried to erase.

A shipwrecked traveller named Frumentius rose to advise the Aksumite court and later persuaded King Ezana to accept Christianity, probably in the 340s; Athanasius of Alexandria then consecrated Frumentius as the first bishop of the Ethiopian church. The change shows up on Aksum's own coinage, where the crescent and disc that had marked earlier issues gave way to a cross, among the first uses of that symbol on any coin.

Aksum controlled trade across the Red Sea from its highland capital in modern Ethiopia and Eritrea, and its royal conversion made it one of the earliest states anywhere, alongside Armenia, to adopt Christianity as policy rather than as a private practice among some subjects. Ezana's own inscriptions shift from invoking multiple gods to invoking one, in step with the coinage.

Al-Ghazali had taught at Baghdad's leading madrasa and studied the Greek influenced philosophy of Avicenna and al-Farabi closely enough to summarise it fairly before attacking it. His book, written in the early 1090s, argued that philosophers who claimed reason alone could prove the world's eternity or deny bodily resurrection had overstepped what logic could actually establish.

The book did not end philosophical study in the Islamic world, but it forced later thinkers, including the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, to answer it directly; his rebuttal was itself titled The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Al-Ghazali left teaching soon after for a period of wandering and ascetic withdrawal before returning to write on mysticism and law.

Al-Jazari finished the Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Devices in 1206, at the end of about twenty five years serving as chief engineer to the Artuqid court at Diyarbakir. The book describes roughly fifty devices in detail: water clocks marked by moving figures, automated palace gates, a hand washing basin that released water only once a servant figure's hands passed under it.

Each device is set out with diagrams alongside the text so a craftsman could rebuild it from the page, an unusual level of practical instruction for the period. Later copies were made across the Islamic world and into Ottoman workshops, and surviving illustrated manuscripts, none from al-Jazari's own hand, are now held in museum and library collections from Istanbul to Washington.

The island in San Francisco Bay had already held a military prison for decades before the Department of Justice took it over in 1934, converting it into a maximum-security federal penitentiary meant to hold the inmates other prisons could not control. Cold currents and the mile and a quarter of open water to the mainland were treated as security features in their own right, cheaper than extra guards.

Al Capone and kidnapper Machine Gun Kelly were both sent there in its early years, and the prison operated for 29 years before closing in 1963 when the cost of running an island facility, including shipping in fresh water, outweighed its usefulness. No escape from Alcatraz was ever confirmed successful, though three men who vanished in a 1962 raft escape were never found alive or dead.

Bill Wilson, a New York stockbroker who had nearly drunk himself out of his career, was on a business trip to Akron, Ohio when he grew afraid of relapsing and started calling local ministers to find another alcoholic to talk to instead of a drink. That search led him to surgeon Robert Smith, and the two men met on 10 June 1935, a date the fellowship marks as its founding because it was the day Smith took his last drink.

Their method, developed in the Christian Oxford Group before the two men split from it, rested on alcoholics helping one another rather than doctors treating them, kept anonymous so members were not identified publicly. Wilson wrote the group's core text, known informally as the Big Book, in 1939, and the twelve-step model it set out was later adapted by dozens of other recovery groups.

Alexander founded or refounded dozens of cities on his march east, many named Alexandria after himself, and garrisoned them with veterans who married local women and stayed. Greek became the administrative language from Egypt to the Indus, and Greek coinage, gymnasiums and theatres followed the garrisons even after his empire split among his generals.

The result, later called Hellenistic culture, mixed rather than simply replaced what it found: Egyptian priests kept writing in demotic script alongside Greek, and a Greco-Bactrian kingdom in modern Afghanistan minted coins with Greek gods on one face for centuries after Alexander's death in 323 BC. Buddhist sculpture in Gandhara later borrowed Greek drapery and facial modelling from soldiers' descendants settled in the region.

The Dorset culture occupied the Arctic coasts of what are now Canada and Greenland for around fifteen hundred years without ever adopting the bow and arrow or the dog sled, tools their Thule successors used to hunt on land and travel further. Instead they hunted seals at breathing holes cut in sea ice, working with finely struck stone microblades and harpoon heads shaped for that single purpose.

Carved ivory figures of bears, seals and human faces, some no larger than a thumbnail, are the clearest trace of Dorset belief that survives, though nothing written explains what the carvings were for. Genetic studies of Dorset remains find no descendants among later Arctic peoples, suggesting the culture ended in replacement by incoming Thule groups rather than gradual absorption.

Around the first and second centuries, communities across the Four Corners region of the American Southwest began digging pit houses into the ground, lined with stone and roofed with timber and earth, growing maize alongside squash and beans on the mesas above. These pit houses, later excavated at sites such as Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde, are the earliest structures used to trace the culture now called Ancestral Puebloan.

Over the following centuries the pit house gave way to above-ground masonry rooms joined into blocks, the form that produced the multi-storey villages the region is known for. The early farming settlements left behind pottery, turkey pens and irrigated fields, evidence of a settled life built well before any of the stone towns that came later.

Tree ring records from the Colorado Plateau show a severe drought running from about 1276 to 1299, a stretch dry enough to fail crops repeatedly across a region already farming near the edge of what its soils could support. Communities at Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings and at Chaco Canyon's great houses, some occupied for generations, emptied out within this window.

People moved south and east toward the Rio Grande and Little Colorado river valleys, where permanent water sources were more reliable, and their descendants built the pueblos still occupied today at places such as Acoma and Zuni. Archaeologists no longer treat the move as a single event: households appear to have left in stages over years, following whichever farmland still held water.

Chaco Canyon's Pueblo Bonito rose in stages over two centuries into roughly six hundred rooms and multiple kivas, built from sandstone blocks quarried nearby and roofed with timber carried, on foot, from mountains over fifty miles away since no draft animals or wheeled transport existed to move it. Roads radiating from the canyon connected it to dozens of outlying great houses across the San Juan basin.

At Mesa Verde, families built multi storey stone dwellings directly into sandstone alcoves in canyon walls, reachable only by hand and toe holds carved into the rock. Both sites were largely abandoned by the late 1200s, likely under sustained drought, and their descendants moved into the Rio Grande and Hopi pueblos that Spanish explorers later encountered.

Monasteries in Northumbria and elsewhere in England produced illuminated gospel books whose decoration drew on three sources at once: Irish knotwork brought by missionary monks, Germanic animal ornament carried over from pagan metalwork, and figure drawing copied from Italian manuscripts reaching English scriptoria through Rome and Wearmouth-Jarrow.

Pigments came from as far as lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan and insect dyes from the Mediterranean, ground and mixed by hand for pages that could take a scribe months to complete. Surviving examples besides the Lindisfarne Gospels include the Book of Durrow and the Echternach Gospels, made in linked scriptoria that shared exemplars and, in places, individual artists.

The National Party won South Africa's 1948 general election on a platform built around the Afrikaans word apartheid, meaning apartness, and began passing laws to enforce it soon after taking office. The Population Registration Act of 1950 classified every resident by race, and the Group Areas Act of the same year assigned separate residential zones, forcibly removing people who lived in the wrong one.

Further laws over the following decade banned interracial marriage, segregated schools, hospitals and beaches, and required Black South Africans to carry passes restricting where they could live and work. The system remained in place until negotiations in the early 1990s led to South Africa's first fully democratic election in April 1994.

Apuleius, born in Roman North Africa, wrote a novel in eleven books that he called Metamorphoses; readers later renamed it The Golden Ass to distinguish it from Ovid's poem of the same title. Its narrator, Lucius, dabbles in magic ointment and is accidentally turned into a donkey, then spends most of the book passed between owners while waiting to find a way back to human form.

Bound into the story are inset tales told by other characters along the road, the best known being the story of Cupid and Psyche, which has no earlier surviving source and may be Apuleius's own invention. The final book turns serious: the donkey is restored to human shape after praying to Isis and is initiated into her priesthood, an ending that has led some readers to treat the whole novel as a religious allegory rather than pure comedy.

Thomas Aquinas wrote the Summa Theologica as a teaching text for students new to theology, structured as a long sequence of questions, each stating objections before Aquinas's own answer and his replies to the objections. He worked on it while teaching in Rome and later Paris, dictating much of it to secretaries, and it drew heavily on Aristotle, whose works had recently reached western Europe through Arabic and Latin translations.

He never finished it. In December 1273 Aquinas stopped writing after what he described as an overwhelming experience during Mass, reportedly telling a companion that everything he had written now seemed small; he died a few months later in 1274. Later theologians completed the unfinished third part from his other writings.

The frame story is simple: Scheherazade delays her execution night after night by never finishing a story before dawn. Ninth century Arabic versions grew from a smaller Persian collection called Hazar Afsana, a thousand tales, and Baghdad copyists added stories set in their own city alongside older material carried in from India and Persia.

No single author signed the collection, and no two manuscripts agree on its contents. Stories such as Aladdin and Ali Baba, now inseparable from the title in the West, are not in the earliest Arabic manuscripts at all; they entered through the eighteenth century French translator Antoine Galland, who added them from other sources.

A finished Quran of this period could carry gold leaf on every opening page, laid over a red bole ground and burnished with an agate stone so it caught light without a brushstroke showing. Copyists worked in relay: one scribe wrote the text in black ink, another added vowel marks in red, and a third filled the margins with interlace before the illuminator touched the page at all.

The geometric patterns were built with compass and straightedge from a small set of repeating stars and polygons, not sketched by eye. Workshops in Baghdad, Cairo and Granada shared the same underlying grids, which is why a page from one city can be mistaken for another without a signature or colophon naming its scribe.

Leonardo of Pisa, later called Fibonacci, had learned the Hindu-Arabic numeral system as a boy from an Arab tutor in the North African port of Bugia, where his father worked for Pisan merchants. In 1202 he set the system out in Liber Abaci, a mathematics manual written for traders.

The book showed how nine digits and a zero, arranged in place-value columns, made multiplication, division and currency conversion far quicker than counting on an abacus or working through Roman numerals. Adoption by Italian merchants and bankers over the following two centuries gradually displaced Roman numerals from everyday accounts and ledgers.

The Umayyad general Hassan ibn al-Nu'man took Carthage in 698, defeating a Byzantine force sent from Constantinople to hold what remained of its African province. His troops tore down the city's walls, blocked its harbours and cut off its water supply, leaving it unusable rather than simply occupied.

A year later a new settlement, Tunis, rose nearby to serve as a naval base for further campaigns west. Carthage never recovered its population or its harbours, and the administrative and trading role it had carried for over a thousand years, first for Phoenicia, then Rome, then Byzantium, passed permanently to its replacement a few miles along the coast.

Historians mark the start of Greece's Archaic period around 800 BC, following the poorly documented Dark Age after the collapse of Mycenaean palace centres. There is no single founding event: the boundary is drawn from a cluster of changes, including the adoption of an alphabet adapted from Phoenician traders and the first stone temples replacing earlier wooden shrines.

Greek city-states began sending settlers across the Mediterranean and Black Sea in this period, founding colonies from Sicily to the Crimea while competing at home through early forms of hoplite warfare. The first recorded Olympic Games, traditionally dated to 776 BC, fall within this same stretch, though the earliest surviving victor lists were compiled later.

Arius, a priest in Alexandria, argued that the Son had a beginning and was therefore not equal in eternity to the Father, since anything begotten must come after the one who begot it. His bishop Alexander disagreed, and the dispute spread through Egyptian congregations quickly enough that Constantine summoned bishops from across the empire to settle it at Nicaea in 325.

That council condemned Arius and produced the creed that names the Son as of one substance with the Father, but it did not end the argument. Arian and Nicene factions kept contesting bishoprics and imperial favour for another two generations, with emperors switching sides more than once before Theodosius finally enforced the Nicene position by law in 380.

Aristophanes' earliest surviving play, The Acharnians, was staged in 425 BC and argued, in the middle of the Peloponnesian War, that an ordinary farmer was right to make his own private peace with Sparta. He named living Athenians on stage by their own names, including the general Cleon, who is said to have sued him over an earlier, lost comedy that mocked him more directly.

Eleven of his plays survive complete out of roughly forty he is credited with writing, more than for any other Greek comic poet, because later grammarians in Alexandria and Byzantium kept copying his texts as school and reference material long after the political jokes had stopped landing. The rest are known only from fragments and the titles later writers happened to quote.

Philip II brought Aristotle to Macedon around 343 BCE and gave him the use of a retreat at Mieza, away from the court at Pella, to teach the thirteen year old Alexander and a small group of noble boys. In return Philip is said to have rebuilt Aristotle's home city of Stagira, which he had destroyed in an earlier campaign.

The lessons covered logic, ethics, medicine and poetry, and Aristotle later produced an edited text of Homer's Iliad for his pupil to carry on campaign. Alexander funded natural history collecting for his old teacher once he began conquering Persia, sending back specimens from as far as India, though the two men's politics diverged sharply as the empire grew.

Asante oral tradition holds that the priest Okomfo Anokye summoned a wooden stool sheathed in gold from the sky, which settled onto the lap of the first Asante king, Osei Tutu, before an assembly of chiefs around the start of the eighteenth century. The stool was said to hold the soul of the Asante people, not merely the ruler's authority, and no one, including the king himself, was permitted to sit on it.

Whatever the founding moment actually looked like, the stool was afterward the empire's central symbol, kept away from public view except at major ceremonies and guarded so closely that a British governor's 1900 demand to see it triggered an uprising known as the War of the Golden Stool. It remains in Asante custody in Kumasi, never sat upon, matching the original prohibition.

The Ashikaga shoguns ruled from Kyoto rather than from a distant military camp, and living close to the imperial court's older aristocratic culture, they spent heavily on building it a rival of their own. Shogun Yoshimitsu retired to a villa at Kitayama in the 1390s whose gold covered pavilion still stands, rebuilt after a 1950 arson fire, as Kinkakuji.

Zen temples in Kyoto became the setting for tea gatherings, garden design using rock and raked gravel to suggest mountains and water, and ink paintings imported from Song and Yuan China that Japanese monk painters began copying and adapting. These tastes, cultivated first inside temple walls and shogunal villas, spread outward over the following century to become touchstones of later Japanese aesthetics generally.

When the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus in January 27 BCE, marking the settlement that ended two decades of civil war, he and his ally Maecenas began drawing writers into their circle rather than commissioning propaganda outright. Maecenas's patronage supported Virgil and Horace directly, giving each a country estate and time to write, while Ovid worked at Rome's margins without that same backing.

The results included Virgil's Aeneid, Horace's Odes, and Ovid's Metamorphoses, works read in schoolrooms and quoted by Latin authors for centuries afterward. Augustus's tolerance had a limit: when Ovid's own conduct or writing displeased him, the same regime that had funded Virgil banished the poet to the Black Sea coast for the rest of his life.

Augustine led a group of monks sent from Rome by Pope Gregory in 596, who nearly turned back partway through Gaul on hearing frightening reports of the Anglo-Saxons. They landed on the Isle of Thanet in Kent in 597 and were received by King Ethelbert, whose wife Bertha was already a Christian from the Frankish court.

Ethelbert converted within the year, and Augustine was consecrated archbishop with a see at Canterbury rather than the abandoned Roman city of London. The mission answered directly to Rome rather than to any surviving British church, a distinction that mattered later when Roman and older Celtic Christian practice came into conflict over matters as small as how to calculate the date of Easter.

The jizya was a tax non-Muslim subjects paid in exchange for exemption from military service, and earlier Mughal emperors, including Aurangzeb's great-grandfather Akbar, had abolished it to keep the empire's mostly Hindu population content. Aurangzeb reversed that policy in 1679, reimposing the tax and directing that revenue toward Islamic religious institutions.

The decision followed earlier moves against Hindu temples and festivals during his reign and provoked open resistance, including revolts by Rajput and Maratha nobles who had previously served the Mughal court. Aurangzeb kept expanding Mughal territory to its largest extent even as this unrest spread, leaving an empire that looked strongest on the map just as its internal loyalties were fraying.

Ibn Rushd, a judge in Cordoba known in Latin as Averroes, wrote three tiers of commentary, short, middle and long, on nearly all of Aristotle's surviving works. He aimed to recover what Aristotle had actually argued rather than the Neoplatonist reading that earlier Arabic and Syriac translators had layered over the text.

Latin translations, mostly made by Michael Scot in the early thirteenth century, reached the arts faculties of Paris and Oxford within decades, and Thomas Aquinas cited Ibn Rushd simply as the Commentator. In 1195 the Almohad caliph had his books burned and exiled him to Lucena, recalling him to Marrakesh shortly before his death in 1198.

Clement V, a Frenchman elected in 1305 after a stalemated conclave, never went to Rome, where factional violence among noble families made the city dangerous for an outsider pope. He settled the curia at Avignon in 1309, technically papal territory but surrounded by lands the French crown controlled, and later popes built a fortified palace there that still stands.

Seven successive popes, all French, governed from Avignon rather than Rome, a run critics inside and outside the church read as proof of French influence over appointments and policy. The arrangement also let the papacy build an efficient, centralised bureaucracy for taxation and correspondence, tools later popes carried back to Italy once the court finally returned.

Gregory XI left Avignon in September 1376 and reached Rome in January 1377, urged home partly by the preaching of Catherine of Siena and partly by a revolt of Italian cities against papal governors, the War of the Eight Saints, which threatened to strip the papacy of its Italian territory entirely. He found the Lateran Palace, the traditional papal residence, in poor repair after decades of neglect and settled instead near St Peter's.

His return did not settle the underlying strain between French and Italian cardinals over where the papacy belonged. Gregory died the following year, and the conclave that followed split so badly it produced two rival claimants, one of the direct causes of the schism that opened almost immediately after his death.

Ruhollah Khomeini died on 3 June 1989 at 86, ten years after returning from exile to lead Iran's revolution. His open bier drew a crowd estimated at over ten million, roughly a sixth of Iran's population, that swelled through a night of vigil in Tehran's summer heat.

Mourners broke through the barriers around the coffin, tearing his burial shroud and pulling the body partly from its casket; the wooden coffin itself was smashed. Officials called off the burial and returned days later, flying the body in by helicopter under guard to complete it. Iranian reports at the time put the dead and injured in the crush at several thousand.

Ayutthaya, founded in 1351 on an island in the Chao Phraya river, controlled routes linking the Gulf of Siam to inland Southeast Asia and grew rich taxing the ships that passed. By 1500 its port hosted merchants from China, Japan, India and the Persian Gulf, and foreign communities kept their own quarters along the riverbank.

Kings funded temple building on a large scale, including the royal temple of Wat Phra Si Sanphet within the palace grounds, its three chedi eventually holding the ashes of Ayutthaya kings. The kingdom's court records and much of its temple art were destroyed when a Burmese army burned the city in 1767, leaving ruins that are now a protected historical park.

Bach had spent his last 27 years as director of music for Leipzig's main churches, writing cantatas week after week alongside teaching Latin to choirboys at the Thomasschule. His eyesight had been failing for years, and in 1750 an English eye surgeon operating on his cataracts in Leipzig left him blind and weakened.

He died on 28 July 1750, likely from complications following the operation or a stroke. Leipzig's council had already been discussing his replacement before he died, and much of his music went unpublished and scattered among his sons' collections; Felix Mendelssohn's revival of the St Matthew Passion in 1829 brought wide attention back to it.

Bach assembled the Mass in B minor in the final year of his life, largely by reworking music he had already written for earlier church cantatas into a full setting of the Latin mass text. He had sent an early Kyrie and Gloria to the Dresden court years before, seeking a royal title that never fully materialised.

As a Lutheran cantor writing a Catholic mass, Bach produced a work too long and too demanding for ordinary church use in either tradition; it went unperformed as a complete piece in his lifetime. The manuscript passed through his sons and a scattering of collectors before receiving a full public performance in the following century.

Bach wrote out the first book of the Well-Tempered Clavier while working as court musician in Cothen, a set of 24 preludes and fugues, one pair in every major and minor key. The title page states he wrote it partly for the instruction of young musicians eager to learn.

Keyboards of the time were tuned unevenly, so some keys rang sweet and others sour; a well-tempered instrument, tuned with small adjustments, could play in any of them without an ugly clash. Bach later assembled a second book of 24 more preludes and fugues two decades on.

The Bagobo people of Mindanao's Mount Apo region wove cloth from abaca fibre, stripped from the leaf stalks of a banana relative, dyeing bundles of fibre before weaving in a resist technique that produced repeating geometric patterns. Brass obtained through trade was cast into anklets, belts and betel-nut boxes.

Status among Bagobo men was marked by red clothing and fuller sets of ornament, worn by those who had taken part in a raid or paid a ceremonial fee. The anthropologist Fay-Cooper Cole documented these grades of dress during fieldwork in the early twentieth century, before much of the material was dispersed to museums abroad.

Catherine de Medici commissioned the piece to celebrate a courtly wedding, and it was staged in the great hall of the Hotel de Bourbon in Paris on 15 October 1581, running from ten at night past three the following morning. Balthasar de Beaujoyeulx, an Italian violinist working at the French court, choreographed it to follow rules on matching verse, music and movement drawn up by a Parisian academy of poets and musicians.

The plot, drawn from the legend of the sorceress Circe, unfolded through sung verse, instrumental interludes and dance rather than spoken dialogue, performed before the king and queen on a floor marked with geometric patterns the dancers traced. Beaujoyeulx published a detailed account with illustrations the following year, which survives and let later scholars reconstruct the performance.

Two colossal figures were cut into the cliff face at Bamiyan, in the Hindu Kush valley of central Afghanistan, roughly a century apart; the larger, about 55 metres tall, stood beside a smaller 38-metre figure carved earlier nearby. Both were shaped directly from the sandstone cliff, with details such as robes and faces built up afterwards in mud plaster over a wooden armature rather than carved whole from the rock.

Bamiyan sat on a branch of the Silk Road connecting Central Asia to India, and pilgrim monks including the Chinese traveller Xuanzang recorded the statues, painted and gilded, in the seventh century. Both figures stood for roughly a millennium and a half until the Taliban destroyed them with explosives in March 2001, leaving only the empty niches now visible in the cliff.

Around 1680, Arcangelo Corelli was working in Rome under cardinal patronage, publishing trio sonatas that fixed the standard instrumentation later composers borrowed wholesale, while Henry Purcell in London was writing anthems for the Chapel Royal and incidental music for the London stage. Both were building on a newer habit of writing instrumental music as its own art form rather than an accompaniment to voices or dance.

Corelli's concerto grosso format, pitting a small group of soloists against a larger string body, gave composers across Europe a reusable structure, while Purcell's opera Dido and Aeneas, written around 1689, showed English audiences that homegrown opera could carry serious tragedy. Printed scores travelled between Italy, England, France and Germany fast enough to shape a shared Baroque style.

By the middle of the seventeenth century, patrons across Catholic Europe wanted art that moved viewers physically, not just informed them. Gian Lorenzo Bernini was carving marble to look like flesh and fabric caught mid motion in Rome, Peter Paul Rubens ran an Antwerp workshop turning out large, muscular canvases for churches and courts, and Rembrandt in Amsterdam was working oil paint thickly enough to catch real light on a sitter's skin.

None of the three worked for the same audience: Bernini answered to popes, Rubens to Catholic courts and diplomats, Rembrandt to Dutch merchants and civic guards who paid to appear in group portraits. That range across patron and purpose is part of why the period is described as a peak rather than a single school, since its unifying trait was technique and drama rather than one style.

Walter Gropius merged Weimar's existing arts and crafts academy with its fine art academy in April 1919 and wrote a manifesto arguing that painters, sculptors and architects should train alongside carpenters and metalworkers rather than above them. Students called their instructors masters, not professors, and began each course with a shared foundation year regardless of the craft they intended to specialise in.

Political pressure forced the school out of Weimar in 1925 into a purpose built campus in Dessau, and the Nazi government closed it outright in 1933 after moving it once more, to Berlin, under its final director Mies van der Rohe. Many of its teachers, including Gropius, Mies and Laszlo Moholy-Nagy, emigrated to the United States and carried its teaching methods into American architecture schools.

Al-Ma'mun's father had already gathered manuscripts in Baghdad, but the caliph pushed the institution toward organised translation, paying scholars to render Greek philosophy and science into Arabic. Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian physician from al-Hira, became its most prolific translator, producing well over a hundred Arabic versions of Galen and other Greek medical writers.

The texts moving through the House of Wisdom included Aristotle's logical works, Ptolemy's astronomy and Euclid's geometry, often relayed through earlier Syriac versions rather than straight from Greek. Baghdad's own scholars, among them the mathematician al-Khwarizmi, worked alongside the translators, and their combined output shaped Islamic science for centuries.

Sullivan had happened to be at London's Heathrow airport in late 1963 when thousands of screaming fans met the Beatles' returning flight, and booked the band on the spot without having heard much of their music. They arrived in New York on 7 February 1964 to a similar crowd at Kennedy Airport, twelve weeks after their manager Brian Epstein had first pitched Sullivan by transatlantic phone.

Roughly 73 million Americans watched the broadcast on 9 February, a figure later cited as proof of the audience television could deliver in one sitting. New York police reported unusually low juvenile crime that Sunday night, which several papers attributed, only half seriously, to every teenager being at home in front of a set.

John Lennon's skiffle group the Quarrymen, formed at his Liverpool school in 1957, had already added Paul McCartney and George Harrison and shed most of its founding members by 1960. That year the remaining players tried out names including Johnny and the Moondogs and the Silver Beetles before settling, reportedly at Stuart Sutcliffe's suggestion, on the Beatles.

The lineup still lacked a steady drummer; Pete Best joined only that August, just before the band left for a residency in Hamburg's red light Reeperbahn district, playing punishing nightly sets in clubs there. Ringo Starr would not replace Best until 1962, after the group had already signed with EMI.

Bede finished his Ecclesiastical History of the English People at the monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow in 731, having spent his whole adult life there since arriving as a child of seven. The book traces Christianity's arrival in England from Roman times through Augustine's mission of 597 to his own day, drawing on letters, oral testimony and papal archives he requested by post.

He is also the reason English dates count years from Christ's birth: his adoption of the anno domini system in this history helped fix it as the standard reckoning across Western Europe. He died in 735, reportedly dictating the final lines of a translation of John's gospel from his deathbed.

Beethoven premiered the Fifth Symphony on 22 December 1808 at Vienna's Theater an der Wien, in a marathon benefit concert that also debuted his Sixth Symphony, his Fourth Piano Concerto and the Choral Fantasy, all in an unheated hall through several hours. The orchestra was under-rehearsed, and at one point a collapse mid-performance forced a restart.

The opening four notes, three short and one long, became one of the most recognisable phrases in orchestral music, and Beethoven's pupil and biographer Anton Schindler later claimed the composer called it fate knocking at the door, a story with no earlier source. Beethoven was already losing his hearing by the time he wrote it.

Beethoven conducted the first performance of his First Symphony in Vienna on 2 April 1800, at a benefit concert he organised for himself at the Burgtheater that also included one of his piano concertos and improvisations at the keyboard. He was thirty years old and already known in Vienna chiefly as a pianist rather than a composer of large orchestral works.

Critics noted how heavily the piece leaned on Haydn and Mozart, his teacher and the composer whose style dominated Viennese concert life, though some found the wind writing unusually prominent for a symphony's opening movement. It was the first of nine symphonies he completed, the last delivered under near-total deafness decades later.

At the Karntnertor theatre in Vienna on 7 May 1824, Beethoven stood at the front of the stage turning pages and marking tempo, while the actual conducting was done by Michael Umlauf. Beethoven had been profoundly deaf for years, and the singers and orchestra had been told beforehand to watch Umlauf and ignore Beethoven's beat entirely.

When the final chord ended, Beethoven kept marking time, unaware the piece had finished. The contralto soloist, Caroline Unger, is said to have turned him around to face the audience so he could see them applauding rather than hear it. The symphony's choral finale, setting Schiller's Ode to Joy, needed a chorus and soloists Beethoven had never combined with an orchestra before.

Beijing had lost its bid for the 2000 Games to Sydney before winning the right to host in 2001, and spent an estimated 40 billion dollars building venues including the steel-lattice National Stadium, nicknamed the Bird's Nest, and the bubble-walled Aquatics Centre known as the Water Cube. Director Zhang Yimou staged the opening ceremony on 8 August 2008, timed for the number eight's association with prosperity.

American swimmer Michael Phelps won eight gold medals, a single-Games record, while Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt set world records in both the 100 and 200 metres. China topped the gold medal table for the first time, ahead of the United States, finishing with 51 golds to the Americans' 36.

Guild casters working for the Oba of Benin used the lost wax method to cast brass and bronze plaques and heads, working metal supplied largely through trade with Portuguese merchants active on the coast from the late fifteenth century. Ivory tusks were carved with figures of the Oba, his warriors and Portuguese traders themselves, and hung or displayed at the royal court.

Many plaques recorded specific rulers, wars and court ceremonies rather than generic scenes, giving historians a dated visual record where written sources are thin. Most of this material left Benin City in 1897, seized by a British force after a punitive expedition, and pieces are now held in museums across Europe and North America, some subject to ongoing restitution claims.

Casting in Benin City was restricted by law to a single guild, the Igun Eronmwon, who worked exclusively for the Oba and lived in their own quarter of the palace grounds. The metal itself was often manilla bracelets brought by Portuguese traders from the 1480s, melted down and recast using the lost wax method the guild had practised for generations before Europeans arrived.

The workshops produced commemorative heads for royal altars, plaques nailed to palace pillars showing warriors and court officials, and ivory carvings for ceremonial dress. Most of what survives left Benin City only in 1897, seized by a British punitive expedition and dispersed into museum collections abroad, which is largely how the corpus is dated and studied today.

Brass and bronze plaques from the Edo kingdom's palace once lined the pillars of the royal compound, showing warriors, court officials and the oba, or king, holding audience surrounded by attendants. Craftsmen cast them by the lost wax method, sculpting each figure in wax over a clay core, coating it in more clay, then melting the wax out before pouring in molten metal, so no two plaques repeat exactly.

Metal for the plaques arrived largely through trade with Portuguese merchants, who reached the Edo coast in the 1480s and exchanged brass manillas for pepper, ivory and cloth. British forces looted thousands of these plaques and other palace bronzes during a punitive expedition in 1897, and most now sit in museums in Europe and North America rather than in Benin City, where restitution claims continue.

No one knows who wrote the poem or exactly when. Estimates for its composition range from the early eighth century to the tenth, and it survives in a single manuscript copied around the year 1000, damaged by a fire in 1731 that scorched its edges and cost some lines permanently.

The poem is set among the Geats and Danes of Scandinavia several centuries before its own composition, and its hero fights Grendel, Grendel's mother and finally a dragon that kills him. Its language mixes Christian references with a plainly pre-Christian warrior culture, a combination scholars still argue over, since the poet never says which world he thought he was describing.

Four brothers working at the Thanjavur court under Maratha rulers set down a fixed sequence of items for temple and court dance, running from a pure movement opening through pieces built on rhythm, mime and devotional text, ending in a closing dance. That sequence, the margam, is still the basic structure a dancer performs in a debut recital.

The brothers also trained musicians and dancers attached to the Thanjavur temple and composed much of the music the repertoire still uses today. Colonial-era laws later banned temple dancers from performing, and the tradition survived largely because teachers passed the Thanjavur repertoire on privately outside the temple.

The verses attributed to Bhartrihari are usually grouped into three sets of roughly one hundred each, on policy and worldly conduct, on love, and on renunciation of the world, though no single manuscript agrees with another on which poem belongs where or even how many are genuinely his. Some are addressed to a king weighing the cost of pleasure against the cost of duty; others simply describe watching desire lose its grip with age.

Indian tradition also credits a Bhartrihari with a treatise on grammar and the philosophy of language, and disagrees over whether this is the same poet, a namesake, or a legend that merged two people into one. Nothing datable, no inscription or colophon, fixes when either lived, and estimates for the poet's life still range across several centuries either side of 450.

Pope Damasus I had commissioned Jerome in 382 to revise the existing Latin Gospels, a patchwork of earlier translations that disagreed with each other. Jerome went further than asked, working from Bethlehem and translating most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than from the Greek Septuagint that other Christian scholars trusted.

That choice drew criticism from contemporaries, including Augustine, who worried a Hebrew-based text would split Latin Christians from the Greek-speaking church. Jerome's version nonetheless became the standard Bible of Western Christianity for over a thousand years and was declared the Catholic Church's official Latin text at the Council of Trent.

Orphaned young, Bihzad was raised in Herat by the painter Mirak Naqqash and came under the protection of Mir Ali Shir Nava'i, a statesman and poet at the Timurid court. He worked in the city's royal workshop during the reign of Sultan Husayn Bayqara, and by 1486 he was its head, directing the copying and illustration of manuscripts for the court library.

His figures broke from flat, symmetrical convention: faces turn, bodies twist in motion, and crowd scenes such as building sites and battle camps are arranged with individual gesture rather than repeated poses. Little is documented of his life beyond these court records, but paintings bearing his name illustrate copies of the Zafarnama and other histories commissioned in Herat.

Alexander was born in Pella, the Macedonian capital, in 356 BCE, the son of Philip II and Olympias of Epirus. Plutarch, writing centuries later, reports omens around the birth, a temple of Artemis burning at Ephesus the same night, that cannot be checked against any contemporary record and were likely added once his conquests made the story worth improving.

His father was already turning Macedon's army into the most effective infantry force in Greece, built around the long sarissa pike. Alexander inherited that army at twenty after Philip's assassination in 336 BCE, along with a kingdom most of Greece still regarded as a backward frontier state rather than the centre of anything.

No contemporary record fixes the date. Sri Lankan chronicles place his death around 483 BCE and count backwards to a birth eighty years earlier, near Lumbini in the Terai lowlands, then part of the Shakya republic rather than any kingdom of Nepal in the modern sense. A sandstone pillar Ashoka raised at the site around 249 BCE, inscribed to mark his own visit, is the earliest physical trace anyone agrees on.

The name Siddhartha Gautama comes from texts compiled centuries after the events they describe, written down only once Buddhist communities began using script. Archaeologists excavating beneath the Mayadevi Temple at Lumbini in the 1990s found a brick shrine layered over a still older timber structure, consistent with a site venerated long before any building stood there.

Robert Darwin's household in Shrewsbury already had money from medicine and pottery when his son arrived in February 1809; the Darwin and Wedgwood families were intertwined by marriage on both sides. The boy showed little early promise at school and was sent to study medicine at Edinburgh, which he found unbearable, before switching to Cambridge for a degree in theology.

A near-accidental berth on HMS Beagle in 1831, arranged through a Cambridge professor who thought the ship's captain needed a gentleman companion, took him around South America and the Galapagos for five years. The notebooks he filled on that voyage became the raw material for the argument he spent the next two decades testing before publishing it.

Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, compiled some four centuries later, gives the birthplace as Qufu in the small state of Lu and names his father as an elderly minor official who died when the boy was three. The family was left poor; Confucius later described working as a shepherd, a clerk and a bookkeeper before he began teaching for a living, a career then open to almost no one outside the aristocracy.

Lu kept its own court archive of ritual and precedent, and much of what became Confucian teaching drew directly on that record rather than on any doctrine he invented from nothing. He is not known to have written a book himself; the Analects were assembled by students after his death from remembered conversations, which is why the text reads as fragments rather than argument.

Almost nothing about Hippocrates' life is independently confirmed. He is said to have been born around 460 BCE on the island of Kos, where a plane tree still shown to visitors is claimed, without evidence reaching back that far, as the spot where he taught. The roughly seventy medical texts bundled under his name were written by many hands over generations.

What that collection, the Hippocratic Corpus, argues for is disease explained by imbalance in the body rather than by offended gods, and treatment by diet, rest and observation before drastic intervention. The oath later attributed to him, promising to do no harm, was not his composition either, but it carried his name into medical schools for over two thousand years.

Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 in Eisleben, in the County of Mansfeld, to a family that had recently moved off the land into copper mining. His father Hans wanted him trained as a lawyer, and he was studying law at Erfurt when a thunderstorm in 1505 reportedly frightened him into vowing to become a monk instead.

He entered an Augustinian friary that same year and was ordained a priest in 1507, later teaching theology at Wittenberg. The University of Wittenberg is where, three decades after his birth, he would post his objections to the sale of indulgences and set off the split within Western Christianity that followed.

Ancient sources disagree on the year by decades, and 372 BCE is a modern reconstruction rather than anything the surviving record states outright. He was born in the small state of Zou, and a much later tradition credits his mother with moving house three times, away from a graveyard and then a market, to find a neighbourhood fit for raising him, though the story is first recorded well after his death.

He travelled between the courts of Qi, Liang and Song offering rulers advice they mostly did not take, arguing against the philosopher Mozi's utilitarian ethics and against Xunzi's later claim that human nature tends toward disorder. His arguments survive as the book that bears his name, a series of recorded exchanges rather than a treatise he sat down to compose.

Islamic tradition places Muhammad's birth in Mecca in the Year of the Elephant, remembered for an Abyssinian army's failed assault on the city with war elephants, an event some historians link to a documented Aksumite campaign of around 570. No contemporary record fixes the exact year, and biographical detail about his early life was written down generations after his death.

He was orphaned young, raised first by his grandfather and then an uncle, and worked as a merchant on caravan routes before, tradition holds, receiving the first revelations around 610 in a cave outside Mecca. What followed reshaped the Arabian Peninsula within his own lifetime, ending in the unification of tribes that had spent centuries at war with each other.

Napoleon Bonaparte was born on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, a year after France bought the island from the Republic of Genoa in 1768. His family, the Buonapartes, were minor Corsican nobility who had briefly backed the island's independence movement under Pasquale Paoli before it was crushed.

That timing meant Napoleon was born a French subject rather than a Genoese or independent Corsican one, and he was sent to French military schools on a scholarship reserved for the island's nobility. He later dropped the Italian spelling of his surname as he rose through the French army.

No writing by Socrates survives, because he apparently left none. Everything known of him comes filtered through Plato, Xenophon and the comic playwright Aristophanes, who mocked him on stage while he was still alive. Even his birth year, usually given as 470 BCE, is a back calculation from Plato's account of his age at death in 399.

He worked as a stonemason's son in Athens before turning to argument as his trade, questioning generals, priests and craftsmen about what they meant by courage or piety until they contradicted themselves. He wrote nothing down and charged no fees. Athens eventually tried him for corrupting its youth and impiety, and he drank hemlock rather than flee.

A person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a nine-page paper titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System to a cryptography mailing list on 31 October 2008, proposing a currency that needed no bank to verify transactions. Nakamoto mined the first block, called the genesis block, on 3 January 2009, embedding a newspaper headline about a bank bailout as a timestamp.

Programmer Hal Finney downloaded the software the day it went public and received the first bitcoin transaction, ten coins, from Nakamoto on 12 January 2009. Nakamoto corresponded with early developers by email and forum post for about two years, then stopped replying in 2011 without ever being conclusively identified.

Alicia Garza wrote a Facebook post the night a Florida jury acquitted George Zimmerman on 13 July 2013 for shooting Trayvon Martin, an unarmed seventeen year old, the year before. Patrisse Cullors, a friend, turned Garza's closing line into the hashtag BlackLivesMatter, and Opal Tometi helped build the online network that carried it beyond their own circles.

The phrase moved from a hashtag to street organising after Michael Brown was killed by police in Ferguson, Missouri, in August 2014, when Cullors led a bus of activists there and local chapters began forming nationwide. By the mid 2010s the network Garza, Cullors and Tometi started had grown into dozens of affiliated chapters across the United States.

Phil Knight, a middle distance runner at the University of Oregon, and his coach Bill Bowerman agreed on a handshake deal on 25 January 1964 to split a shoe importing business fifty fifty, each putting in 500 dollars. Knight had written a business school paper on importing cheap, well made athletic shoes from Japan rather than Germany, then travelled there to find a supplier.

They struck a deal with the Onitsuka Tiger company and sold the shoes from the back of Knight's car at track meets around Oregon, since no store would stock an untested brand. The company kept the Blue Ribbon Sports name for seven years before renaming itself Nike in 1971 and commissioning its swoosh logo for 35 dollars.

Boccaccio frames his hundred stories with seven women and three men who leave plague stricken Florence for a country villa and pass the time telling tales, one each per day over ten days, which gives the book its title. His opening account of the 1348 outbreak, bodies left in the street and families abandoning the sick, is among the fullest surviving descriptions by someone who lived through it.

The tales themselves range from bawdy tricks played on foolish husbands to stories of patient suffering and clever escape, drawn from French fabliaux, Italian folk tale and classical sources. Boccaccio wrote in Tuscan vernacular rather than Latin, and the book's mix of registers, comic and tragic within the same collection, gave later Italian prose writers a model distinct from Dante's poetry or Petrarch's Latin scholarship.

Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy while awaiting execution at Pavia in 524, imprisoned by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric on a charge of treason he denied to the end. The book is a dialogue: a woman personifying Philosophy visits the prisoner in his cell, and prose argument alternates with poems as she talks him through his complaint that a good man's life had collapsed into a condemned cell.

Her answer rests on Fortune's wheel, the idea that rank, wealth and reputation turn regardless of merit and so were never truly his to lose, alongside arguments drawn from Plato on the nature of real goods. Translated into Old English under Alfred the Great and later into Middle English by Chaucer, the book carried Boethius's own case for accepting misfortune's turn to readers who never learned Latin.

Boethius set out to translate every surviving work of Plato and Aristotle into Latin and reconcile the two, a project his execution in 524 left far from finished. What he completed of Aristotle, chiefly the Categories and On Interpretation, along with his own commentaries and textbooks on logic, became for centuries the only route most of Latin Europe had into Greek philosophy at all.

Later medieval scholars called this surviving core the logica vetus, the old logic, to distinguish it from Aristotle's other logical works recovered only after translations from Arabic and Greek resumed in the twelfth century. Until then, a student in Paris or Oxford met Aristotle almost entirely through Boethius's Latin and his own added commentary.

What is called the Book of the Dead was never one fixed book. Scribes copied whichever spells a family could afford from a pool of roughly 200, onto papyrus rolled inside the coffin or wrapped with the mummy, so that a poor burial might carry a handful of texts and a wealthy one nearly all of them.

The spells named the heart's weighing before Osiris, when it was balanced against the feather of the goddess Maat, and gave the words needed to answer the judges and pass among the reeds of the afterlife. The best-preserved copy, the Papyrus of Ani, runs to nearly 24 metres of illustrated text.

The manuscript's exact origin is unrecorded; scholars generally place its production at a Columban monastery, possibly Iona, before the community moved to Kells in County Meath after Viking raids around 806. It contains the four Gospels in Latin, written on calfskin vellum, and was never finished: some pages of decoration were left as outline sketches.

Its pigments came from as far as the Mediterranean and Afghanistan, ground for colours that still show under raking light after twelve centuries. The book was stolen from Kells in 1007 for its gold cover, which was never recovered, and the manuscript itself was found buried some months later, stripped but intact. It has been kept at Trinity College Dublin since the 1660s.

Joseph Smith brought his manuscript to Egbert Grandin, a printer in Palmyra, New York, who ran off 5,000 copies through the winter of 1829 into March 1830. Smith said he had dictated the text from behind a curtain, translating characters on a set of golden plates using a seer stone, with a scribe named Oliver Cowdery writing down what he spoke.

Grandin priced the finished book at a dollar twenty-five, a considerable sum for a first-time author to guarantee, and Martin Harris mortgaged his farm to cover the printing costs. Smith organised the Church of Christ, later renamed the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, within weeks of the book reaching Palmyra's shelves.

The text names its author only as John, writing from exile on the Aegean island of Patmos, and the identification with John the Apostle is a later church tradition; some early Christian writers, including Dionysius of Alexandria, argued the Greek style differed too much from the fourth Gospel for one author. Most scholars date the work to Domitian's reign, around 95, from its references to persecution and to seven named churches in Roman Asia.

It opens as a letter addressed to those seven congregations before turning to visions of beasts, seals and a final battle, written in a coded style scholars call apocalyptic, common in Jewish writing under foreign rule. Its place in the Christian canon was contested longer than most other New Testament books; some eastern churches still do not read it aloud in liturgy.

Botticelli painted the goddess on canvas rather than the wood panel usual for the period, likely because canvas suited a country villa rather than a formal chapel; the work is generally linked to the Medici family, probably commissioned for a villa outside Florence. Venus stands on a scallop shell blown ashore by the wind god Zephyrus, with a figure usually read as the Hour of Spring waiting to clothe her.

The nude female form had almost no precedent in Christian-era Florentine painting at this scale, and Botticelli drew instead on classical sculpture and poetry, including verses by Poliziano describing Venus's birth. The painting survived a period late in Botticelli's life when he reportedly turned against his own earlier secular work under the preacher Savonarola's influence; it hangs today in the Uffizi Gallery.

Robert Baden-Powell, a British army officer known for defending Mafeking during the Boer War, tested his ideas about outdoor training on twenty boys camped on Brownsea Island in Dorset in August 1907. He wrote up the exercises in Scouting for Boys, published in fortnightly instalments through 1908, and boys began forming troops on their own before any organisation existed to run them.

Baden-Powell had not planned a mass movement, but he found himself running one within two years as membership spread across Britain and then abroad. By 1910 troops had formed in the United States, and Baden-Powell resigned his army commission that year to devote himself to scouting full time.

A printer, Colin Macfarquhar, and an engraver, Andrew Bell, launched the Encyclopaedia Britannica in Edinburgh, issuing it in weekly sixpenny instalments starting in December 1768 rather than as a finished book. William Smellie, a 28-year-old scholar hired as editor, compiled most of the entries himself, reportedly using a stack of borrowed books and scissors and paste.

By the time the last instalment appeared in 1771, the parts had been bound into three quarto volumes running to roughly 2,500 pages, illustrated with 160 copperplate engravings by Bell. It sold well enough that a second, ten-volume edition followed within a decade, and the title kept being revised and reissued for more than two centuries afterward.

The Slave Trade Act passed Parliament in March 1807, after William Wilberforce had introduced abolition bills in the Commons for two decades, backed by a campaign that included the Quaker-led boycott of slave-grown sugar and Josiah Wedgwood's kneeling-figure medallion. It banned British ships from carrying enslaved people, but did not free anyone already enslaved in the colonies.

The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron was later tasked with intercepting slave ships from other nations, though smuggling to Brazil and Cuba continued for decades. Slavery itself remained legal in British colonies until the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, and even that act paid compensation to slave owners rather than to the enslaved.

Around 1413 Filippo Brunelleschi painted a small panel of the Florence Baptistery and had viewers check it against the real building through a hole drilled in the back, holding a mirror up to the panel's face. Where the sky should have been he laid burnished silver, so the real clouds reflected in the mirror moved across his painted scene.

The panel itself is lost; what survives is a description by his biographer Antonio Manetti, written decades later. Brunelleschi worked out that lines receding into distance should converge on a single point at the viewer's eye level, a rule Leon Battista Alberti wrote down formally in 1435 and that Florentine painters adopted within a generation.

Siddhartha Gautama had already tried extreme fasting and given it up as useless before he sat beneath a fig tree at Bodh Gaya and resolved not to move until he understood the cause of suffering. Tradition holds he stayed through a night of temptation by the demon Mara before reaching his insight at dawn.

What he arrived at, later summarised as the Four Noble Truths, held that craving causes suffering and that a specific path, not birth or ritual, ends it. The tree said to be descended from that original fig still stands at the site, now the Mahabodhi Temple, and cuttings from it have been replanted across Asia.

Buddhist teachers travelled the caravan routes out of northern India into the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin, places such as Khotan and Kucha, carrying texts and images alongside the merchants whose caravans they joined for safety. Kushan rule across much of this network gave the travelling monks a single political umbrella to move under rather than a string of separate borders.

Local rulers along these routes endowed monasteries and had scripture translated into Central Asian languages, cave shrines were cut into cliffs near towns such as Dunhuang, and merchants carried both goods and Buddhist manuscripts onward into China. The oasis towns became way stations where a text picked up in Gandhara could be copied, translated and passed further east before it ever reached a Chinese court.

Bukhara's madrasas were built and endowed one at a time by rulers and wealthy citizens rather than as a planned system, each supported by a waqf, an endowment of land or shops whose rents paid teachers' salaries and fed students. The Kalyan minaret, over 45 metres tall and finished in the twelfth century, still marked the city's skyline through this period and reportedly survived Genghis Khan's siege of 1220 when much else was burned.

Students travelled from Persia, India and the Arab lands to study law, theology, grammar and astronomy in Bukhara's colleges, and the city kept exchanging scholars and manuscripts with Samarkand, a few days' journey south, throughout the fourteenth century. Copies of works produced in one city routinely turned up in the other's libraries within a generation.

The Samanid rulers kept their capital's palace library stocked with books on every subject then known, Ibn Sina later wrote, including Greek philosophy in Arabic translation that he had never seen collected elsewhere. He was given access as a teenager after treating the reigning emir, and used the time there before the library burned to work through texts unavailable to him anywhere else in the region.

Persian poets including Rudaki and Daqiqi worked at the Samanid court in Bukhara, writing in New Persian at a moment when Arabic still dominated formal prose across the wider Islamic world. The dynasty's patronage helped New Persian literature re-establish itself as a written language of scholarship and verse, alongside Arabic rather than replaced by it.

Edmund Burke published Reflections on the Revolution in France in November 1790, cast as a long open letter to a young Frenchman who had asked his opinion of events in Paris. Burke, an Irish-born member of the British Parliament who had earlier supported the American colonists, warned that abstract rights torn loose from tradition and inherited institutions would end in violence rather than liberty.

The book sold tens of thousands of copies within months and split Burke from former allies such as Charles James Fox, while provoking Thomas Paine's reply, Rights of Man, the following year. Later readers have treated Burke's argument for gradual reform over revolutionary rupture as the founding statement of a distinct political tradition.

Iconoclasm ended in 843, when the regent Theodora, ruling for her young son Michael III, restored icon veneration, an event the Orthodox Church still marks each year on the first Sunday of Lent as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. Painters afterward worked to fixed theological rules: a saint's pose, colours and inscription followed patterns copied from model books rather than an individual painter's invention.

Icons were held to make a holy figure present rather than simply portray one, which is why painters avoided signing their names and why panels were painted on wood prepared with gesso and gold leaf before pigment was added. Surviving early examples are rare, since so many were destroyed during the iconoclast decades; a notable group escaped in the remote monastery of Saint Catherine in Sinai.

In 726 Emperor Leo III had a large icon of Christ removed from above the Chalke Gate, the ceremonial entrance to the imperial palace in Constantinople. The soldier sent to take it down was reportedly killed by a crowd of women. By 730 Leo had made opposition to religious images official policy, ordering their removal from churches across the empire.

The dispute ran in two phases separated by a period of restored icons, the first from 726 to 787 and the second from 815 to 843. Monasteries, often centres of icon veneration, bore much of the enforcement, and defenders like John of Damascus argued in writing that honouring an image was not the same as worshipping it.

San Vitale in Ravenna was consecrated in 547, funded by a banker named Julianus Argentarius rather than by the emperor directly, though its apse mosaics show Justinian and his wife Theodora each flanked by their retinue. The tesserae are cut from glass backed with gold leaf and set at slight angles, so the surface catches light unevenly rather than reflecting it flat.

Ravenna was a Byzantine outpost in Italy, not the imperial capital, and its churches survive largely intact because the city fell out of major strategic importance after the sixth century. Justinian and Theodora never visited Ravenna themselves; their portraits asserted a rule the mosaics announced rather than recorded a real ceremony that took place there.

Ottoman troops took Constantinople on 29 May 1453, and the Byzantine court and its libraries scattered west. Some scholars had already settled in Italy in the decades before the siege; John Argyropoulos and others taught Greek in Florence and Rome, bringing manuscripts of Plato and Aristotle that western readers had known mainly through Latin summaries.

Their arrival fed a Florentine appetite already stirred by Cosimo de' Medici's patronage. Cardinal Bessarion, a Greek convert who had argued for church union at Constantinople's own council, carried his personal library of Greek texts to Rome, where it later formed part of the founding collection of the Marciana Library in Venice.

The Umayyad caliphate based in Cordoba had already fractured through a civil war known as the fitna, with rival claimants and Berber garrisons fighting through the city itself. In 1031 the Cordoban council abolished the office of caliph altogether rather than back another claimant, ending the line founded there in 929 by Abd al-Rahman III.

What followed was a patchwork of roughly thirty taifa kingdoms, ruled from cities such as Seville, Toledo and Granada, each paying tribute to Christian kingdoms further north to survive. That tribute, and the rivalry between the taifas, gave Castile and Aragon leverage that outlasted the caliphate itself.

In 1209 the mayor of Oxford hanged two or three clerks after a woman's accidental death, even though scholars were supposed to answer only to church courts. Oxford's chancellor suspended lectures in protest, and within days a group of masters and students, perhaps a few hundred, had packed their books and left for the market town of Cambridge on the River Cam.

They began teaching in borrowed rooms, churches and rented houses rather than any purpose built hall. It took over two decades for the arrangement to gain formal backing: in 1231 King Henry III issued a charter recognising the scholars at Cambridge and granting them specific legal privileges, the point at which the loose gathering became a chartered university.

Roman writers dated the city to 814 BCE and credited its founding to Elissa, a Tyrian princess fleeing her brother's court. No inscription from the settlement itself survives to confirm the year. The earliest archaeological layers excavated on the site, pottery and tophet burials, point instead to sometime in the eighth century BCE.

What is certain is the location: a peninsula jutting into the Gulf of Tunis, with two natural harbours and easy access to Sicily and Sardinia. Phoenician traders used it to reach tin and silver routes across the western Mediterranean. Within a few centuries it had outgrown Tyre itself and was fielding its own fleets and colonies.

Ingrid Bergman later said she played every scene without knowing which man her character loved, which gives her uncertainty on screen a genuine source.

Warner Bros. rushed the New York premiere to November 1942 to trade on the Allied landings in North Africa days earlier, then held the wider release until January 1943 to coincide with the Casablanca conference between Roosevelt and Churchill. Most of the cast, including Bergman, were European emigres.
