John Cassian had spent years among the hermits of Egypt before settling at Marseille around 415, where he founded a convent for women and the abbey of Saint Victor for men, one of the earliest such foundations in the western Mediterranean. He wrote from that experience rather than from theory, aiming to translate the practice of the Egyptian desert into a form communities in Gaul could actually sustain.

His two books, the Institutes and the Conferences, cover everything from a monk's daily clothing and work to conversations attributed to individual desert fathers on prayer and temptation. Benedict of Nursia later drew directly on the Institutes when writing his own monastic rule, and recommended the Conferences be read aloud to his monks.

Joseph Heller drew on his own missions as a bombardier over Italy, though he flew far fewer than the seventy missions his fictional airman Yossarian faces as the required number keeps rising. Simon and Schuster published the novel on 10 October 1961 after Heller spent roughly eight years writing it in the evenings while working an advertising job.

The title had originally been Catch-18, changed late because Leon Uris's novel Mila 18 was appearing that same season and the publisher wanted no confusion. The book's circular rule, that a flier judged insane to keep flying missions cannot be grounded because asking to be grounded proves he is sane, gave English the phrase catch-22.

Cathars in Languedoc held that the material world was the creation of an evil power, not the Christian God, and that the spirit alone could be saved. Their leaders, called bons hommes and bonnes femmes, lived austerely, rejected the sacraments of the Catholic church, and won backing from local nobles who valued the movement's independence from Rome as much as its theology.

Church councils condemned the belief through the twelfth century without suppressing it, and in 1209 Pope Innocent the third launched the Albigensian Crusade, a campaign of northern French armies against the towns that sheltered Cathars. Decades of siege and burning, including the mass killing at Beziers, broke the movement's open practice in the region by the mid thirteenth century.

Cathedral schools existed to train clergy in reading, chant and Latin grammar under the bishop's authority, attached to the cathedral itself rather than to any town government. In Paris, the school at Notre Dame drew masters teaching logic and theology to students from well beyond the diocese, more than the cathedral's own clerical needs required.

Independent teachers without a formal cathedral post began lecturing nearby anyway, competing with the bishop's licensed masters for students willing to pay for instruction directly. That informal, overlapping teaching around Notre Dame is what the University of Paris grew out of within a few decades, once masters organised themselves into a guild with its own seal and statutes.

A hand stencil in the cave of El Castillo in northern Spain was dated by measuring the decay of uranium in the thin mineral crust that grew over it. The result, at least 40,800 years old, made it among the oldest confirmed painted marks anywhere, predating the Lascaux images by roughly 25,000 years.

The pigment is red ochre, blown or spat around a hand pressed to the rock. No brushes, no scaffolding, no single artist can be named. Similar stencils and dots appear across a dozen caves in the region, work by people who left nothing else of themselves behind but the shape of a hand.

Cervantes was in his mid-fifties when the book appeared in Madrid in 1605, after a life that included fighting at the naval battle of Lepanto, where he lost the use of his left hand, and five years enslaved in Algiers after Barbary pirates captured his ship home. None of that fortune shows in the book's success, which he did not live to see fully rewarded.

The story sends an ageing minor nobleman out to revive chivalry, tilting at windmills he mistakes for giants alongside his practical squire, Sancho Panza. A rival author published an unauthorised sequel in 1614, prompting Cervantes to rush out his own continuation in 1615, a year before he died.

Champa was never one kingdom but a string of Cham principalities along the coast of what is now central and southern Vietnam, each built around a river mouth port that traded with India, China and the wider Indian Ocean. Their kings took Sanskrit titles and dated inscriptions using the Saka calendar, borrowed through centuries of trade contact with Indian merchants rather than conquest.

Their brick temple towers, called kalan, cluster at My Son in a valley the Cham treated as a royal sanctuary, each tower raised for a king to honour Shiva under a local name. My Son's towers were badly damaged by American bombing during the Vietnam War, and only a fraction of the original complex still stands.

OpenAI put the tool online on 30 November 2022 as a free research preview, built on a version of its GPT-3.5 model and refined with human feedback on which answers read better. There was no launch event; the company expected modest interest and had not built for scale.

It reached an estimated one million users within five days and roughly 100 million monthly users by January 2023, faster than any consumer application before it. Schools banned it within weeks over essay writing, Microsoft added a version of it to Bing that spring, and rival labs accelerated their own chatbot releases in response.

Chaucer set his frame story on the road from London to the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury, a route packed with real pilgrims, and gave his fictional travellers a storytelling contest with a free dinner at stake, judged by their host at the Tabard Inn. He wrote it in Middle English rather than the French or Latin still common among educated writers, drawing on his own work as a customs official and diplomat for details of trade and law.

He planned over a hundred tales, one for most pilgrims on the way there and back, but died in 1400 with only twenty four written and the return journey never told. The Wife of Bath's and the Miller's tales, both bawdy, sit beside pious ones like the Knight's, giving a cross-section of voices rare for the period.

Chavin de Huantar, a temple complex high in the Peruvian Andes, drew pilgrims from both the coast and the eastern jungle between roughly 900 and 200 BCE, long before the Inca. Its builders cut stone galleries and drainage tunnels inside the temple mound, channelling river water to create sounds and effects for visitors moving through the dark passages.

Carved stone monuments there, including the Lanzon, a dagger shaped monolith standing inside the temple's core, show fanged deities blending human, feline and serpent features. Motifs from Chavin, particularly its jaguar and snake imagery, appear on pottery and textiles found hundreds of kilometres away, evidence that the site's religious ideas travelled along trade routes across the central Andes.

Fan Kuan's Travelers Among Mountains and Streams, painted around 1000 on a silk hanging scroll over two metres tall, places a sheer cliff filling two thirds of the picture above a tiny mule train on a path below. The scale is deliberate: a human traveller is barely visible, dwarfed by rock formed over ages that no single dynasty could claim to control.

Guo Xi's Early Spring, dated 1072 by an inscription in his own hand, uses mist and twisting pine branches to suggest a mountain still settling after winter, painted for the Song court decades after Fan Kuan's death. Together with Li Tang's later work, these three hanging scrolls are treated in Taiwan's National Palace Museum as the defining monuments of Northern Song landscape painting.

Cacao arrived in Spain from the Americas in the early sixteenth century, carried back among the goods of conquistadors who had encountered it prepared as a bitter, spiced drink in Mesoamerica. Spanish households altered the recipe, stripping out the chilli the Aztecs used and adding sugar, vanilla and cinnamon to suit European taste.

For decades Spain kept the recipe close, and chocolate stayed a costly drink for court and clergy rather than a food anyone ate. It spread slowly outward through royal marriages and monastic contacts, reaching France and Italy over the following century, well before it was ever moulded into a solid bar.

Rajaraja Chola and his son Rajendra built up a Tamil fleet capable of open-water operations, unusual for a South Asian state whose wars were normally fought on land. Under Rajendra it sailed against Srivijaya, the maritime power controlling the Strait of Malacca, in 1025.

The Cholas sacked the Srivijayan port of Kadaram in modern Kedah, seized its ceremonial gateway of jewelled war gates as plunder, and captured its king, Sangrama Vijayottunggavarman. It is the only large scale, long-distance naval campaign launched from South Asia recorded before the colonial era, undertaken to force open trade routes to China that Srivijaya had been taxing heavily.

The Primary Chronicle, written well over a century later, says Vladimir sent envoys to compare Islam, Judaism, Latin and Orthodox Christianity before choosing Constantinople's faith, partly to secure marriage to the Byzantine emperor's sister Anna. He was baptised, by most accounts at Chersonesus in Crimea, then returned to Kiev and had the wooden idol of Perun dragged through the streets and thrown into the Dnieper.

Mass baptisms followed at the river for the city's population, an event later Russian painters turned into a single orderly ceremony rather than the uneven, years-long process historians think it actually was outside the capital. The choice tied the Rus principalities to Byzantine liturgy, script and church law rather than Rome's, a split that widened over the following centuries.

Dickens wrote the story in about six weeks that autumn, partly to cover debts and partly after visiting a ragged school for poor children in London. He paid for the first printing himself, choosing a red cloth binding, gilt edges and hand-coloured illustrations by John Leech, which ate most of the profit from the initial run of six thousand copies.

It sold out within days of its release on 19 December 1843 and went through further printings before the new year. Weak international copyright law meant pirated American editions appeared almost immediately, and Dickens took one pirate publisher to court, winning a judgment he never managed to collect.

Marlowe was a shoemaker's son from Canterbury who studied at Cambridge on a scholarship meant for future clergymen, then went to London and wrote for the stage instead. Tamburlaine, staged around 1587, gave English drama a hero speaking in unrhymed iambic pentameter with a fluency the public stage had not heard before.

Doctor Faustus followed, built around a scholar who trades his soul to Mephistophilis for twenty-four years of forbidden knowledge. Marlowe was killed in a Deptford lodging house in 1593, stabbed above the eye during a dispute over a bill, at twenty-nine, after years also under suspicion as a government informer.

Out of office since his election defeat the year before, Churchill delivered the speech, titled The Sinews of Peace, at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946. President Truman had arranged the invitation and introduced him, then sat on the platform through a forty-six-minute address to an audience of about fifteen hundred.

Churchill said an iron curtain had descended from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic, listing the capitals of Central and Eastern Europe he judged now cut off from the West. Stalin denounced the speech within days as a call to war; both American and British opinion at the time was divided over whether Churchill had spoken too soon.

Bernard arrived at the young abbey of Citeaux as a sickly novice in 1113 and within two years was sent out to found his own house in a clearing called the Valley of Wormwood, renamed Clairvaux. He rebuilt its reputation for austerity, sleeping little, eating less, and writing letters that made Clairvaux the model other Cistercian houses copied.

Cistercian monks worked their own fields rather than relying on tenants, kept their churches undecorated, plain stone with no coloured glass or carving, and settled in remote valleys rather than towns. By the time Bernard died in 1153 Clairvaux alone had founded around sixty eight daughter houses, part of an order that had grown past three hundred abbeys across Europe.

RKO gave a 25 year old radio actor final cut on his first film, a deal no other studio would offer. William Randolph Hearst recognised the thinly veiled portrait of himself and tried to buy every print to destroy it, then had his newspapers refuse to mention the film or its studio.

The picture cost about 800,000 dollars, modest for RKO, and lost money on its first run because many theatre chains, wary of Hearst, would not book it. Its deep focus photography and overlapping narrators, told through five conflicting witnesses, unsettled reviewers more than audiences, who mostly stayed away.

The National Assembly reorganised French dioceses to match the new administrative departments, made bishops and priests salaried state employees, and had them elected by local citizens rather than appointed by Rome. Clergy were then required to swear a public oath of loyalty to the new constitution.

Roughly half of French priests refused the oath, and Pope Pius VI condemned the whole arrangement the following year, splitting French Catholics into oath taking and refusing clergy. The refusing priests, driven underground or into exile, became a lasting source of resistance to the Revolution in the countryside.

William the Pious, Duke of Aquitaine, signed the founding charter on 11 September 910, handing over a hunting estate in Burgundy along the Grosne river and naming Berno, already abbot of two other houses, as Cluny's first head. The unusual clause in that charter placed the new monastery under the pope alone, free of any bishop or lay lord, including William's own heirs.

That independence let a chain of Cluniac priories spread across France, Spain, England and Italy over the following two centuries, all following customs set at the mother house rather than a local bishop's rule. The abbey church built there in the twelfth century was, until Saint Peter's in Rome was completed, the largest in Christendom; revolutionary demolition after 1791 left only a single transept tower standing.

The text is attributed to Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, or to his son Shulgi, and survives only through later Old Babylonian copies. A damaged pair of tablets found at Nippur was translated by the Sumerologist Samuel Kramer in 1952, and better-preserved copies recovered later let scholars reconstruct about forty of an original fifty-seven laws.

The code fixes compensation in silver for specific injuries rather than the mutual retaliation of later Babylonian law: a broken bone or a severed nose has a set price. It predates the Code of Hammurabi by roughly three centuries and shows a legal system already keeping written, numbered rulings rather than relying on custom alone.

Two traders from Syria opened houses selling the drink to the public in the Ottoman capital in the 1550s, offering benches, board games and readings aloud from poetry and news alongside the coffee itself. Customers paid a small entry fee and could sit for hours, which unsettled some officials who worried about idle talk and unlicensed gathering.

Religious authorities briefly argued over whether coffee itself counted as an intoxicant banned to Muslims, and sultans periodically closed houses they suspected of harbouring plots or gossip against the government, only for them to reopen. Coffeehouses spread from Constantinople along Ottoman trade routes to Cairo, then to European ports, reaching London within a century.

Coffee reached Cairo from Yemen by the sixteenth century, and the qahwa khana, the coffeehouse, became a fixture of the city under Ottoman rule, open to men of different ranks who could not otherwise sit together. Patrons played chess and backgammon, listened to hired storytellers recite epics in instalments, and heard news carried by travelling merchants.

Religious and civic authorities periodically shut the coffeehouses down, worried less about the drink itself than about what unsupervised gathering and talk might lead to, including gossip against the government. Each closure proved temporary, and the houses reopened once the immediate alarm passed.

Columba left Ireland after a dispute over a copied manuscript escalated into a battle, and tradition holds his penance was to convert as many souls abroad as had died in it. He landed on Iona, a small island off Scotland's west coast, with twelve companions and built a monastery of wood and wattle rather than stone.

From Iona, monks carried Christian teaching to the Picts of the Scottish mainland and later to Northumbria, and the community became a training ground for missionaries and a stop for pilgrims and kings. Columba died on Iona in 597; his biographer Adomnan, writing roughly a century later, is the main source for his life, since no contemporary account survives.

Travelling troupes in northern Italy worked from a scenario, a one-page plot outline pinned backstage, rather than a written script, and improvised the dialogue in performance. Actors specialised in one fixed character for a career: Arlecchino the hungry servant in patched costume, Pantalone the miserly old merchant, and masked lovers who never wore masks themselves.

The earliest individual actor's name to survive in a document is Lucrezia Di Siena, on a contract dated 10 October 1564. Companies carried their few props and costumes between town squares and noble courts, and by the later sixteenth century Italian troupes were touring as far as Paris, where their masked improvisation influenced French and English stage comedy for generations.

The Communist League, a small group of German exiles based partly in London, commissioned Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels to write a statement of aims for the organisation, and the pamphlet appeared in London in German in February 1848, just weeks before revolutions broke out across much of continental Europe. Neither author's name was printed on the original edition.

It opens by declaring that a spectre is haunting Europe, and closes urging working men of all countries to unite, framing history as a sequence of struggles between opposing classes. Marx had already been expelled from Germany and France for his writing before the Manifesto, and Belgium expelled him within days of the revolutions reaching Brussels that spring.

Thirteen delegates met in a girls' school building in Shanghai's French Concession starting 23 July 1921, representing a movement of only about fifty members nationwide. Two Comintern agents, a Dutchman using the name Maring and a Russian known as Nikolsky, attended to advise on organisation and funding.

Police attention forced the congress to relocate partway through, and its final sessions were held aboard a rented boat on South Lake near Jiaxing on 2 August. Mao Zedong, then a Hunan schoolteacher and library assistant, was one of the delegates and took minutes; he did not lead the party for another two decades.

The order came not from an emperor with power over all China but from Feng Dao, a court official of the Later Tang, one of several short lived states fighting over the north after the Tang collapse. He set scribes and carvers to reproducing the Confucian classics from woodblocks rather than by hand copying, a project meant to fix one authoritative text rather than spread cheap copies.

The carving and proofreading ran for roughly twenty one years, into the 950s, under successive dynasties, and produced 130 volumes of the classics with their commentaries. The government controlled every stage, since the point was an approved text scholars across the fractured north could cite without dispute, not a wider reading public.

Confucius spent much of his life a minor official in the state of Lu, and only turned to teaching in earnest after failing to win a ruler willing to adopt his ideas about government by moral example rather than harsh law. He accepted students regardless of birth in exchange for a modest bundle of dried meat.

He wrote no book himself. What survives as his teaching is the Analects, sayings and short exchanges with students, assembled by his followers after his death in 479 BCE. Those students carried his ideas into rival courts, and the tradition eventually became the basis for the imperial civil service examinations.

Before the battle at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome in October 312, Constantine is said to have ordered his soldiers to paint a Christian symbol on their shields. He defeated his rival Maxentius, who drowned in the Tiber during the retreat, and Constantine credited the victory to the Christian god rather than to the pagan cults his predecessors had favoured.

He did not make Christianity the state religion, that step came from Theodosius decades later, but he ended official persecution, funded churches including St Peter's in Rome, and was baptised only on his deathbed in 337. He kept the title of pontifex maximus, head of the old Roman priesthood, throughout his reign.

Constantine VII spent much of his reign as a junior or sidelined co-emperor before ruling in his own right from 945, and he used the years of enforced study to become a scholar rather than a soldier. His Book of Ceremonies runs to more than 150 chapters detailing exactly how the imperial court staged processions, festivals and audiences with foreign envoys, down to the order of march and the colour of robes.

He commissioned a companion volume, later called De Administrando Imperio, advising his son on the empire's neighbours, and oversaw agricultural and military handbooks compiling older Greek and Roman knowledge. None of these works read as original composition; they gathered and preserved earlier material at a court that valued precedent over innovation.

Waxaklajuun Ubaah Kawiil, known to modern archaeologists as 18 Rabbit, ruled Copan from 695. Between 711 and 736 he raised a series of stelae in the city's Great Plaza, among them Stela A, dated by its own glyphs to 731, each carved with his portrait in the round, full body rather than the flatter relief of earlier rulers.

His reign shifted Copan's carving from angular Early Classic forms toward deeper, rounder sculpture in the round. It ended badly: in 738 the ruler of the smaller city Quirigua, once a subordinate lord, captured and executed him, a reversal recorded in Quirigua's own inscriptions rather than Copan's.

Corneille's tragedy, staged in Paris in the winter of 1636 and 1637, dramatised the Castilian knight known as El Cid, forcing its heroine Chimene to choose between loving Rodrigue and pursuing him for killing her father in a duel over honour. Audiences responded strongly, but rival playwrights attacked the play for breaking rules drawn from classical drama.

Cardinal Richelieu asked the newly founded Academie francaise to judge the dispute, and its verdict criticised the play's construction while conceding its popular success. The argument, remembered as the Querelle du Cid, pushed French theatre toward tighter observance of the unities of time, place and action for decades afterward.

Roughly 500 bishops, almost all from the eastern half of the empire, gathered at Chalcedon in 451 on the orders of Emperor Marcian, after an earlier council at Ephesus had been denounced as a rigged proceeding pushed through by intimidation. The Pope in Rome, Leo I, sent legates rather than attending in person.

The bishops ruled that Christ had two complete natures, divine and human, united in one person without either being changed or blended. Churches in Egypt, Syria and Armenia rejected that formula and broke away rather than accept it, a split between Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian Christianity that has never fully healed.

Bishops meeting at Antioch in 341, for the dedication of a new cathedral there, issued a set of creeds intended to restate Christian doctrine on Christ's nature without using the exact wording of Nicaea. None of the bishops present openly called themselves Arian, but the council's avoidance of Nicaea's term homoousios, of one substance, let opponents of that formula gather under cover of dedicating a church.

The council also passed canons on church discipline, including rules against a bishop appealing directly to the emperor over his own synod's ruling. Historians reading the surviving creeds disagree on how far the bishops at Antioch actually favoured Arius's teaching, since the texts read as a deliberate compromise rather than a clear statement either way.

Three men claimed to be pope when the council opened at Constance in November 1414: a Roman, an Avignon claimant and a Pisan one backed by the emperor. Delegates voted by nation rather than by head count, a rule meant to stop the Italian bishops simply outnumbering everyone else. It took until 1417 to strip all three of their claims.

The council had also promised the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus safe passage to defend his teaching. It tried him instead, and burned him at the stake on 6 July 1415 for refusing to recant. Martin V was elected pope the following year, ending the Western Schism, and Hus's execution helped set off the Hussite wars in Bohemia.

Paul and Barnabas travelled to Jerusalem around 49 to settle a dispute that had split the young church: whether a Gentile convert had to be circumcised and keep the Jewish food laws before being baptised. The account in Acts has Peter and James siding against the requirement, after Paul and Barnabas argued that their converts in Antioch were already receiving the same spirit without it.

The ruling asked Gentile Christians to avoid food offered to idols, meat from strangled animals, and sexual immorality, but dropped circumcision as a condition. It is the first recorded instance of the church settling a doctrinal argument by meeting and voting rather than by a single leader's decree, and it kept the new movement from splitting along ethnic lines at the outset.

Pope Paul III convened the council in the northern Italian city of Trent in December 1545, after years of delay caused by war between the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and France. Bishops met there on and off for eighteen years, in three separate periods broken up by plague, politics and two more popes, and did not finish until 1563.

The bishops restated Catholic doctrine on the sacraments and scripture against Luther's positions, ordered every diocese to open a seminary for training priests, and standardised the Latin Mass. The decrees were printed and circulated across Catholic Europe, and the reforms they set in motion shaped Catholic worship into the twentieth century.

Italian court weddings and state visits in the fifteenth century were marked with elaborate danced entertainments called balli, staged between courses of a banquet and combining dance, verse and costumed allegory. A wedding at Tortona in 1489, organised for the marriage of Isabella of Aragon and Gian Galeazzo Sforza, is often pointed to for its danced courses matched to each dish served.

These entertainments travelled to France when Catherine de Medici brought Italian dancing masters to the French court in the mid sixteenth century, feeding directly into the ballet de cour staged there. The formal steps, turned out legs and codified positions later associated with ballet developed gradually out of this social dancing over the following two centuries, not from any single invented form.

Cyprian was a trained rhetorician before his conversion, and was elected bishop of Carthage in 249, only a few years into his Christian life. The Decian persecution broke out almost immediately afterward, and Cyprian went into hiding outside the city, governing his congregation through letters while some members bought certificates proving they had sacrificed to Roman gods to avoid arrest.

When the persecution eased, Cyprian argued that those who had lapsed could be readmitted only after penance, and later that baptisms performed by breakaway or heretical clergy did not count at all and had to be repeated. A council he led in Carthage in 256 backed rebaptism, putting sixty-one bishops in direct conflict with Pope Stephen in Rome, who threatened excommunication over the dispute.

Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings opened the Cabaret Voltaire in a rented Zurich tavern room in February 1916, gathering exiled writers and artists who had fled conscription in a Europe at war. Ball performed sound poems in a cardboard costume that made him look like an obelisk and could barely move, chanting syllables that were not words in any language.

The word Dada itself is said to have been picked at random, possibly from a French dictionary, though the various founders gave conflicting accounts of who chose it and why. The group treated nonsense and deliberate bad taste as a rejection of the reasoned culture they blamed for the war, staging noisy readings and exhibiting torn-up posters and found objects rather than crafted art.

Louis Daguerre had been experimenting with his late partner Nicephore Niepce's light-sensitive processes for years when he found that mercury vapour could bring out a latent image on an iodine-coated silver plate in minutes rather than the hours Niepce had needed. The French government bought the rights and announced the process to the Academy of Sciences on 19 August 1839, releasing it for free public use.

Each daguerreotype was a unique image on metal, easily scratched and reversed left to right, usually cased in velvet and glass for protection. Studios opened within months across Europe and the United States, and a sitting that had cost a fortune in painted portraiture now cost a few dollars, though the sitter still had to hold still for up to a minute.

Damascus lent its name to damask, a weave in which the pattern is formed by the weft threads themselves catching light differently rather than by added embroidery or dye. Workshops in the city drew raw silk along overland routes from further east and combined it with local dyeing and finishing skills built up over centuries of trade.

The cloth travelled west through Mediterranean ports, and European buyers who could not pronounce or spell the city's name simply named the fabric after it, a label that stuck long after the weaving itself had spread to Italy and beyond. Surviving fragments in museum textile collections show the same repeating floral and geometric bands that made the pattern recognisable at a glance.

The Hamburg publisher Otto Meissner released the first volume of Das Kapital on 14 September 1867, in an edition of about a thousand copies. Marx had spent years in the British Museum's reading room compiling it from parliamentary factory reports and trade statistics, and he was still revising the French translation when he died in 1883.

He never finished the second and third volumes; Friedrich Engels assembled them from Marx's notebooks and published them in 1885 and 1894. Engels also translated the surviving correspondence between the two men into the source material later scholars used to reconstruct how the argument changed as Marx wrote it.

A Bedouin shepherd named Muhammed edh-Dhib, searching a cliffside near Qumran for a lost goat in 1947, threw a stone into a cave opening and heard it break pottery rather than land on rock. Inside were clay jars holding seven leather and papyrus scrolls, the first of what became the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Ten more caves, found between 1949 and 1956, yielded fragments of roughly 800 more manuscripts, copied by scribes over some three centuries. Among them is the oldest known complete copy of the Book of Isaiah, over a thousand years older than any Hebrew Bible text known before the find.

Miguel de Cervantes died in Madrid on 22 April 1616, having spent his later years poor despite the success of Don Quixote, whose first part had appeared in 1605 and second in 1615. He had earlier lost the use of his left hand at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571 and spent five years enslaved in Algiers after capture by corsairs.

Because Spain still used the Julian calendar while England had adopted the Gregorian, his death predates Shakespeare's by ten days despite both being recorded as 23 April by their respective calendars, a coincidence often mistaken for the same date on the same day.

Cleopatra died in Alexandria in August 30 BCE, days after Mark Antony's own suicide and weeks after Octavian's forces had taken the city. Roman writers settled on an asp smuggled in a basket of figs as the method, a detail already contested in antiquity: Plutarch lists it alongside a poisoned hairpin and a self administered ointment as rival accounts.

Her death removed the last independent ruler of Egypt and the last monarch descended from Alexander's general Ptolemy, who had taken the country three centuries earlier. Octavian annexed Egypt outright rather than leaving it a client kingdom, and its grain shipments became one of the pillars feeding Rome for the next several centuries.

Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar died in Valencia in July 1099, the city he had ruled since taking it from its Muslim governors five years earlier, holding it as an independent lord rather than for the Castilian crown that had once exiled him. He had fought for both Christian and Muslim rulers over his career, earning the title El Cid, likely from the Arabic al-sayyid, meaning the lord.

The Poema de Mio Cid, composed around a century later, turned his life into Castile's founding epic, adding scenes and speeches with little basis in the surviving charters and legal documents that record the real man. A later legend claims his corpse was strapped upright on his horse Babieca to frighten besieging Almoravid forces after his death, a story with no contemporary support.

Lenin had suffered a series of strokes from 1922 that left him largely unable to speak or write; he died at his estate in Gorki, outside Moscow, on 21 January 1924, at fifty-three. Against his own stated wishes, his body was embalmed and put on permanent display in a wooden mausoleum on Red Square, later rebuilt in granite.

In his final months he had dictated notes criticising several colleagues, including Stalin, and proposing he be removed as party general secretary. The Politburo suppressed the document, and Stalin used his control of the party apparatus over the following years to outmanoeuvre Trotsky and the other rivals for leadership.

Leonardo da Vinci died on 2 May 1519 at Clos Luce, a manor house near Amboise given to him by King Francis I of France, who had invited him there in 1516 with the title of First Painter, Engineer and Architect to the King. He was around sixty-seven and had brought the Mona Lisa with him rather than leaving it in Italy.

He left behind roughly 13,000 pages of notebooks covering anatomy, hydraulics, flight and fortification, most never published in his lifetime and scattered after his death among collectors. His assistant Francesco Melzi inherited the manuscripts and paintings, and it was centuries before scholars pieced together how much of his scientific work had gone unread.

Louis XIV died at Versailles on 1 September 1715, four days short of his seventy-seventh birthday, after gangrene spread from a leg injury that his doctors treated too late. He had become king in 1643 at four years old and only began ruling personally in 1661, after the death of his chief minister Cardinal Mazarin.

His seventy-two years on the throne remain the longest confirmed reign of any monarch of a sovereign European state. He outlived his son, his eldest grandson and his eldest great-grandson, so the crown passed to a five-year-old great-grandson, who became Louis XV under a regency.

Mao died in Beijing on 9 September 1976 at the age of 82, after years of declining health that included Parkinson's disease. State radio announced the death hours later, and factories, schools and offices across China halted for a week of mourning. His embalmed body was placed on public display in the Great Hall of the People before burial in a purpose built mausoleum on Tiananmen Square.

Within a month, his widow Jiang Qing and three allies, later named the Gang of Four, were arrested in a move led by Hua Guofeng and marshal Ye Jianying. That arrest ended the radical faction that had driven the Cultural Revolution, and within two years Deng Xiaoping had outmanoeuvred Hua to begin the market reforms that reopened China's economy.

Napoleon spent his last six years on Saint Helena, a British-held island in the South Atlantic more than 1,900 kilometres from any continent, chosen precisely because it was hard to escape. He lived at Longwood House with a shrinking retinue of followers, dictating memoirs and complaining about the damp climate and his British custodian, Governor Hudson Lowe.

He died there on 5 May 1821 at fifty-one. British doctors recorded stomach cancer; later tests on preserved hair samples raised, then largely undermined, a theory of arsenic poisoning. His body was moved to Paris in 1840 and placed in a tomb at the Invalides, where it remains.

Oliver Cromwell died on 3 September 1658 at Whitehall, probably of a urinary infection following a bout of malaria, on the anniversary of his victories at Dunbar and Worcester. He had ruled as Lord Protector since 1653 and named his son Richard as successor days before his death.

Richard lacked his father's support among the army and resigned within eight months, and the resulting political collapse led Parliament to invite Charles II back from exile in 1660. Cromwell's body was later exhumed on royal order, and his head was displayed on a pole outside Westminster Hall for decades.

Pericles had already lost his sister and two legitimate sons to the same epidemic that killed him. Thucydides, who caught the disease himself and survived, described its symptoms in detail: fever, thirst, blistered skin, a cough that would not settle. It arrived in Athens in 430 BCE, carried in by a population crammed behind the city walls to shelter from Spartan raids.

He died in 429 BCE, two years into the Peloponnesian War he had argued Athens should fight defensively, letting its navy and walls do the work rather than meeting Sparta's army in the field. His cousin Alcibiades and other successors abandoned that caution soon after his death. The war dragged on for another twenty five years and ended with Athens defeated.

William Shakespeare died on 23 April 1616 in Stratford-upon-Avon, where he had retired some years earlier after his London playing company, the King's Men, had made him a wealthy man. His will, signed weeks before his death, left his wife Anne Hathaway the notorious 'second best bed', a bequest scholars still debate the meaning of.

None of his manuscripts survive, and roughly half his plays existed only in performance until two former colleagues, John Heminges and Henry Condell, gathered them into the First Folio of 1623. Without that later printing, plays including Macbeth and The Tempest would likely have been lost.

Steve Jobs died at his home in Palo Alto on 5 October 2011, aged 56, eight years after being diagnosed with a rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour. He had resigned as Apple's chief executive only six weeks earlier, handing the role to Tim Cook while staying on as chairman, and had undergone a liver transplant in 2009 as the disease progressed.

Apple stores worldwide became informal shrines overnight, with mourners leaving flowers, apples and handwritten notes below darkened storefronts. The company held a private memorial on its campus and later released a biographical film and an authorised biography by Walter Isaacson, published weeks after his death, that Jobs had cooperated with while ill.

CT scans and DNA testing on Tutankhamun's mummy have pointed to a broken leg, malaria and the effects of his parents being siblings, rather than the murder once suspected from a mark on his skull. He left no surviving children; two mummified foetuses were buried in his tomb.

Because he died young and his tomb was small by royal standards, it was cut into rubble left by later burials and escaped the notice of the grave robbers who stripped nearly every other pharaoh's resting place. Howard Carter's workers cleared a stairway to its sealed door on 4 November 1922, and Carter first looked inside by candlelight on 26 November.

Democritus, working in the northern Greek city of Abdera, argued that everything is made of tiny, uncuttable pieces of matter, atomos, moving through empty space, and that differences between things come only from the shape, size and arrangement of these particles rather than any quality added to them. He built the idea on an earlier theory proposed by his teacher, Leucippus, whose own writings survive only as fragments quoted by later authors.

None of Democritus's own books survived complete; what remains is roughly three hundred quoted fragments preserved by writers such as Aristotle, who mostly cited him to argue against him. Aristotle rejected an empty void, so atomism lost the argument in its own lifetime and was not taken up seriously again until the physics of the early modern period.

Rene Descartes published Discourse on the Method anonymously at Leiden in 1637, writing in French rather than the Latin scholars used, so that readers outside the universities could follow his argument. He appended it to three scientific essays, on optics, meteors and geometry, presenting the philosophy as a preface to his method for the sciences.

The book sets out his resolve to doubt everything that could conceivably be false and rebuild knowledge from what survived that doubt, arriving at the certainty of his own thinking existence. He had settled in the Dutch Republic partly to write with less risk of censure than Catholic France allowed.

Luther arrived in Worms in April 1521 under a promise of safe conduct, the same kind of guarantee that had not saved Jan Hus a century earlier. He was shown a table stacked with his own pamphlets and asked a single question: would he retract them. He asked for a day to consider his answer.

His reply the next day is remembered as ending in the German phrase hier stehe ich, though the earliest printed transcript does not record those exact words. The emperor Charles V issued the Edict of Worms weeks later, declaring Luther an outlaw. He left the city under his safe conduct and went into hiding at Wartburg Castle.

The sound grew out of clubs serving Black, Latino and gay audiences in New York and Philadelphia in the early 1970s, where DJs such as David Mancuso and Nicky Siano strung records together on continuous mixes rather than playing single tracks. Philadelphia International Records, run by Kenneth Gamble and Leon Huff, supplied much of the lush, string-heavy production that defined the style before it reached the charts.

Donna Summer's I Feel Love and the Bee Gees' songs for Saturday Night Fever, both from 1977, carried the sound into mainstream radio and packed venues like Studio 54. The backlash arrived quickly: a 1979 promotional stunt at Chicago's Comiskey Park, where a crate of disco records was blown up between baseball games, drew a crowd that rioted onto the field.

The 17 July 1955 opening, broadcast live on ABC and hosted by Ronald Reagan, went wrong almost immediately. Counterfeit tickets let in far more people than the park could hold, asphalt laid that morning was still soft in the summer heat and trapped women's high heels, and a plumbers' strike had forced Walt Disney to choose between working toilets and working drinking fountains.

He chose the toilets, and on a hot day guests went thirsty, a decision the press seized on. Disney had spent about 17 million dollars building the park in Anaheim orange groves, financed partly by a deal giving ABC a stake in exchange for airing a weekly television show to promote it.

Dante wrote the poem in exile, banished from Florence in 1302 on trumped-up corruption charges after backing the losing side in a factional split, and threatened with burning if he returned. He wrote it in Tuscan Italian rather than Latin, and cast the Roman poet Virgil as his guide through Hell and Purgatory before handing the guide's role to Beatrice, a Florentine woman he had loved from a distance and who had died young.

He finished the final section, Paradiso, shortly before his death in Ravenna in 1321, having never returned to Florence. The poem's Tuscan dialect, spread by its popularity, became a major influence on standard modern Italian, and later commentators added the word Divine to its title.

Dogon farmers moved onto the Bandiagara escarpment in what is now central Mali over several centuries, most intensively from around the thirteenth century, settling into and above cliff dwellings that an earlier people, the Tellem, had already cut into the sandstone before them.

Villages were built directly against the rock face, with granaries set into ledges out of reach of raiders and floodwater. French anthropologist Marcel Griaule's fieldwork in the 1930s brought Dogon cosmology to outside attention, though his later claims about their astronomical knowledge of the star Sirius have been disputed by other researchers since.

Dolly was born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, made by taking a nucleus from a mammary cell of a six year old Finn Dorset ewe and inserting it into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed. Of 277 attempts by Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell's team, only this one produced a live lamb.

The birth stayed secret for seven months while a patent was filed, and the announcement in February 1997 startled governments already debating the limits of genetic science. Dolly lived a normal sheep's life at Roslin, bred six lambs of her own, and was put down in 2003 after a lung disease common in older sheep kept indoors.

No charter or founding document marks the start of teaching at Bologna. The 1088 date carved into the university's crest is a nineteenth century commemorative choice, picked for an anniversary celebration rather than drawn from a surviving record, and the earliest solid evidence of organised law teaching there dates closer to the 1090s.

What is documented is the subject: masters teaching Roman law from Justinian's Corpus Juris, drawing students from across Europe who organised themselves into guild like nations for protection in a foreign city. That student organised structure, students hiring and paying their teachers, set Bologna apart from Paris, where the teachers held the power.

No single grant or charter starts Oxford's story. Clerics were teaching there by the 1090s, drawn perhaps by a existing tradition of scholarship around its churches, and the town's position on a river crossing gave it easy access from London and the Midlands without the university being planned as an institution from the outset.

Growth accelerated later, in 1167, when Henry the second barred English students from studying at Paris, pushing many home to Oxford instead. Colleges as separate endowed institutions inside the university, Merton and Balliol among the first, only appeared from the 1260s, more than a century and a half after teaching had already begun there.

Masters teaching around Notre Dame's cathedral school had no legal existence as a body until they began organising themselves into a guild in the mid twelfth century, electing officers and setting rules for who could teach. Unlike Bologna, where students hired and paid their own masters, Paris put power in the hands of the teaching masters themselves.

Theology, taught nowhere else in Europe with Paris's standing, drew students from England, Germany and Italy into a single foreign community inside the city, organised into nations for mutual protection and support. A papal charter under Pope Innocent the third later in 1200 confirmed the masters' independent legal status, protecting them from the city's civil courts.

Nobody recorded when Donatello cast his bronze David or who paid for it first; the earliest mention of the statue only turns up in 1469, standing in the courtyard of the Medici palace in Florence. Scholars have proposed dates from the 1420s to the 1460s, with the 1440s now the most common guess, commissioned by Cosimo de' Medici for his own house rather than for a church or public square.

The figure stands nude but for boots and a shepherd's hat, one foot resting on the severed head of Goliath, a plume from Goliath's helmet trailing up the inside of his leg. It was the first freestanding bronze nude cast in Europe since antiquity, made to be walked around and viewed from every side rather than set into a niche or wall.

In 311 Caecilian was consecrated bishop of Carthage by a group that included Felix of Aptunga, who had handed scripture to imperial officials during Diocletian's persecution. A rival council of North African bishops declared the consecration void on those grounds and elected Majorinus in his place; when Majorinus died the see passed to Donatus, who gave the movement its name.

Both sides agreed on doctrine and disagreed only on who counted as a traditor, someone who had cooperated with the persecutors, and whether such a person's sacraments were valid at all. Rome and most of the wider church backed Caecilian, but Donatist congregations persisted across Roman North Africa for a century, outlasting several imperial attempts to suppress them by law.

Fyodor Dostoevsky serialised the novel in the journal Russky Vestnik across nearly two years, finishing the last instalment in November 1880. He had planned it as the first part of a longer work following its youngest brother, Alyosha, but died in January 1881, only months after completing it, leaving that sequel unwritten.

The plot turns on the murder of a father, Fyodor Karamazov, and the suspicion that falls on his eldest son Dmitri while another son, Ivan, argues fiercely against the idea of a just God in a world that allows children to suffer. Dostoevsky drew partly on a real murder case he had followed in the press while researching the courtroom scenes.

Athens had relied on unwritten custom, enforced unevenly by aristocratic judges, until it appointed Draco to set its laws down around 621 BC. Having them in writing meant a defendant could at least know in advance what he was accused of breaking, a real change from judgement handed out case by case.

The code was remembered afterward for its severity: later writers claimed even minor theft or idleness could carry the death penalty, and the word draconian entered English from his name alone. Only fragments of the actual text survive, mostly concerning homicide, and Solon replaced most of the rest with milder statutes within a few decades.

Siena had commissioned the altarpiece from Duccio in 1308, and when it was finished the city treated its arrival at the cathedral as a civic event. On 9 June 1311 the bishop led clergy and officials in a procession that carried the panel from Duccio's workshop outside the walls, through the main piazza, past the town hall and up to the high altar, accompanied by musicians and lit candles.

The front shows the Virgin enthroned among saints and angels, watched over by Siena's own patron saints kneeling at her feet. The back carries scenes from Christ's life and a predella beneath the main panel adds seven episodes from his childhood. Later cutting of the frame for sale scattered several of those panels to museums outside Siena, so the altarpiece as installed in 1311 no longer survives whole.

The caves at Dunhuang were cut into a cliff face where routes converging from Central Asia entered China proper, and merchants paid for shrines there in thanks for a safe crossing or in hope of one. By the mid sixth century the site held hundreds of grottoes, each painted floor to ceiling with Buddhas, donor portraits and scenes from scripture, then sealed behind carved wooden facades bolted to the rock.

A walled side chamber, opened only in 1900, held tens of thousands of manuscripts and paintings sealed away around the eleventh century, untouched for roughly nine hundred years. Among them was a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra dated 868, among the oldest complete printed books known to survive, alongside contracts, letters and paintings that never left Dunhuang before that hidden library was found.

Duns Scotus, a Franciscan friar who taught at Oxford, Paris and Cologne around 1300, argued that the word being applies to God and to created things in exactly the same sense, not merely by analogy as earlier theologians such as Aquinas had held. For Scotus, this univocity was needed for any human reasoning about God to get a foothold at all.

He also proposed that what makes one horse or one person a distinct individual, rather than just an instance of the species horse or person, is a further principle he called haecceitas, roughly this-ness, added to the shared nature. Scotus left much of his major work as lecture notes rather than a finished treatise, and later scholars have argued over which surviving manuscripts record his own final positions.

The Book of Durrow is a small gospel book, roughly the size of a hand, made around 650 to 700 in an Irish or Northumbrian scriptorium and later kept at the monastery of Durrow in County Offaly. Its full page carpet designs mix Celtic spiral and interlace patterns with animal ornament closer to Anglo-Saxon metalwork, evidence that scribes on both sides of the Irish Sea were borrowing from each other.

A colophon added later claims the book was written by Columba himself, though its style points to a date roughly a century after his death, so the claim was likely added to raise the manuscript's standing rather than record its real authorship. It survived at Durrow into the 1660s before passing to Trinity College Dublin, where it remains, predating the more elaborate Book of Kells by over a century.

The Beeldenstorm began at Steenvoorde on 10 August 1566, when a crowd left a field sermon by the preacher Sebastian Matte and broke into a nearby monastery to smash its statues and paintings. Within weeks the destruction had spread through Flanders, Brabant and Holland, hitting hundreds of churches whose images Calvinist iconoclasts treated as idolatry.

Regent Margaret of Parma initially negotiated concessions with nobles who had petitioned against religious persecution, but Philip II sent the Duke of Alva and an army the following year to punish both the rioters and the nobles seen as too lenient. The crackdown that followed helped push the Low Countries toward the revolt against Spanish rule.

Antonin Dvořák wrote the symphony while running the National Conservatory in New York, a post he took partly because it admitted women and Black students at a time most conservatories did not. He drew on spirituals he had heard from his student Harry Burleigh and on his own reading about Native American music, without quoting either directly.

The Philharmonic Society premiered it at Carnegie Hall on 16 December 1893, and the audience applauded between movements, unusual enough that newspapers reported it. Dvořák insisted the symphony was Czech in spirit rather than American, but its themes, especially the largo, were borrowed almost immediately into American hymn and folk arrangements.

On 25 July 1965, Dylan walked onto the Newport Folk Festival stage with a Fender Stratocaster and a pickup band including members of the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, having spent the afternoon rehearsing in a rented cottage rather than with the festival's usual acoustic performers. He opened with Maggie's Farm, a song about refusing to keep working for someone else's rules.

Accounts differ on why parts of the crowd booed, some blamed the electric sound as a betrayal of folk tradition, others said the sound mix was simply bad and too loud for the field. Dylan played only three songs before leaving the stage, returned alone with an acoustic guitar at the urging of festival organiser Peter Yarrow, and closed with It's All Over Now, Baby Blue.

Egyptian sculptors under Ramesses II carved four seated colossi, each about 20 metres tall, into the sandstone cliff face at Abu Simbel to front a temple cut deep into the rock rather than built up from a foundation. Twice a year sunlight still reaches down the temple's axis to light statues in the innermost sanctuary, an alignment the builders calculated without instruments beyond sight lines and patience.

Further north at Amarna, the sculptor Thutmose kept a painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti in his workshop, likely as a model for apprentices rather than a finished commission; it was found there in 1912 by a German expedition led by Ludwig Borchardt. Both survive because they were buried or abandoned rather than deliberately preserved, the sand and rubble that hid them also protecting their paint and stone.

Tomb walls in the Valley of the Kings were plastered, then painted with mineral pigments bound in gum: ochre for red and yellow, malachite for green, ground azurite for blue. Painters worked from grid lines snapped in red onto the wall, so a figure's proportions could be copied from a master pattern rather than drawn freehand each time.

The scenes followed set formulas rather than a painter's own choices: the deceased before Osiris, the weighing of the heart, boatmen fishing on a canal. Because the tombs were sealed after burial, many paintings kept their original colour for three thousand years, hidden from sunlight until archaeologists reopened the chambers.

Domenikos Theotokopoulos, a painter trained in Crete and then Venice and Rome, is first recorded in Spain in 1577, when a document names him in connection with a commission for the high altar of the church of Santo Domingo el Antiguo in Toledo. He may have hoped for work decorating El Escorial for Philip II, but that royal patronage never materialised.

He settled in Toledo instead and stayed until his death in 1614, becoming known there as El Greco. Commissions from the cathedral chapter and local monasteries, rather than the crown, supported the elongated figures and unusual colour that mark paintings such as The Disrobing of Christ and later View of Toledo.

Ed Sullivan had publicly said he would never book Presley after seeing complaints about his stage moves, then paid 50,000 dollars for three appearances once a rival host's broadcast of him drew huge ratings. Sullivan himself was recovering from a car accident and did not host the first of the three shows, on 9 September 1956; actor Charles Laughton introduced Presley instead.

Cameras on the third appearance, on 6 January 1957, are best remembered for showing Presley only from the waist up, though he had already been shown full length during the two earlier broadcasts, which undercuts the usual censorship story. His first appearance, in September 1956, drew more than 60 million viewers, a majority of the American television audience that night.

Elvis Presley, a nineteen year old truck driver, was fooling around between takes at Sun Studio in Memphis in July 1954 when he sped up Arthur Crudup's blues song That's All Right, and producer Sam Phillips ran back into the room asking what they had just played. Guitarist Scotty Moore and bassist Bill Black had no idea they were making a record until Phillips said to do it again from the top.

Phillips pressed it as a single with a bluegrass number, Blue Moon of Kentucky, sped up on the other side, blending styles that radio stations usually kept apart. Memphis disc jockey Dewey Phillips played it repeatedly on WHBQ the night he got the acetate, and callers jammed the station asking who the singer was.

Diderot took over what had begun as a French translation of an English reference work and turned it into something far larger, recruiting Jean d'Alembert to handle the science and mathematics articles. The finished set ran to 17 volumes of text and 11 of plates, with contributors that eventually included Voltaire and Rousseau.

French censors suspended its printing licence twice over articles judged hostile to the church and crown, and the publisher secretly softened some entries without telling Diderot. Subscribers who had paid in advance kept receiving instalments anyway, smuggled or printed under cover of a foreign address.

Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in November 1534, naming Henry VIII head of the Church of England after Pope Clement VII refused to dissolve his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, who had not given him a surviving son. Thomas Cromwell drafted much of the legislation that followed, and Thomas More, who would not swear to it, was executed within a year.

The break did not immediately change church doctrine or the mass; it transferred authority and, from 1536, wealth, as Cromwell's commissioners began dissolving England's monasteries and selling their land to the crown's supporters. Henry married Anne Boleyn the same year the Act passed, and beheaded her within three.

Historians commonly mark the Enlightenment's start near 1687, when Isaac Newton published Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, laying out laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form. The book gave European thinkers a working example of what reasoned method could achieve, and writers across the continent began applying that same confidence to government, law and religion rather than only to physics.

Over the following decades, figures such as Locke, Voltaire and Diderot argued that political authority needed justification by reason rather than by inherited right or scripture. Salons, coffee houses and printed pamphlets carried these arguments beyond universities, and the questioning of monarchy and church authority that followed shaped the American and French revolutions later in the eighteenth century.

The story of the Sumerian king Gilgamesh circulated for centuries as separate poems before a Babylonian scribe, traditionally named Sin-leqi-unninni, wove them into one continuous narrative on twelve clay tablets. Copies were kept in the library at Nineveh, where fragments were unearthed by archaeologists in the nineteenth century.

Its flood story, in which a man builds a boat to survive a god-sent deluge, closely matches the later biblical account of Noah. George Smith read the flood tablet aloud to the Society of Biblical Archaeology in London in 1872, reportedly becoming so excited he began undressing at the lectern.

A scholar named Sin-leqi-unninni is credited with editing the twelve-tablet Standard Babylonian version from older Sumerian and Akkadian poems about the king of Uruk, in the centuries after 1200 BCE. About two thirds of that edition survives, largely from copies kept in the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.

Its eleventh tablet contains a flood story close to the biblical account of Noah, with a boat, a bird sent out to test for dry land, and a mountain landing. British Museum scholar George Smith identified the parallel in 1872 while translating tablets that had been excavated at Nineveh decades earlier.

Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof, an ophthalmologist in Warsaw, grew up hearing Polish, Russian, Yiddish and German argued over in the same streets and blamed language division for much of the hostility between them. In 1887 he published Lingvo Internacia under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, meaning one who hopes, and the name attached itself to the language rather than to him.

The grammar fits on a few printed pages, with sixteen rules and no irregular verbs, built from roots drawn mainly from Latin and Germanic languages. Zamenhof funded the first pamphlet partly with his wife's dowry. Esperanto speakers held their first world congress in France in 1905, and the language is still used today with no country and no native population.

Emperor Fasilides moved his court to the shores of Lake Tana in 1636, ending a long tradition of shifting royal camps and giving Ethiopia a fixed capital at Gondar for the first time in centuries. He built a stone castle there, the core of what became the Fasil Ghebbi complex, and founded several of the city's earliest churches during his reign.

Successor emperors added more palaces within the same walled compound, and later rulers founded churches decorated with murals in a distinctive Ethiopian style. Gondar remained Ethiopia's capital for roughly two centuries after Fasilides, until civil wars in the mid nineteenth century fractured the empire into rival regional powers and the court moved elsewhere.

Medea was staged at the City Dionysia in 431 BC against two other tragedians, and it lost. Euphorion, son of Aeschylus, won first prize that year and Sophocles took second, leaving Euripides in last place with a play in which a wronged wife kills her own children to punish the husband who abandoned her.

Athenian audiences already knew the story of Jason and the Golden Fleece, so the shock was not the plot but where Euripides put the camera: on Medea's reasoning, weighed out in a monologue before she acts rather than reported afterwards by a messenger. The play was revived and reread for centuries after its poor showing at the festival that first judged it.

The Book of Exodus describes ten plagues sent against Pharaoh, a sea parted for the fleeing Israelites and forty years of wandering before reaching Canaan. No Egyptian record mentions any of it, and archaeologists have found no trace in the Sinai of a migration on the scale the text describes.

The story nonetheless became the reference point for later liberation movements: it structures the Jewish festival of Passover, and it was quoted directly by abolitionists and by leaders of the American civil rights movement as an account of bondage ending in deliverance, regardless of what happened on the ground in the Bronze Age.

Edward I issued the Edict of Expulsion on 18 July 1290, a date that fell on the Jewish fast of Tisha B'Av, and ordered the roughly 3,000 Jews of England to leave before All Saints' Day, 1 November. Those who lent money at interest, a trade the crown had both taxed heavily and restricted them to, lost that livelihood along with their homes.

No formal readmission followed for over three and a half centuries. Jewish settlement in England was not permitted again until the 1650s, under Oliver Cromwell, when a small community was allowed to resettle without a new royal edict reversing the old one.

Ferdinand and Isabella signed the Alhambra Decree on 31 March 1492, giving Spain's Jews until the end of July to convert to Catholicism or leave the kingdom, taking no gold, silver or coined money with them. The decree came months after the fall of Granada ended Muslim rule in Iberia, and the crown framed the expulsion as completing that religious unification.

Estimates of how many left rather than converted vary widely, from tens of thousands to well over a hundred thousand, since many conversions were forced and some converts were later tried by the Inquisition as secret Jews. Many exiles resettled in Portugal, North Africa and the Ottoman Empire, which took in large numbers of Sephardic refugees.

Mark Zuckerberg opened thefacebook.com on 4 February 2004 from his Kirkland House dorm room at Harvard, restricting membership at first to students with a harvard.edu email address. Roommates Dustin Moskovitz, Eduardo Saverin and Chris Hughes helped run it as it spread to other Ivy League campuses within weeks.

The site opened to other universities that spring, then to high schools in 2005, and to anyone over thirteen with an email address in September 2006. Saverin, an early co-founder and initial financier, was later pushed out of the company in a dispute over shares, a rift dramatised in the 2010 film The Social Network.

The Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli began building Al-Azhar in Cairo in 970, shortly after founding the city itself as a new capital for a caliph who had just conquered Egypt. Construction finished in 972, and the mosque opened as a base for Ismaili Shia teaching under a dynasty that saw itself as a rival caliphate to the Sunni Abbasids in Baghdad.

Formal instruction was organised there by 988, and the institution changed character sharply after the Fatimids fell in 1171, when new Sunni rulers under the Mamluks turned it into a centre of Sunni scholarship instead. It has taught continuously since, its curriculum built around Islamic law, theology and Arabic long after the dynasty that founded it disappeared.

Filippo Lippi grew up an orphan placed in the Carmelite friary of Santa Maria del Carmine in Florence, the same building where Masaccio was then painting the Brancacci chapel, and later accounts say he learned to paint by watching the older man work there. Lippi took his own religious vows but spent much of his life in trouble with his order over money and, more than once, women.

His Madonnas soften Masaccio's weight and perspective into rounder faces and finer linear drapery, painted for patrons including the Medici family in Florence and Prato. Sandro Botticelli trained in his workshop as a boy, and the profile of Lippi's faces reappears, refined further, in Botticelli's own later work.

On 2 December 1982, surgeons at the University of Utah led by William DeVries implanted a Jarvik 7, a grapefruit sized pump of polyurethane and aluminium, into retired dentist Barney Clark. Compressed air lines ran through his chest wall to an external console the size of a washing machine, so Clark could never be disconnected from the equipment beside his bed.

He lived 112 days, suffering repeated seizures, kidney failure and bouts of confusion before dying on 23 March 1983. The trial drew criticism over whether Clark, 61 and already gravely ill, could meaningfully consent to an experimental device, but later Jarvik hearts were used as bridges to transplant rather than as a permanent replacement.

Wisconsin senator Gaylord Nelson proposed the idea after seeing a 1969 oil spill off Santa Barbara, and organised it with activist Denis Hayes, who built a national staff to coordinate events. It was held on 22 April 1970, deliberately scheduled between college spring breaks and final exams so students could take part.

Rallies, teach-ins and clean-up drives were held in cities and on campuses across the country, drawing roughly twenty million participants by later estimates, at a time when the United States had no federal agency dedicated to pollution. Congress created the Environmental Protection Agency that December, and Nelson later received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for founding the day.

Ray Tomlinson, an engineer at Bolt Beranek and Newman, wrote the first message sent between two separate computers over the ARPANET in 1971. He has said he cannot recall the exact wording, guessing it was something like QWERTYUIOP, since the content did not matter, only that the transfer worked.

Tomlinson chose the @ symbol to separate a user's name from the machine holding their mailbox, since it did not appear in any name and was rarely used elsewhere on a keyboard. The convention spread across ARPANET sites within the early 1970s and survived the network's later growth into the internet largely unchanged.

Christiaan Barnard led a team of about thirty at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town through the night of 2 to 3 December 1967, transplanting the heart of Denise Darvall, a young woman killed in a car accident, into Louis Washkansky, a grocer dying of heart disease. Barnard had trained partly in the United States and had practised the technique on dozens of dogs beforehand.

Washkansky survived the surgery but died eighteen days later of pneumonia, his immune system weakened by the drugs used to stop his body rejecting the new heart. Barnard's second transplant patient the following year lived for nearly nineteen months, and the operation was repeated at hospitals worldwide within a year of the first attempt.

Thirty-one artists, including Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Degas and Berthe Morisot, rented studio space from the photographer Nadar on the boulevard des Capucines in April 1874 after years of rejection from the official Paris Salon jury. They called themselves the Societe Anonyme rather than Impressionists, a name none of them had chosen yet.

A critic named Louis Leroy wrote a mocking review of Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, sneering that even wallpaper showed more finish, and the label he coined as an insult stuck to the whole group. Roughly 3,500 visitors came through in a month, far fewer than the Salon drew, and reviewers were mostly hostile to the loose brushwork and unfinished-looking surfaces.

Friedrich Froebel opened his school in Bad Blankenburg in 1837 under the name Care, Play and Activity Institute for Small Children, built around songs, finger games and a set of wooden blocks and balls he called his gifts. He believed young children learned through structured play rather than rote drilling, an idea most German schools at the time did not share.

He did not settle on the name that stuck until 1840, when he renamed the institute Kindergarten, garden of children, a term that spread through German-speaking Europe and then abroad as teachers trained under him opened their own schools. Prussia briefly banned kindergartens outright in 1851, suspecting Froebel's circle of harbouring radical politics.

On 5 September 1882, about ten thousand workers took unpaid leave to march from City Hall to a park uptown, carrying banners for the eight-hour day. The Central Labor Union organised the march, and a picnic with speeches and fireworks followed in the afternoon. No one is certain whether the idea came from Peter McGuire of the carpenters' union or Matthew Maguire, a machinist.

Oregon made Labor Day a state holiday first, in 1887, and by 1894 thirty states had followed. Congress made it a federal holiday that same year, days after federal troops broke the Pullman railroad strike, a timing many took as a deliberate gesture toward organised labour rather than toward the more radical May Day.

Atlantic City hoteliers organised the contest to keep tourists in town past Labor Day, when the summer crowds usually left. On 8 September 1921 at the Million Dollar Pier, sixteen-year-old Margaret Gorman of Washington, D.C. was crowned, chosen from entries that had begun as a newspaper photo contest rather than a stage competition.

Gorman received a trophy shaped like a golden mermaid and a modest cash prize rather than a scholarship, the tuition prize that later pageants became known for. She returned the following year to defend the title, an arrangement soon dropped once organisers settled on a fresh winner each year and built the contest into an annual fixture rather than a one-off publicity stunt.

Pierre de Coubertin persuaded delegates at a Paris congress in 1894 to revive the games, and Athens was chosen partly because Greece could claim the ancient original. King George I opened the games on 6 April 1896 in a marble stadium rebuilt with funding from the Greek businessman Georgios Averoff, before a crowd estimated at around 60,000.

Roughly 245 athletes from fourteen countries competed, all of them men, in sports including cycling, wrestling, swimming and gymnastics. Greece hoped to make Athens the permanent host, but the games moved to Paris in 1900, and a rotating host city became the settled arrangement instead.

Auguste and Louis Lumiere charged an entrance fee for the first time on 28 December 1895, in the basement salon of the Grand Cafe on Paris's Boulevard des Capucines. Around thirty-three paying customers watched roughly ten short films, each under a minute, including workers leaving a factory and a train arriving at a station platform.

The brothers' own camera, the Cinematographe, doubled as a projector and a printer, which made it lighter than rival machines and easier to carry abroad. Within a year the Lumieres had sent operators to film and screen in cities from London to Bombay, and their patents briefly gave France a lead in an industry the United States would soon overtake.

The Olympic Games of 776 BCE at Olympia is the earliest date ancient Greek record-keepers agreed on, taken from a list of victors in the sole event, a footrace called the stadion, roughly 192 metres down the length of the stadium. The winner recorded that year was Coroebus of Elis, a cook.

Competitors were free adult men and boys, all Greek, all competing naked, and married women were barred even as spectators. The games were held every four years at the same site for over a millennium, until the Roman emperor Theodosius I banned pagan festivals in 393 CE and the Olympiad ended.

Around 1826 or 1827, Joseph Nicephore Niepce coated a pewter plate with light-sensitive bitumen of Judea and set it inside a camera obscura pointed out an upstairs window of his house at Le Gras, near Chalon-sur-Saone. The exposure needed roughly eight hours, long enough that sunlight reaches both sides of the courtyard buildings in the finished image at once.

Niepce called his process heliography, sun writing, and this pewter plate is the oldest known surviving camera photograph rather than the first he ever attempted. It shows a dovecote, a barn roof and a tree, rendered as a rough, low-contrast grey image, and it went unrecognised in a private collection until a historian identified it in 1952.

Warner Bros. built the film around its Vitaphone system, which played synchronised sound from large discs run alongside the projector rather than printed onto the film strip itself. Most of it was still a silent picture with a music score and intertitles; the spoken lines were confined to a handful of scenes where Al Jolson, playing a cantor's son turned jazz singer, ad-libbed dialogue the crew had not planned to record.

It opened at Warners' Theatre in New York on 6 October 1927 and its commercial success pushed other studios to convert to sound within a few years, ending the careers of some silent stars whose voices did not suit the new format. Vitaphone's disc system itself was abandoned by the early 1930s in favour of sound printed directly onto the film.

From studios built inside Alexandra Palace in north London, the BBC began broadcasting on 2 November 1936, alternating week by week between two rival systems: John Logie Baird's mechanical 240-line picture and the Marconi-EMI company's electronic 405-line system. Only a few thousand households owned a receiver capable of picking up either signal, most of them within range of the single transmitter mast.

Programmes ran for only an hour at a time, split between an afternoon and an evening slot, and the BBC dropped Baird's mechanical system within months once picture quality made the choice obvious. The service went off air entirely on 1 September 1939, the day before Britain declared war on Germany, in case its transmissions helped guide enemy bombers toward London.

The organisers in Chamonix did not call it an Olympics at all. It opened on 25 January 1924 as an International Winter Sports Week, a meet the International Olympic Committee sponsored without formally sanctioning, because members worried snow and ice events had no place alongside the summer Games.
