About 250 athletes from 16 countries competed in events including speed skating, ski jumping, bobsleigh and curling.

American speed skater Charles Jewtraw won the 500 metres, the meet's first event, making him its first individual champion, while Finland's Clas Thunberg took three golds, a silver and a bronze across the skating oval. The week ran well enough that the IOC retroactively recognised it as the first Winter Olympic Games the following year and voted to hold a separate Winter Games every four years after that.

The earliest cuneiform signs were pressed into wet clay at Uruk to track grain, sheep and beer owed to temple stores, not to record speech. A scribe used a cut reed to leave wedge-shaped marks, and the tablets were baked or sun-dried, which is why so many survived a fire that would have destroyed a scroll.

Pictographs came first, drawings of jars and animal heads standing for the things themselves. Only over centuries did the signs come to stand for sounds, letting scribes spell names and words that had no picture of their own. Tens of thousands of these tablets have been recovered from Mesopotamian sites.

As plague spread through Europe from 1348, bands of penitents walked from town to town whipping their own backs and chests with knotted cords, sometimes fitted with metal points, in processions that could last thirty-three days, one for each year of Christ's life. Chroniclers in German and Low Countries towns describe crowds gathering to watch and sometimes join.

The movement alarmed both bishops and secular rulers, who saw self-appointed lay preachers gaining followings outside church control, and some flagellant bands turned on Jewish communities, blaming them for the plague. Pope Clement VI condemned the practice in October 1349, and rulers in France and the German lands began suppressing the processions by force.

Seven sculptors were told to fit the sacrifice of Isaac, Abraham, a donkey, two servants, an altar, a ram and an angel into a bronze quatrefoil no bigger than a large dinner plate. The Calimala cloth guild, which paid for the Baptistery's doors, judged the panels in Florence in 1401. Only two entries survive complete.

Lorenzo Ghiberti cast his figures in fewer pieces than his rival Filippo Brunelleschi, saving bronze and, the judges apparently felt, showing more grace. Brunelleschi lost, or the vote tied and he withdrew rather than share the commission. He turned to architecture instead, and would later raise the Duomo's dome across the piazza.

Ford's board announced the change on 5 January 1914, roughly doubling the pay of most workers on the Highland Park assembly line, from about 2.34 dollars a day to 5. The wage was not unconditional: it applied only after six months' service and was withheld from workers Ford's own investigators judged to drink, gamble or otherwise mismanage their home life.

Newspapers called it madness and Wall Street predicted ruin, but the plant's punishing turnover, which had run above 300 percent a year on the new moving assembly line, fell sharply once workers had a reason to stay. Ford also cut the working day to eight hours across three shifts, which let the factory run around the clock without lengthening anyone's individual workday.

Francesco di Pietro di Bernardone, a cloth merchant's son from Assisi, gave away his possessions after what he described as a call from Christ speaking through the crucifix at San Damiano. He and a handful of followers began preaching and begging in the countryside around Assisi, owning nothing individually or communally, and in 1209 he travelled to Rome to ask Pope Innocent III for permission to live this way.

Innocent hesitated, reportedly wary of a movement that resembled banned heretical sects, but approved an oral rule after a dream in which Francis propped up a collapsing Lateran basilica. The order grew fast enough that Francis wrote a stricter rule in 1223 to hold it together; disputes over how literally to keep his vow of poverty split his followers within decades of his death in 1226.

The 1818 title page carried no author's name at all, only a dedication to William Godwin. Mary Shelley was nineteen when she wrote the core of the story and twenty when it appeared in print, and reviewers who assumed a man had written it argued over whether Percy Shelley or Godwin himself was the true source.

The idea grew out of a wet summer at Lake Geneva in 1816, when Lord Byron proposed that everyone in the house write a ghost story to pass the time confined indoors. Mary Shelley later said the image of the creature came to her in a waking dream, and she did not put her name to the novel publicly until a revised edition appeared in 1831.

Named for the Fremont River in Utah, where archaeologists first defined it in the 1930s, this culture occupied the eastern Great Basin and Colorado Plateau growing maize alongside continued hunting and gathering, unlike neighbouring foraging groups who never took up farming. Villages were small, often a handful of pit houses, and shifted as families balanced fields against wild resources.

Fremont people pecked and painted anthropomorphic figures with trapezoidal bodies and elaborate headdresses onto canyon walls across Utah, alongside basketry and unfired clay figurines left in caves. The culture's population declined and its farming settlements were largely abandoned by around 1300, for reasons still debated among archaeologists working the region today.

Voltaire had recently returned from exile in England, where he had watched Isaac Newton buried in Westminster Abbey with state honours, and he brought back a taste for English scientific method and religious tolerance that he pressed into his own writing. Montesquieu was travelling Europe gathering material for a comparative study of governments and laws.

Neither man worked alone. Salons, coffee houses and a growing trade in printed pamphlets let arguments about censorship, taxation and monarchy travel between Paris, London and the German states faster than any one writer could carry them himself.

Freud's publisher dated Die Traumdeutung 1900 to make it look current, though it went on sale in Vienna in November 1899. Freud had analysed his own dreams for the book, most famously one about a patient he called Irma, and argued that dreams were disguised fulfilments of repressed wishes rather than random noise.

The first printing of 600 copies took eight years to sell out, and Freud earned little from it at the time. He revised the book repeatedly over three decades, adding new case material and a chapter on dream symbolism, and later called the interpretation of dreams the surest foundation of his whole theory of the unconscious.

The Indian National Congress adopted Gandhi's non-cooperation programme in September 1920, asking Indians to resign government jobs and titles, boycott British courts and schools, and stop buying imported cloth in favour of hand-spun khadi. It followed the Amritsar massacre of 1919, in which troops under General Dyer killed hundreds of unarmed civilians at a public meeting.

Gandhi called the campaign off in February 1922 after a mob at Chauri Chaura killed several police constables, which he saw as proof the movement had turned violent before independence could be won by non-violent means. He was arrested weeks later and served roughly two years of a six-year sentence.

British law taxed salt and banned Indians from making or selling their own, even though it lay free for the taking along the coast. Gandhi picked the tax because it touched every household regardless of religion or caste, and on 12 March 1930 he set out from his ashram at Sabarmati with a small group of followers, walking roughly 240 miles to the coastal village of Dandi.

He reached the shore on 6 April and broke the law in public by scooping up natural salt, a gesture with almost no material value that thousands of Indians copied in coastal towns over the following weeks. British authorities arrested more than 60,000 people during the wider campaign it sparked, and Gandhi himself was jailed without trial that May, though the tax itself stayed on the books for years afterward.

The Genroku era, an official reign name running from 1688 to 1704, fell during a long stretch of peace under Tokugawa rule that let merchant wealth accumulate in cities such as Osaka and Edo even though merchants sat at the bottom of the formal social order. That wealth, without an outlet in politics or land ownership, went instead into theatre tickets, prints and fashion.

Kabuki actors such as Ichikawa Danjuro built star followings, the puppet theatre writer Chikamatsu Monzaemon turned contemporary scandals into stage tragedies, and ukiyo-e printmakers supplied portraits of both. The period's name became shorthand for this burst of urban commoner culture, even though the peace and prosperity that produced it had been building for decades before the era officially began.

Britain granted independence to the Gold Coast on 6 March 1957, and the new state took the name Ghana after the historic West African kingdom rather than keeping its colonial label. Kwame Nkrumah, who had organised strikes and a boycott campaign through his Convention People's Party, became its first prime minister and later its president.

It was the first sub-Saharan colony to gain independence through a largely negotiated, non-violent process rather than a war of liberation, and Nkrumah used the moment to push pan-African unity, hosting the first Conference of Independent African States in Accra in 1958. More than thirty African nations followed Ghana out of colonial rule within the next decade.

Edward Gibbon published the first volume of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in 1776, the same year the American colonies declared independence, and it sold out its first printing quickly. He eventually completed six volumes by 1789, tracing more than a thousand years from the second century to the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Two chapters on the early Christian church, arguing that its rise had weakened Roman civic and military virtue, provoked accusations of impiety that Gibbon answered in a published vindication. He wrote much of the later volumes at Lausanne, in Switzerland, having left a seat in Parliament behind him.

Enrico Scrovegni built his family chapel in Padua partly to atone for his father's money lending, a trade the church treated as sinful, and hired Giotto to cover its walls. Giotto gave Mary and the apostles weight and turned bodies, faces creased with grief or surprise rather than fixed in the flat frontal stare of earlier Italian church painting.

The cycle runs from Joachim's expulsion from the temple to the Last Judgement on the entrance wall, where Scrovegni himself kneels offering the chapel to the Virgin. Giotto worked in true fresco, applying pigment to wet plaster section by section so each patch had to be finished before it dried, a method that fixed the colours into the wall itself rather than sitting on its surface.

Juliette Gordon Low had met Robert Baden-Powell in England and run a small troop of Girl Guides there before bringing the idea home. On 12 March 1912 she registered a troop of eighteen girls in Savannah, Georgia, initially also calling them Girl Guides, and taught them first aid, astronomy and outdoor skills at a time when most organised activities for girls stopped at needlework.

Low renamed the organisation Girl Scouts within the year and ran it from her own house and her own money for much of the early period. She died of breast cancer in 1927 without knowing how large it would grow; membership had already passed 140,000 by the time of her death.

Portugal set up a tribunal at Goa in 1561, modelled on the Inquisition at home, to police the faith of new converts and the Portuguese settler population itself. Its first target was less Hindus and Muslims than crypto-Jews, converted Portuguese Jews suspected of secretly keeping their old practice, some of whom had fled Portugal for Goa to escape exactly this scrutiny.

The tribunal's own building and archive were destroyed after Goa's Inquisition was abolished in 1812, so most of what is known comes from a single detailed account written by a Frenchman, Charles Dellon, who was imprisoned and tried there in the 1670s and published his memoir after release. Public autos de fe were held in the main square of Old Goa for over two centuries.

In Games Workshop's Warhammer 40,000 setting, the Emperor of Mankind is mortally wounded by his own son Horus during a civil war fought across the galaxy, and his ruined body is interred on the Golden Throne, a life support device housed in the Imperial Palace on Terra. The year belongs to that setting's own future history rather than to any real calendar.

Ten thousand years further on, the fiction has the Throne failing, sustained by continuous psychic sacrifice and patched endlessly by the tech priests of the Adeptus Mechanicus, who no longer fully understand the machine they maintain. Whether the Emperor is dead, dying or something else is left deliberately unresolved, a question the novels and games have kept open rather than answered.

Goethe had been working on the Faust story since his twenties, and an early draft known to scholars as the Urfaust circulated among friends decades before he finished the first part for print. The finished text opens not with Faust but with a theatre director and a poet arguing about what will draw an audience.

The story follows an ageing scholar who trades his soul to the demon Mephistopheles for renewed youth and knowledge, and it borrows from a German legend already centuries old by Goethe's time. Goethe kept working on a second part almost until his death in 1832, published only after he died.

Goguryeo nobles were buried in stone chambers under earth mounds, and painters covered the chamber walls and ceilings with plaster and pigment before the tomb was sealed, so the images were made for the dead rather than for any living viewer. Subjects range from hunting on horseback and wrestling to processions of servants, alongside guardian spirits meant to protect the occupant.

Many tombs also carry the four directional animals, a blue dragon, white tiger, red phoenix and black tortoise-snake, painted on the chamber's four walls to orient the dead within the cosmos. Most of these tombs survive around the old Goguryeo capitals at Ji'an in China and Pyongyang in North Korea, sealed underground and largely undisturbed until modern archaeologists reopened them.

Producer David O. Selznick burned old studio sets, including the King Kong backlot, for the film's Atlanta fire sequence months before he had cast Scarlett O'Hara, betting that any delay finding an actress would cost more than losing that footage. He went through more than 1,400 candidates before settling on the British actress Vivien Leigh, who was not American and had almost no Hollywood profile at the time.

It premiered in Atlanta on 15 December 1939 with a segregated cast list: Hattie McDaniel, who played Mammy, could not attend the Georgia premiere under the state's segregation laws, though she later became the first black performer to win an Academy Award for the role. Adjusted for inflation, it remains among the highest-grossing films ever released in the United States.

Larry Page and Sergey Brin met as Stanford graduate students and built a search tool called BackRub, which ranked pages by counting links to them rather than just matching keywords, the method most rivals used. They renamed it Google, a misspelling of googol, and incorporated the company in a friend's Menlo Park garage on 4 September 1998.

Their first outside cheque came from Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, who wrote a hundred thousand dollars to a company that did not yet exist, made out to Google Inc. before the paperwork was filed. The firm moved out of the garage within months as its index grew past the tens of millions of pages other engines were still working from.

At kilns near Gangjin and Buan, Goryeo potters fired a glaze whose colour came from iron oxide reduced in a low-oxygen kiln. The Song envoy Xu Jing, visiting Korea in 1123, recorded in his Gaolitujing that the ware's colour was praised among his contemporaries as unmatched by ordinary green stoneware.

From around the mid twelfth century, potters added sanggam inlay: cutting a design into the wet clay, packing the cuts with white or black slip, then shaving the surface flat before glazing. No earlier Chinese celadon used the method, which let a single glaze surface carry a pattern set beneath rather than painted onto it.

King Gojong ordered the carving after an earlier set of woodblocks was destroyed in a Mongol invasion, and work began in 1236 on Ganghwa Island, where the Goryeo court had taken refuge. Carvers finished the project in 1251, having cut the entire Buddhist canon, roughly 81,258 double sided blocks, each checked against earlier printed editions for accuracy.

The blocks were later moved to Haeinsa Temple in the southern mountains, where they still sit in two storage halls built with staggered windows that keep airflow even through the seasons. No block is known to have warped or rotted badly enough to need replacement, a survival owed as much to that building as to the wood itself.

Scribner's printed roughly 20,000 copies on publication and the book sold through only a fraction of them before Fitzgerald died in 1940, thinking himself a failure. He drew Gatsby's mansion and lifestyle from Long Island's Gold Coast, where he and Zelda rented a house in Great Neck among the newly rich commuters and bootleg fortunes he was writing about.

Fitzgerald wanted to title it Trimalchio, after a vulgar social climber in the Roman Satyricon, and only accepted the publisher's preferred title under protest. Sales recovered after his death, helped by a wartime paperback edition distributed free to American servicemen, and the novel is now a fixture of American high school reading lists.

Diocletian's first edict, issued in February 303, ordered Christian churches demolished, scriptures burned and Christians stripped of the right to hold office or sue in court. Further edicts that year and the next required sacrifice to the traditional gods on pain of imprisonment, forced labour or execution, enforced with the most severity in the eastern provinces under his co-emperor Galerius.

The killing was uneven across the empire: Gaul and Britain, under the western ruler Constantius, saw little of it. It ended piecemeal between 311 and 313, when Galerius and later Constantine issued edicts of toleration. Constantine's own conversion followed within a decade, reversing in one generation a policy meant to eliminate the faith entirely.

The break came to a head in Constantinople when papal legate Cardinal Humbert, after a heated dispute with Patriarch Michael Cerularius over practices such as using unleavened bread in the Eucharist, laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of the Hagia Sophia and walked out. Cerularius responded by excommunicating Humbert in turn, though the pope who had sent him, Leo IX, had died before the confrontation took place.

Neither side saw this as a permanent break at the time; the split hardened over the following century through separate ritual practice, disputed authority over the Balkans and the sack of Constantinople by Catholic crusaders in 1204. Mutual excommunications from 1054 were formally lifted only in 1965, when Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras met in Jerusalem.

Early Greek floor mosaics were made from uncut river pebbles pressed into wet plaster, giving soft outlines and a limited palette of natural stone colours. At Pella in Macedonia, capital of the kingdom that raised Alexander, pebble floors from the fourth century BC show hunting scenes and a lion hunt with the pebbles set closely enough to suggest shading.

The technique changed when workshops began cutting stone and glass into small regular cubes, tesserae, which could be laid to follow a curved line or a shaded fold of cloth far more precisely than a rounded pebble allowed. That shift, visible already in some Pella floors, let mosaic copy panel painting rather than only imitate it.

Black-figure ware paints silhouettes onto the natural orange clay, incising details with a needle. Around 530 BCE Athenian workshops reversed the technique: the background was painted black and the figures left in the clay's colour, then outlined in fine brushstrokes instead of scratched lines. The change let painters draw foreshortened limbs and turned faces that the older silhouette method could not manage.

Painters such as the Andokides Painter worked in both styles on the same vessel, black-figure on one side and the new red-figure technique on the other, as workshops tested which would sell. Corinth had led the export trade in painted pottery a century earlier, but the Athenian potters' quarter, the Kerameikos, took over the market and supplied households and tombs across the Mediterranean.

Pope Gregory I died in 604, more than two centuries before the melodies bearing his name were written down. Carolingian monks under Charlemagne's successors collected and notated the chant repertoire used across Frankish churches, and crediting it to Gregory lent the resulting standard the authority of Rome rather than of any living composer.

The notation itself was new: neumes, small marks placed above the words, recorded the rise and fall of a melody without fixed pitch or rhythm, a system singers had to already know the tunes to read. That single-line, unaccompanied style, sung in Latin for the Mass and the divine office, became the basis against which later Western polyphony was measured.

Gregory had governed Rome as a civil administrator before becoming a monk, and he brought that administrative habit into the papacy when he was elected in 590, reportedly against his own wishes. Rome was battered by plague, flooding of the Tiber and Lombard armies pressing on its territory, with little help arriving from a Byzantine government based far off in Constantinople.

He negotiated directly with the Lombards, reorganised the church's substantial estates to feed the city, and wrote extensively on pastoral care and liturgy, work later credited, without firm proof, with shaping the chant that bears his name. In 596 he sent a mission under Augustine to convert the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, extending papal reach into a Britain Rome had abandoned as a province two centuries earlier.

Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, working as librarians and philologists in the German state of Hesse, published the first volume of their tale collection in December 1812, drawing mostly on stories told to them by acquaintances and neighbours rather than gathered from peasants in remote villages, as they later claimed. One key source, Dorothea Viehmann, was a tailor's widow from a nearby town.

The first edition included stories far more violent than the versions read to children today, and the brothers kept softening and revising them across seven editions over four decades, adding Christian moralising and cutting sexual content. Later editions sold widely across German-speaking lands and were translated into English within a generation.

Picasso had already accepted a commission for a mural at the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the 1937 Paris World's Fair when, on 26 April 1937, German and Italian planes bombed the Basque town of Guernica in support of Franco's forces. Contemporary estimates of the dead ranged into the hundreds, and later research by Basque historians settled on a lower figure than the thousands first reported in the international press.

Working in a borrowed Paris studio over about a month, Picasso filled a canvas roughly eleven feet high and twenty-five feet wide with a screaming horse, a gored figure and a woman carrying a dead child, all in flat greys, whites and blacks like a newspaper photograph. The painting toured to raise money for Republican Spain and did not reach Spain itself until 1981, after Franco's death.

Under Gupta rule from the fourth century, the astronomer Aryabhata calculated the solar year's length to within minutes of the modern figure and used a place value number system that included a symbol for zero, ideas that later reached the Islamic world and then Europe. Sanskrit court poetry flourished alongside this, including the plays of Kalidasa, though his exact dates within the period remain debated.

The dynasty's wealth came from trade routes across northern India, and its coinage, struck in gold rather than the more common silver, advertised that wealth with kings shown hunting lions or playing the veena. Gupta power weakened after Hun invasions in the fifth century, and its temples, built in stone rather than the brick and wood of earlier centuries, are among the oldest surviving Hindu shrines.

Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith by training, had spent years developing metal type that could be cast in identical, reusable pieces, along with an oil-based ink and a modified wine press. His edition of the Latin Vulgate ran to roughly 180 copies, most on paper and about 35 on vellum calfskin, each of two volumes printed in double columns of 42 lines, and it took his Mainz workshop about two to three years to complete.

Gutenberg had borrowed heavily from the financier Johann Fust to fund the press and lost the equipment to him in a lawsuit before the Bible was even finished. Around 49 copies survive today, only 21 of them complete, scattered across libraries from Mainz to the United States Library of Congress.

Haida carvers worked in red cedar, a wood soft enough to carve with hand adzes yet resistant to rot in the wet coastal climate. A pole raised outside a house recorded the lineage's crests, animals such as raven, eagle or bear owned by a family, and the specific stories that gave them the right to display each figure.

Raising a pole required a potlatch, a ceremony where the host family gave away wealth to validate the carving in front of witnesses from other clans. Iron tools obtained through maritime fur trade with European and American ships let carvers work larger poles faster than earlier stone and shell tools had allowed.

In spring 1689, Matsuo Basho sold his house in Edo and set out on foot with a companion toward Japan's northern interior, a journey of roughly 150 days and some 2400 kilometres through country still considered remote and unsafe. He kept notes of the villages, shrines and chance encounters along the way, pairing short prose passages with seventeen syllable verses composed on the spot.

The account, Oku no Hosomichi, was not published until 1702, eight years after Basho's death, and its verses treat ordinary sights such as frogs, cicadas and roadside inns with the same seriousness earlier poets had reserved for court subjects. That shift in what counted as worth writing about became the model later haiku poets worked from long after his own travels ended.

Handel wrote Water Music for a Thames river party ordered by King George I, who travelled by barge from Whitehall to Chelsea while musicians played from a boat alongside. Newspapers reported the King liked the suite enough to have it repeated at least three times over the journey.

Decades later Handel turned to sacred oratorio, and Messiah became his most performed work, written in under a month while he was in financial difficulty. He conducted charity performances of it at London's Foundling Hospital for the rest of his life, and left a copy of the score to the institution in his will.

Handel wrote the oratorio in about three weeks in 1741 and took it to Dublin rather than London, arriving that November. It was first performed on 13 April 1742 at Neal's Music Hall on Fishamble Street, as a charity concert for three causes: a society relieving imprisoned debtors, Mercer's Hospital and the Charitable Infirmary. Ladies were asked to leave their hoops at home so more seats would fit.

More than 700 people crowded in, against the hall's usual capacity of about 600, and ticket sales raised roughly 400 pounds, split between the three charities. London did not hear it until the following year, and reception there was cooler than in Dublin; Handel kept revising the score for later performances for the rest of his life.

A single Manhattan neighbourhood held Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Duke Ellington and the painter Aaron Douglas within walking distance of one another through the 1920s. The magazine Opportunity ran writing contests that gave many of them their first paid publication, and the Cotton Club on Lenox Avenue booked black performers for a whites-only audience, a contradiction the era never resolved.

Alain Locke's 1925 anthology The New Negro gathered the movement's fiction, poetry and essays under one cover and gave critics a name for what was already under way in rent parties and church basements. The 1929 stock market crash and the Depression that followed cut the private patronage much of it depended on, though its writers kept publishing into the 1930s and beyond.

The earliest surviving mention of a harpsichord is a 1397 note by a jurist in Padua recording that a man named Hermann Poll claimed to have invented an instrument called the clavicembalum. No description of what Poll's instrument looked like or sounded like survives alongside the claim, only the name and the year.

The earliest known image of one appears carved into an altarpiece from Minden, Germany, made in 1425, and the oldest surviving instrument itself was built in Bologna in 1521. Unlike a piano, a harpsichord's strings are plucked by small quills rather than struck by hammers, giving every note the same volume regardless of how hard a key is pressed.

Bloomsbury printed only five hundred copies of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in June 1997, most going to libraries, after twelve publishers had turned the manuscript down. J.K. Rowling had written much of it in Edinburgh cafes as a single mother on benefits, typing drafts on an old manual typewriter.

An American edition followed a year later retitled Sorcerer's Stone, a change made because Scholastic's editors thought US children would not recognise the word philosopher in a title. Six sequels followed through 2007, and the series was translated into more than eighty languages.

Harun al-Rashid became Abbasid caliph in 786 at about twenty, ruling from Baghdad while his mother Khaizuran and his vizier family, the Barmakids, ran much of the administration for years before he moved against them in 803, executing one and imprisoning the rest.

His reign is the setting later Arabic storytellers gave to One Thousand and One Nights, though the tales were compiled centuries after his death in 809 and mix invented episodes with real figures from his court, including the poet Abu Nuwas and the executed vizier Jafar al-Barmaki.

Prince Paul Anton Esterhazy hired Haydn in 1761 as vice-Kapellmeister for his court in Hungary, a contract that required him to compose whatever music the prince asked for on demand and kept him subordinate to the ageing Kapellmeister Gregor Werner. Haydn took full charge of the musical establishment after Werner died in 1766, running an orchestra housed on the estate.

Isolated from other composers for much of the year, Haydn later said the position forced him to experiment because he had no one nearby telling him how a symphony ought to sound. He wrote most of his eventual total of 106 symphonies during his decades of Esterhazy service, several nicknamed for a joke or an instrumental effect buried inside them.

Mono no aware, roughly the pathos of things, named a sensitivity to beauty precisely because it does not last: cherry blossoms scattering, a season turning, a correspondence ending. Heian courtiers built entire social codes around registering that feeling correctly, judging character by how someone reacted to a fading flower or a poorly matched robe colour.

Court rank depended on skill at composing waka poetry on demand, layering multiple colours of silk in a visible sleeve edge and recognising incense blends by scent alone. Sei Shonagon and Murasaki Shikibu, both palace women rather than professional writers, left the fullest record of these standards, because so much of court life left no other trace once the objects and gestures were gone.

Emperor Kanmu moved the capital from Nara to Heian-kyo, later Kyoto, partly to escape the political power Buddhist temples had built up in the old city and partly after a series of deaths and disasters were blamed on the ghost of a rival he had exiled. The new city, like Nara before it, followed a Chinese grid plan, with the emperor's palace at its northern end.

Court life there produced writing largely by women, since men wrote in Chinese for official business while women used the newer phonetic kana script for diaries, poetry and fiction. Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book and Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel, both came out of this court around the turn of the eleventh century.

Kyoto, then called Heian-kyo, had been laid out as the imperial capital in 794 on a grid modelled on Tang Chinese cities, and by 1000 its court had turned inward, cultivating writing, calligraphy and etiquette over the military campaigns that occupied earlier Japanese rulers. Court women wrote in Japanese script rather than the classical Chinese reserved for men's official documents, producing the era's most enduring literature.

Buddhist temples built during the period, among them structures later reflected in the Phoenix Hall at Byodo-in, paired gilded statuary with gardens designed to evoke the Pure Land paradise described in Buddhist texts. Provincial governors, meanwhile, ran the countryside with less central oversight, a gap that let regional military families grow into the power the court later lost.

Men at the Heian court wrote in Chinese, the language of government and scholarship. Women were largely barred from it, so they wrote in kana, a simplified syllabary derived from Chinese characters, which was considered too informal for official use. That exclusion is why a body of diaries, poetry and fiction from the court's women survives in the vernacular Japanese that men of the period rarely committed to paper.

Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book records court anecdotes and lists of things she found pleasing or irritating; Izumi Shikibu and others left poem collections built around love affairs and mourning. Almost nothing is known of these women beyond what they wrote, since court records tracked fathers and husbands, not the women themselves.

Ruprecht I, elector of the Palatinate, asked Pope Urban VI for permission to found a school of general studies, and the pope granted it in October 1385; the decision to actually open the university at Heidelberg followed in June 1386. It was modelled on the University of Paris, with faculties of theology, law, medicine and philosophy, and its first rector was Marsilius of Inghen, a Dutch scholar who had taught in Paris.

Founding a German university under papal charter mattered politically as well as academically, since it meant clergy and lawyers no longer had to travel to Paris or Bologna for a doctorate. Heidelberg remains Germany's oldest university, and the institution has continued teaching on and near its original site through repeated wars and rebuilding in the centuries since.

Muhammad left Mecca in 622 after years of hostility from the Quraysh, travelling to Yathrib, a town later renamed Medina, where rival Arab clans had invited him to arbitrate their disputes. He did not travel alone or first: his companion Abu Bakr went with him, while other followers had already been slipping out of Mecca ahead of him in small groups.

In Medina, Muhammad drew up a document known as the Constitution of Medina setting out relations between the Muslim migrants, the local converts and the town's Jewish clans under his arbitration. The Islamic calendar counts its years from this migration rather than from Muhammad's birth or first revelation, so year one begins with an emigration, not a battle or a birth.

Trials for witchcraft rose sharply across parts of Germany, France, Scotland and Switzerland from the 1560s through the early 1600s, driven by local courts rather than any single order from Rome or a Protestant church. Accusations most often came from neighbours after a death, a failed harvest or a sick child, and confessions were frequently extracted under torture that local law permitted in witchcraft cases specifically.

Estimates for the whole period across Europe run to roughly forty thousand to sixty thousand executions, concentrated heavily in certain German territories rather than spread evenly. Women made up the large majority of the accused. Prosecutions declined through the seventeenth century as courts required stronger evidence and as scepticism about the trials themselves grew among judges.

Rapper's Delight was recorded by the Sugarhill Gang, a group assembled specifically for the session by producer Sylvia Robinson after she heard rapping over records at parties in the Bronx and Harlem. Released on Sugar Hill Records in September 1979, it ran close to fifteen minutes on the twelve-inch pressing, built over a bassline played live by session musicians re-creating Chic's Good Times.

It reached number 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 in early 1980, an unlikely chart position for a record with no radio-friendly length or conventional song structure, and sold roughly two million copies within its first year. The style it introduced to a mass audience had already been developing for several years at Bronx block parties around DJs such as Kool Herc and Grandmaster Flash.

Hiroshige travelled the Tokaido road connecting Edo to Kyoto as part of an official escort delivering shogunal horses to the imperial court, sketching the post stations along the way. His publisher issued a print for each of the 53 stations plus the two endpoints, 55 sheets in total.

The series showed travellers caught in rain, wind and river crossings rather than idealised scenery, and its low price put a share of Japan's own landscape within reach of ordinary city buyers. It sold well enough that Hiroshige produced several later variant editions of the same route over the following years.

Thomas Hobbes wrote most of Leviathan in Paris, where he had fled during the English Civil War, and published it in London in 1651 once the monarchy had been abolished. He opened by imagining life with no government at all, a condition he judged so violent and insecure that people would rationally trade away their freedom for protection under a single unchallengeable ruler.

The book made him enemies on every side: royalists disliked that his sovereign's authority rested on a hypothetical contract rather than divine right, and parliamentarians and churchmen objected to a ruler with power over religious doctrine. Oxford University had copies burned in 1683, more than three decades after publication, showing how long the book kept unsettling English political and religious argument.

Hokusai was in his late sixties when his publisher issued the Fuji series, using a recently affordable imported pigment called Prussian blue that gave the prints their sharp, saturated colour. The set eventually ran to 46 sheets rather than the 36 the title promised, after demand pushed the publisher to add more views.

Under the Wave off Kanagawa shows three fishing boats dwarfed by a curling wave while Mount Fuji sits small in the background. Hokusai signed his work with a changing string of pen names throughout his life and reportedly told students that nothing he drew before age seventy was worth counting.

Most classicists place the Iliad's composition in the eighth century BC, drawing on oral poetry traditions that may have circulated for centuries before being fixed in the alphabet Greeks had recently adopted from Phoenician traders. Whether a single poet called Homer composed both epics, or whether the name covers generations of bards reciting formulaic verse, has been argued since antiquity itself.

The Iliad covers only weeks near the end of a ten year siege, centred on the anger of Achilles after a quarrel with Agamemnon. The Odyssey follows Odysseus's ten year journey home, delayed by a cyclops, a sorceress and a god's grudge. Both poems were transmitted orally for generations before any surviving written copy.

Burials at Hopewell sites in Ohio were accompanied by objects that had travelled hundreds of miles: copper from around Lake Superior, mica sheets from the Carolinas, marine shell from the Gulf coast and obsidian blades traced to Wyoming. None of these materials occur locally, so their presence marks a network of exchange rather than a single trade route.

The mounds themselves were built up in stages over log tombs and clay platforms, and some enclosures nearby, at Newark for instance, cover thousands of acres in circles and an octagon aligned to lunar risings. Who was buried with the imported goods, and why, is argued from the grave goods alone; no contemporary written record survives.

Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr moved into an old mansion at 800 South Halsted Street on 18 September 1889, in a Chicago district crowded with recent Italian, Irish, Greek and Jewish immigrants. The house had been built by Charles Hull in 1856 and was, by then, surrounded by factories and tenements rather than the open land it once stood on.

Hull House grew to thirteen buildings offering a kindergarten, a night school for adults, a public bath, an art gallery and a labour museum, all free. Addams and its residents pushed successfully for child labour limits and factory safety laws in Illinois, and the model spread: by 1913 there were over four hundred settlement houses across the United States.

The project was funded by the US Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health, with the Wellcome Trust and centres in Britain, Japan, France, Germany and China joining as the effort grew. Its budget was set at roughly three billion dollars, spread over what was meant to be fifteen years.

A rival private venture, Celera Genomics under Craig Venter, raced the public consortium through the late 1990s using faster sequencing machines. Both sides announced a draft sequence together at a White House ceremony in June 2000, and the publicly funded project published its finished sequence in April 2003, two years ahead of schedule.

Hus's execution in 1415 turned a reform movement inside the Bohemian church into an armed one. His followers wanted the mass said in Czech rather than Latin, and insisted that ordinary worshippers receive both bread and wine at communion, not bread alone as Rome then allowed; the chalice became their emblem, painted onto shields and banners.

In 1419 crowds in Prague threw royal officials from a town hall window, an act that opened years of fighting known as the Hussite wars. Blind general Jan Zizka built armoured wagon trains into mobile gun platforms that beat back five papal crusades sent against Bohemia before an uneasy religious settlement was reached at Basel in 1436.

The I Ching grew from a practice of cracking heated tortoise shells and reading the pattern of the fractures, later replaced by counting stalks of yarrow into piles. The results were sorted into 64 six-line figures, each built from broken and unbroken lines, and each attached to a short, often cryptic judgement.

Excavated versions on bamboo strips and silk, including a Han-era manuscript recovered at Mawangdui in 1973, show that the line order and some judgements varied by copy before the text settled into the form still consulted for divination. Confucius and his followers later added layers of philosophical commentary to it.

The company had begun in 1911 as a merger of three smaller firms making tabulators, scales and time clocks, run under the plain label Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company. Thomas J. Watson, who took charge in 1914 after leaving a sales job at National Cash Register, pushed the rebrand to match a business that was already selling punch-card machines to clients well beyond the United States.

On 14 February 1924 the company adopted the name International Business Machines Corporation, a title bigger than its product line at the time but one Watson expected the company to grow into. It did: IBM went on to dominate punch-card data processing for decades before the mainframe and personal computer businesses that made the name familiar to later generations.

In 1938 a farmer named Isaiah Anozie was digging a cistern on his land in south-eastern Nigeria when he turned up bronze objects buried in the soil. Excavations two decades later uncovered a burial chamber and a storehouse of ritual vessels, staff ornaments and a bronze roped pot cast in one piece by the lost-wax method, radiocarbon dated to roughly the ninth century.

No copper or tin ore sources have been identified nearby, so the metal reaching Igbo Ukwu almost certainly travelled along trade routes from North Africa or beyond, centuries before regular European contact with the coast. The objects belonged to a single wealthy burial rather than a settlement, and who held that authority in a society without the walled cities of later West African kingdoms remains unresolved.

Books printed in Europe's first decades of movable type are called incunabula, from the Latin for swaddling clothes, a label coined long after the fact by collectors marking off print's infancy. The cutoff is arbitrary, fixed at the year 1500, but it separates a period when printers were still imitating manuscript letterforms from one where print had settled into its own conventions.

Early print runs stayed small, often a few hundred copies, and printers frequently left blank spaces for a scribe to add coloured initials by hand afterward, a habit carried over from manuscript workshops. An estimated 30,000 different editions were produced before 1501, and a large share of them survive in only one or two known copies today.

By around 2600 BCE the cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, now in Pakistan, were laid out on grid plans with baked brick streets, covered drains, and household wells and bathrooms connected to that drainage. No temple or palace has been identified at either site, unlike contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia, leaving archaeologists arguing over how such uniform planning was organised without an obvious ruling monument.

The civilization used a still undeciphered script, stamped onto small steatite seals carved with animals such as the unicorn-like bull, and traded as far as Mesopotamia, where Indus seals turn up in excavated cities. Standardised weights found across its sites, from small settlements to the largest cities, suggest common measures were used over a huge area without any single surviving capital.

Pope Innocent IV's bull Ad extirpanda, issued in 1252, set out procedure for inquisitors already at work against Cathar and Waldensian heresy in southern France and Italy, and it permitted torture provided it stopped short of killing or permanently maiming the accused. Confessions obtained had to be repeated freely afterward, without instruments present, to count as valid.

The bull also required city governments to fund and support inquisitors under threat of excommunication, tying secular authority into what had begun as a church court. Torture had already been used informally before 1252; the bull's significance was in writing limits and procedure into canon law rather than in introducing the practice for the first time.

Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger stripped down a location-sharing app called Burbn to its photo feature and relaunched it as Instagram on 6 October 2010, limiting posts to square images to match old Polaroid and Kodak formats rather than a phone's usual rectangular frame. It reached 25,000 downloads on its first day from Apple's App Store alone.

Filters such as X-Pro II and Lo-fi let users disguise ordinary phone photos as processed film shots, driving much of the app's early word of mouth. Facebook bought the company, then thirteen employees and no revenue, for one billion dollars in April 2012, days before Instagram's Android release.

Steve Jobs announced the iPhone at Macworld in San Francisco on 9 January 2007, describing it as three devices in one: a phone, an iPod, and an internet browser controlled entirely by a finger on a glass screen with no stylus. It went on sale on 29 June 2007 at 499 dollars for the four gigabyte model, tied exclusively to AT&T in the United States.

The first version had no third party apps and ran on the slower EDGE cellular network rather than 3G. Apple opened the App Store in July 2008 alongside the iPhone 3G, and outside developers could then build software for it directly, a decision that reshaped how phones were sold and used well beyond Apple's own products.

Apple unveiled the iPod on 23 October 2001, a white plastic block built around a 1.8 inch Toshiba hard drive that held about a thousand songs and was navigated with a scroll wheel designed by Tony Fadell's team. Steve Jobs pitched it as a way to carry a whole music collection in a pocket, at a launch price of 399 dollars.

It worked only with Macintosh computers and iTunes for its first eighteen months, limiting early sales, until a Windows-compatible version arrived in 2003 alongside the iTunes Store, which sold songs for 99 cents each. Apple sold over 100 million iPods within six years, reshaping how record labels priced and distributed recorded music.

When Iran's electoral authorities declared Mahmoud Ahmadinejad the winner of the June 2009 presidential vote within hours of polls closing, supporters of the runner up Mir Hossein Mousavi took to the streets of Tehran adopting his campaign's green as their colour. Crowds that organisers put in the hundreds of thousands marched in silence for days before security forces moved against them.

A young bystander, Neda Agha Soltan, was shot during a protest on 20 June and filmed dying on a pavement; the video, uploaded within hours, was seen by millions abroad and became the movement's fixed image. Mousavi and fellow candidate Mehdi Karroubi were placed under house arrest in 2011, where both remained for years afterward.

Irish scribes filled the spaces between and inside their letters with ribbon like interlace, spirals and animal heads that chase their own tails around a page, a style with no direct model in the Mediterranean manuscripts the Latin text itself came from. Some initial letters expand to fill an entire page before the surrounding words resume.

The technique demanded a compass and ruler as much as a pen: patterns were pricked out in advance with pin holes, then filled in with pigments made from local plants, minerals and imported materials such as lapis lazuli. The style travelled with Irish missionaries to monasteries in Northumbria and on the continent, where local scribes adapted it into their own gospel books.

Ireland had no Roman occupation and no Roman roads, so its monasteries grew as self contained settlements rather than clustering near old imperial towns. Foundations at Clonmacnoise, Bangor and Clonard drew students from Britain and the continent, and their scriptoria copied Latin grammar, scripture and classical authors that were being lost elsewhere as western Europe's cities emptied.

Monks there also devised the compressed, rounded handwriting known as insular minuscule, later carried to continental monasteries by missionaries such as Columbanus, who left Ireland around 590 to found houses in Gaul and Italy. The copying habit meant Latin texts that barely survived on the continent kept circulating in Irish scriptoria through the centuries after Rome's collapse.

Isidore, bishop of Seville, spent his final two decades assembling the Etymologiae, arranging the sum of ancient learning he could still find under headings from grammar and law to ships, cooking utensils and the names of God. Each entry explains a word by tracing where he believed it came from, a method modern scholars judge unreliable but which he used to organise an entire inherited body of knowledge.

He died in 636 with the work unfinished, and a friend, Braulio of Zaragoza, divided the text into twenty books and issued it after his death. Copied across Latin Europe for centuries afterward, the Etymologiae became one of the most cited authorities of the medieval period, quoted alongside scripture in monastic libraries that held little else from the ancient world.

Muhammad did not leave Mecca by choice. After years of hostility from the city's merchant clans, an assassination plot forced him and his follower Abu Bakr to slip out at night and hide in a cave while pursuers searched nearby. The journey to Yathrib, soon renamed Medina, the city of the Prophet, took about a week and ended a period in which his small community had no legal protection at all.

In Medina, Muhammad drew up a pact among the city's clans, Muslim and non-Muslim, that amounted to a rough constitution. The year of the move, 622 CE, was fixed decades later by the caliph Umar as year one of the Islamic calendar, a lunar reckoning still used today to date religious observances across the Muslim world.

A bound Quran or scientific treatise from this period typically has covers of goatskin or calfskin over pasteboard, tooled while damp with metal stamps to press geometric interlace and vine patterns into the leather itself rather than painting them on top. Gold leaf was pressed into the tooled lines using egg white or a similar binding agent, catching light along the cover's edges.

Binders also built a flap, called a fore-edge or envelope flap, that folded from the back cover across the book's open edge to protect the pages, a feature rarely seen in European bindings of the same centuries. Surviving examples from Baghdad, Cairo and later Persian and Ottoman workshops show the same core structure repeated and refined over several hundred years.

The Ottoman sultanate had already been abolished in 1922, but the family kept the separate, older title of caliph, a religious rather than political office claimed since 1517. Mustafa Kemal Ataturk's new Turkish Grand National Assembly ended even that on 3 March 1924, exiling the last caliph, Abdulmecid II, and closing a position that had, at least in name, linked the Muslim world's temporal and religious leadership.

Ataturk's government paired the abolition with the closure of religious courts and schools as part of building a secular republic out of the empire's remains. Movements to revive or claim the caliphate elsewhere, including a short-lived congress in Cairo the same year, never produced a successor recognised beyond a single country or faction.

Early Quran copies from the seventh and eighth centuries use Hijazi and then Kufic script, angular letters without vowel marks, written on parchment because paper had not yet reached the Arab world from China. A scribe left no signature; the earliest named calligraphers appear only from the tenth century onward, among them Ibn Muqla, credited with proportioning letters by strict geometric rules.

Because figural images were avoided in religious contexts, lettering itself carried the weight given elsewhere to painting or sculpture, appearing on coins, mosque walls and tomb inscriptions rather than only manuscript pages. Later scripts such as thuluth and naskh grew from these early forms, each suited to a different surface, from stone lintels to correspondence.

Florence in the mid fourteenth century was governed by guilds of merchants and bankers, and it was their wealth, built on wool and money lending, that later paid for the painting and building historians group under this label. There was no single opening date; the change is visible instead in scattered commissions, wills and account books that show patrons asking for something different from what their fathers had asked for.

Petrarch and Boccaccio were already collecting and copying manuscripts of Roman authors in these same decades, and their circle treated the recovery of classical Latin as its own kind of achievement, separate from theology. The word Renaissance itself was coined centuries later, by the French historian Jules Michelet in the 1850s, to describe a change that people living through it did not name.

Jan Hus travelled to the Council of Constance under a safe conduct issued by the emperor Sigismund, expecting to defend his teachings in open debate. Instead he was arrested within weeks, held for months in increasingly harsh conditions, and tried by a council that wanted a recantation. He refused to take back positions he did not believe were his own to withdraw.

He was burned outside the city walls on 6 July 1415, his ashes scattered in the Rhine so no relics could be kept. News of his death reached Bohemia within days and set off protests that hardened into open revolt within three years, the start of the Hussite wars that Sigismund himself would spend the next decade trying to put down.

Cornelius Jansen, a Dutch theologian and bishop of Ypres, died in 1638 leaving a manuscript on Augustine's teaching on grace that colleagues published two years later as the Augustinus. It argued that human will, weakened by original sin, cannot choose good without a grace God grants only to some, a position close to positions the Church had already condemned in others.

The book drew support at Port-Royal and among sympathetic French clergy, and open hostility from Jesuit theologians who saw it as reviving Calvinist-leaning ideas about predestination. Rome eventually condemned five propositions drawn from it in 1653, but the dispute over grace and free will continued in France for decades after that ruling.

During the early Heian period, Japanese court scribes wrote Chinese characters alongside a developing native script, kana, simplified from Chinese forms to represent Japanese sounds directly. Monks who had studied in Tang China, among them Kukai, brought back Chinese brush techniques and are credited by later tradition with shaping how those techniques were taught at the Japanese court.

Court calligraphy became a marker of education and status; a courtier's handwriting was judged alongside their poetry, and collections of model letters circulated for students to copy. Kana script eventually allowed vernacular Japanese literature, including court diaries and poetry, to be written without relying entirely on Chinese characters.

Central Java's Sailendra dynasty built Borobudur, a stepped stone monument covered in relief panels illustrating Buddhist texts, over several decades around the turn of the ninth century. Nearby, the Hindu Prambanan complex, begun not long after under the rival Sanjaya line, rises in tall pointed towers around a central shrine to Shiva.

Borobudur's panels, laid end to end, run for several kilometres and would have required visitors to walk its galleries in sequence, reading the story of the Buddha's life and past lives as they circled upward toward the open stupas at its summit. Both sites were abandoned after Javanese political centres shifted east, and Borobudur lay buried under volcanic ash and jungle growth for centuries before nineteenth century clearance.

No single decree created Javanese court dance around 1400. What survives from the Majapahit period is a scatter of stone reliefs at temples such as Panataran, showing dancers in the poses still used in Java: bent knees, turned wrists, a torso held still while the arms move. Court poems from the same centuries describe performances staged for royal weddings and harvest rites.

The dancers drew their stories from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, retold in Old Javanese verse and acted out with masked and unmasked roles alongside gamelan music. When Majapahit's power broke apart in the following century, its dance forms did not disappear with it; they were carried into the courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta, where variants are still taught today.

Matteo Ricci reached the Portuguese trading post of Macau in 1582 and spent the next years learning Chinese and adopting the dress of a Confucian scholar rather than a foreign priest, eventually gaining entry to Beijing in 1601. He translated Euclid into Chinese with a local collaborator and drew a world map that showed China at its centre, adjusted to please his hosts rather than to follow European convention.

Other Jesuits worked at the Mughal court under Akbar and in Japan, where a mission begun by Francis Xavier in the 1540s had grown large enough to alarm local rulers before persecution and later expulsion ended it. Ricci died in Beijing in 1610, and the Chinese court permitted him burial there, an honour rarely extended to a foreigner.

Pope Paul III approved the new order in a papal bull, Regimini militaris ecclesiae, on 27 September 1540, after Ignatius of Loyola and a small group of companions he had met in Paris took vows of poverty and obedience. Ignatius was elected the order's first superior general the following year and ran it from Rome until his death in 1556.

Members added a fourth vow, obedience to the pope on mission, and were sent as teachers and confessors rather than confined to a monastery. Jesuit colleges spread across Catholic Europe within decades, and Jesuit priests travelled to Goa, Japan and later China, carrying instructions written personally by Ignatius on how to adapt to each court they entered.

Neither Gospel account of the birth gives a year, and the two disagree on the ruler in charge: Matthew places it under Herod the Great, who died in 4 BCE, while Luke ties it to a census under the governor Quirinius, who is not attested in that post until 6 CE. Modern historians generally favour a date before Herod's death.

The calendar that later split history into BC and AD was set in the sixth century by the monk Dionysius Exiguus, who calculated the birth year from partial and since-corrected records. His count stuck regardless, which is how a date now widely placed a few years earlier came to sit at year one.

Crucifixion was a Roman method of execution reserved largely for slaves, rebels and provincials, meant to be slow and visible beside a public road. The Gospels place the sentence with the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, at the urging of Jewish religious authorities, on charges tied to claims of kingship, and describe the site as Golgotha, outside Jerusalem's walls.

Historians generally date the event to around 30 or 33 CE, calculated from the overlap of Pilate's governorship, the reported day of the week, and the timing of Passover in those years. Roman and Jewish writers of the following century, including Tacitus and Josephus, mention the execution in passing, outside any Christian source.

Cash played two shows at Folsom State Prison in California on 13 January 1968, backed by the Tennessee Three and joined by June Carter, Carl Perkins and the Statler Brothers. Columbia Records recorded both sets; producer Bob Johnston chose to release material almost entirely from the earlier morning performance for the resulting live album.

The opening track, Folsom Prison Blues, contains the line about shooting a man in Reno just to watch him die, and the recorded cheer that follows it was reportedly added afterward from another take, since inmates were warned beforehand against cheering violence. The album revived Cash's career, which had stalled through the mid 1960s under drug problems and falling sales.

The Joseon dynasty, founded in 1392 by Yi Seong-gye, made Neo-Confucian philosophy the basis of state examinations rather than the Buddhism the previous Goryeo court had favoured. Officials were chosen through the gwageo civil examination, testing command of Confucian classics, and a hereditary scholar official class known as yangban came to dominate government and landholding.

The court funded printing with movable metal type, decades before Gutenberg's press in Europe, to circulate Confucian texts and legal codes across the peninsula. Ancestor rites, mourning rules and family hierarchy were rewritten along Confucian lines by royal decree, reaching into households far removed from the capital at Hanseong.

Hahoe, a village on a bend of the Nakdong river near Andong, is the source of a set of wooden masks carved for a talnori, a masked dance drama performed as part of a village shaman ritual meant to appease a local guardian spirit. The masks, cut from alder wood with hinged jaws on some characters, represent stock figures including a corrupt nobleman, a lecherous Buddhist monk and a foolish servant.

Performers used the drama to mock the yangban scholar class and clergy in front of audiences that included those same officials, protected by convention from open reprisal for what the masks said. Twelve of the original Hahoe masks, along with related masks from nearby Byeongsan, survive and are held as National Treasures of Korea.

Julian had been raised Christian under guardians appointed after his family was purged by Constantine's heirs, and he kept his own conversion back to the old gods secret until he became sole emperor in 361. He reopened temples, restored public sacrifice and barred Christian teachers from lecturing on pagan literature they no longer, in his view, sincerely believed.

He also ordered the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem rebuilt, reversing centuries of Roman policy, a project abandoned when he died. His attempt to build a rival philosophical priesthood modelled loosely on Christian charity and organisation produced no lasting institution. He died in 363 from a wound taken during a campaign against Persia, after barely twenty months in sole power, and Christianity resumed its favoured position under his successors.

Okuni, a shrine attendant from Izumo, drew crowds in Kyoto around 1603 by performing unconventional dances on a dry riverbed stage, sometimes dressed as a man, mixing sacred dance steps with popular song. Troupes of women copied her act across the city's pleasure districts, and the style took the name kabuki, from a verb meaning to lean or tilt away from the ordinary.

The Tokugawa shogunate banned women from the kabuki stage in 1629, citing the performances' association with prostitution, and young men took the female roles instead. Adult male actors playing onnagata, the female-role specialists, became the form the shogunate eventually tolerated and licensed.

Kabuki began around 1600 with performances by women, most famously the dancer Okuni, but the shogunate banned female performers in 1629 on the grounds that troupes doubled as prostitution fronts. Young men then took the female roles, and when the authorities judged that arrangement equally disreputable, they restricted the stage from 1652 to adult male actors only.

Actors specialising in women's roles, called onnagata, developed a codified vocabulary of gesture, voice and costume meant to represent femininity rather than imitate it directly. Some onnagata lived in character offstage as well, and the convention of all male casts, forced by two separate bans within a generation, became the tradition's defining feature rather than a temporary workaround.

No inscription or colophon names Kalidasa's patron or dates his life, so scholars place him anywhere from the first century BC to the fifth century AD by matching his verse to Gupta-era astronomy and place names. The convention followed here, a poet at the court of Chandragupta II, rests on later legend rather than any surviving document.

Beyond his plays he wrote long poems in ornate metre: Kumarasambhava on the birth of the war god Kartikeya, Raghuvamsha tracing a legendary dynasty, and Meghaduta, in which an exiled spirit asks a passing rain cloud to carry a message to his wife across the length of India. Two further plays, Malavikagnimitram and Vikramorvasiyam, complete the attributed body of work.

Abhijnanasakuntalam turns on a curse. The sage Durvasa strips King Dushyanta's memory of his bride Shakuntala after she fails to greet him, distracted by grief over her husband's departure. Dushyanta does not recognise her when she arrives at court pregnant, and only a ring, swallowed by a fish and cut free by a fisherman years later, restores what the curse erased.

William Jones's 1789 English translation carried the play to Europe, and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe answered it with a short verse comparing it to the blossoms of spring and the fruit of autumn held together. The Sanskrit text survives in more than one regional recension, and scholars still disagree over which verses belong to Kalidasa and which were added by later copyists.

Kant worked in near silence on the Critique for roughly a decade after his earlier writing had drawn little notice, then produced the finished book in a matter of months once the arguments had settled in his mind. Its opening pages ask how knowledge that is certain, like mathematics, is possible at all.

Kant argued that the mind supplies structure, such as space, time and cause and effect, to raw experience rather than reading them straight off the world. Early readers found the book so dense that Kant later wrote a shorter Prolegomena explaining it, and lecture audiences in Konigsberg struggled with the original text for years.

Kathak takes its name from kathakars, storytellers who recited Hindu epics and devotional tales in temple courtyards, marking rhythm with their feet as they spoke. Under Mughal patronage the form moved into court settings, where dancers added rapid spins and a more restrained, stylised hand vocabulary suited to performance for an emperor rather than a temple congregation.

Dancers wear rows of small bells, ghungroo, tied around each ankle, and a skilled performer can ring some bells while silencing others through precise footwork, a technique used to display command over rhythm. The form later split into regional schools, chiefly at Lucknow and Jaipur, each favouring a different balance of narrative mime and pure rhythmic dance.

The Bible presents David as a shepherd and harpist who killed Goliath before succeeding Saul, but the only inscription outside scripture that may name him is the ninth century BC Tel Dan Stele, which refers to a beyt david, a house of David, without describing the man himself. No contemporary Israelite record from his own reign has been found.

According to the biblical account he took Jerusalem from the Jebusites and made it his capital rather than ruling from an existing tribal centre, moving the sacred Ark of the Covenant there. The city he is said to have chosen has remained the religious focus of Judaism ever since.

King James I ordered the new translation in 1604 partly to settle disputes at the Hampton Court Conference over the marginal notes in the existing Geneva Bible, which he thought undermined royal authority. Around fifty scholars, split into six committees working at Oxford, Cambridge and Westminster, spent seven years on it before it was published in 1611.

The translators worked from Hebrew and Greek texts and leaned heavily on William Tyndale's earlier sixteenth century translation, reusing much of his phrasing. Read aloud in English parish churches for generations, its rhythms fed directly into later English prose and poetry, and revised editions are still printed today.

Kush grew from Kerma, on the Nile south of Egypt, where a walled town and monumental tombs stood by the mid second millennium BC. Egypt's Thutmose I overran Kerma around 1500 BC, and Egyptian troops occupied Nubia for roughly five centuries afterward, leaving Egyptian gods and hieroglyphic writing embedded in Kushite religion.

When Egyptian rule collapsed around 1070 BC, Kush re-emerged as an independent kingdom centred at Napata, further south. By around 730 BC its king Piye marched north and took control of Egypt itself, founding the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. A civilisation shaped by Egyptian conquest ended by ruling Egypt in turn.

Philip IV of France, deep in debt to the order after wars with England and Flanders, had sealed orders sent to his officers weeks in advance so that Templars across the kingdom were seized in coordinated dawn raids on Friday, 13 October 1307. Grand Master Jacques de Molay was arrested in Paris along with roughly sixty other knights, accused of 127 charges including heresy, idolatry and obscene initiation rites.

Confessions followed torture, and Philip pressed Pope Clement V, himself dependent on French support, to extend the suppression across Europe. The order was formally dissolved by papal bull in 1312, and Molay was burned at the stake in Paris in 1314 after retracting his earlier confession, denying the charges to the end.

Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised on 3 May 1491 by Portuguese missionaries and took the name Joao, in honour of King Joao II of Portugal. His eldest son, Nzinga Mbemba, was baptised the same year as Afonso, and his wife took the name Leonor after initially resisting the missionaries' refusal to baptise women.

The conversion did not hold evenly. Joao I returned to older religious practice within a few years, partly over the church's demand for monogamy in a court built on multiple marriages, while his son Afonso kept the new faith and later ruled as a Christian king who corresponded directly with Lisbon and Rome about priests, books and trade.

Afonso I ruled Kongo from 1509 until his death in 1543, corresponding directly with the Portuguese crown and sending young Kongolese nobles to Lisbon to be trained as priests. One of them, his own relative Henrique, was consecrated a bishop by the pope in 1518, decades before any other sub-Saharan African held that rank in the Catholic church.

After Afonso's death, Christian practice in Kongo did not stay a court import: crosses, saints and baptism were folded into existing beliefs about ancestors and spirits, producing forms of worship distinct from European Catholicism. Kongolese Christianity outlasted Portuguese influence in the kingdom and persisted through the wars and disruptions of the following century.

In the forests south of the Congo River, weavers stripped fibre from raffia palm leaves, wove it into square panels on a single heddle loom, then handed the cloth to embroiderers, usually women, who cut and stitched pile designs across the surface. No two panels repeat the same geometric pattern exactly, since the layout was worked freehand rather than from a fixed template.

The cloth was currency, tribute and burial wealth among Kuba, Ngongo and Ngeende communities, and a chief's wrapped skirt could use dozens of stitched panels sewn together. Because raffia fibre degrades within decades, almost none of the surviving pieces in museum collections predate the nineteenth century, so the craft is dated by technique and oral account rather than by any single surviving cloth.

The Kuba Kingdom, formed from a cluster of central African chiefdoms in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, built a court culture in which certain masks could be worn only by the king or by dancers acting out his authority. Three masks recur in accounts of royal ceremony: Mwaash aMbooy, Ngady aMwaash and Bwoom, tied to a founding story of rivalry between a king and a commoner.

Carvers covered the wood with cowrie shells, beads and raffia cloth rather than leaving it bare, and each mask's design marked a specific rank or episode in that founding story. Kuba textile work, especially raffia cloth stitched with geometric patterns, was traded well beyond the kingdom's own borders.

Kanishka ruled a Kushan empire stretching from Central Asia into northern India, and coins struck under him carry images of the Buddha alongside Greek, Persian and Hindu deities, a sign of how many traditions his court patronised at once. Buddhist tradition credits him with convening a council to settle disputed scripture, though the details come from later monastic accounts rather than a contemporary record.

Under Kushan rule the Gandhara region produced Buddha images carved with a Greco-Roman sense of drapery and anatomy, the first widespread figural sculpture of the Buddha rather than the earlier practice of representing him only through symbols. Monks and merchants travelling Kushan trade routes carried both goods and manuscripts east toward the Tarim Basin and China.

Seven stone pillars found near the Mahakam river in East Borneo carry Sanskrit verse cut in an Indian Pallava script, commissioned to record gifts a king named Mulawarman made to Brahmin priests, including grants of cattle. Dutch and later Indonesian scholars dated the lettering style to around the fourth or fifth century.

The inscriptions are the earliest known writing found in the Indonesian archipelago, and they show an Indian-influenced court with Hindu ritual and a Sanskrit vocabulary already established on Borneo well before written records survive from Java or Sumatra. Mulawarman's kingdom, called Kutai, otherwise left no other surviving texts.

La Venta sits on a swampy island in Tabasco, and its central mound rises nearly 30 metres, an earthen mass built without wheels, draft animals or metal tools. Workers carried basket after basket of clay and fill from surrounding riverbanks over generations, packing it into a shape some archaeologists read as a stylised volcano.

Four colossal basalt heads, each carved from a single boulder weighing many tonnes, were dragged or rafted roughly 100 kilometres from the Tuxtla mountains, the nearest source of that stone. Buried offerings of jade figurines and mosaic pavements beneath the plazas suggest the site was built and rebuilt as an act of ritual closure, not simple habitation.

Named for a site in New Caledonia where it was first excavated, Lapita pottery is marked by geometric patterns stamped into wet clay with a toothed tool before firing, sometimes including small stylised faces. Between roughly 1600 and 1000 BCE, people making this pottery moved from the Bismarck Archipelago out through the Solomon Islands and into Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, carrying pigs, dogs and cultivated plants aboard sailing canoes.

By around 1000 BCE the same pottery style appears as far as Tonga and Samoa, marking the western edge of Polynesia and the limit of Lapita expansion; later Polynesian voyaging into the central and eastern Pacific happened without it, the style having gone out of use. Excavated shards remain the main evidence for this movement, since no written record survives.

Four teenagers and a dog named Robot found the entrance to Lascaux in 1940 after a fallen tree opened a shaft near Montignac. Inside, the walls held over 600 painted animals, mostly horses, stags and aurochs, laid out along passages too dark to see without a lamp burning animal fat.

The cave opened to visitors in 1948 and drew a thousand people a day, whose breath and body heat grew algae and calcite over the paint. It was sealed in 1963. A full-scale replica, Lascaux IV, opened near the original site in 2016 so the images could still be seen without further damage.

Legalist thinkers in the Warring States period argued that a ruler should govern through fixed, publicly known laws and harsh, evenly applied punishment rather than through the moral example that Confucian advisers recommended.
