Qi, a wealthy state on the eastern seaboard, drew on these ideas as it competed with rival states for territory and revenue during the fourth century BC.

The philosophy is better documented in the western state of Qin, where Shang Yang's reforms a few decades later rewarded soldiers by enemy heads taken and organised households into groups collectively liable for each other's crimes; those reforms eventually helped Qin conquer every rival, Qi included, by 221 BC. Qi's own Legalist court advisers are recorded mainly by name, with little of their writing surviving directly.

Ludovico Sforza, the ruler of Milan, commissioned the mural for the refectory wall of the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie, where the monks ate their meals beneath it. Leonardo worked in tempera and oil on dry plaster rather than true fresco, an experimental method that let him rework details slowly but left the paint flaking within decades.

He set the moment just after Christ announces that one of the twelve will betray him, and grouped the apostles in clusters of three, each reacting differently, rather than lining them up as earlier versions of the subject had done. Restorers have worked on the damaged wall repeatedly since the eighteenth century, most recently in a two-decade cleaning completed in 1999.

Leonardo likely painted Lisa Gherardini, wife of a Florentine cloth merchant named Francesco del Giocondo, from which the painting's Italian name, La Gioconda, derives. He kept the small poplar panel with him rather than delivering it to whoever commissioned it, reworking it for years and carrying it to Milan, Rome and eventually France, where he died in 1519 in the service of King Francis I.

The painting entered the French royal collection and hung at Versailles and later the Louvre for centuries before a 1911 theft by a Louvre workman, Vincenzo Peruggia, made it a household name well beyond art circles. He kept it hidden in Paris for two years before trying to sell it in Florence, where he was arrested.

Victor Hugo published the novel in Brussels and Paris in April 1862, having spent much of the previous decade in political exile on the Channel Islands after opposing Napoleon III's coup. He had begun drafting it as early as 1845 under a different title, Les Miseres, and set it aside for years before returning to finish it in exile.

The book runs to five volumes and includes long digressions, among them a chapter-length account of the Battle of Waterloo that has no character from the main plot in it at all. Its central figure, the ex-convict Jean Valjean, is pursued across decades by a police inspector named Javert for breaking parole after stealing a loaf of bread.

The kings of Pergamon, in what is now western Turkey, built up a library said to hold around 200,000 scrolls under Eumenes II, second in scale in the ancient world only to Alexandria's. Pliny the Elder later reported that Alexandria's Ptolemies grew concerned enough about the rivalry to cut off papyrus exports to Pergamon, forcing the library to prepare treated animal skin as a writing surface instead.

That story is likely a later embellishment rather than a documented trade embargo, but Pergamon did become associated with fine parchment, a word descended from the city's Latin name Pergamena. Mark Antony is said to have later given the library's collection to Cleopatra as a gift, folding a rival's holdings into Alexandria's own.

Charles Lindbergh Jr., twenty months old, was taken from his nursery in Hopewell, New Jersey, on the night of 1 March 1932. A ransom note left on the windowsill demanded 50,000 dollars, and a retired schoolteacher, John Condon, acted as go-between at a Bronx cemetery where Lindbergh himself waited nearby in the dark while the money was handed over.

The child's body was found on 12 May 1932 in woods less than five miles from the family home; he had died of a skull fracture, apparently on the night of the kidnapping itself. German carpenter Bruno Hauptmann was tried and convicted after ransom bills were traced to him, and he was executed in April 1936, still maintaining his innocence.

Tradition credits the manuscript to Eadfrith, bishop of Lindisfarne from 698 until his death in 721, working alone as scribe and painter, though some historians think he commissioned rather than made it himself. Made in honour of Saint Cuthbert, whose body lay at Lindisfarne, it pairs Latin gospel text with carpet pages of interlaced knotwork in a Northumbrian style mixing Celtic, Anglo-Saxon and Mediterranean elements.

A colophon added around 970 by a priest named Aldred records the story and supplies a word for word Old English translation squeezed between the Latin lines, the oldest surviving English version of the gospels. The book survived Viking raids on Lindisfarne and now sits in the British Library, its pigments including lapis lazuli that had to travel from Afghanistan.

Bob Geldof and Midge Ure organised twin concerts on 13 July 1985, one at Wembley Stadium in London and one at JFK Stadium in Philadelphia, satellite-linked so acts could be seen performing on both sides of the Atlantic in the same broadcast. Around 72,000 people filled Wembley and roughly 100,000 attended in Philadelphia, with an estimated global television audience in the hundreds of millions.

Queen's Wembley set, opening with Bohemian Rhapsody, is frequently singled out as the day's standout performance, and Phil Collins played both venues, flying across on Concorde between sets. The concerts were organised as a follow-up to Band Aid's charity single from the previous Christmas and were reported to have raised tens of millions of pounds for famine relief in Ethiopia.

Titus Livius began his history of Rome, arranged in books of roughly equal length, in the years after Augustus took power, working from the city's legendary founding through to his own lifetime. Ancient sources credit him with 142 books in total, a scale he sustained for around four decades.

Only 35 of those books survive complete: the first ten, covering Rome's earliest centuries, and books 21 to 45, covering the wars against Carthage and the conquest of Greece and Macedon. The rest are known chiefly through brief summaries called periochae and through later writers who quoted or paraphrased passages now otherwise lost.

Wycliffe taught theology at Oxford and argued that scripture, not the pope or church tradition, was the final authority for Christians, a position that led him to back an English translation of the Bible so ordinary readers could judge doctrine for themselves. Followers nicknamed Lollards, a word probably mocking their habit of mumbling prayers, carried handwritten copies and preached in English rather than Latin.

The church condemned Wycliffe's teachings after his death in 1384, and in 1428 his remains were dug up from consecrated ground at Lutterworth, burned, and the ashes scattered in the river Swift on the order of a church council's ruling. Lollardy nonetheless persisted underground into the following century, and some of its arguments about scripture and church authority resurfaced in England's later Reformation.

Tolkien had finished the manuscript by 1949 but spent years arguing with publishers over releasing it alongside his unfinished Silmarillion mythology, and over its length; Allen and Unwin eventually split it into three volumes to limit the financial risk of one large book. The Fellowship of the Ring appeared in July 1954, with the second volume following that November.

Tolkien, a philologist at Oxford, had built the story's languages and invented histories over more than a decade before writing the plot that used them, working partly on paper rationed during wartime shortages. Early reviewers were split, W.H. Auden praised it while Edmund Wilson dismissed it as juvenile, but ordinary readers kept it in print continuously.

Louis XIV had danced leading roles in court ballets since childhood, most famously as the Sun King himself in a 1653 production, and by 1661 he wanted the art placed on a professional footing rather than left to noble amateurs. He chartered the Académie Royale de Danse that year, gathering thirteen dancing masters to set standard technique and teaching methods for the first time in France.

The academy fixed the five foot positions and much of the turned out leg work still taught in classical ballet training. Louis himself stopped performing publicly by the mid 1660s as he gained weight, but the institution he founded outlived his own dancing career, and its resident company later grew into the Paris Opera Ballet.

The Louvre had been a royal palace since the sixteenth century, abandoned as a royal residence once Louis XIV moved the court to Versailles in the 1680s. Revolutionary authorities opened part of it to the public on 10 August 1793, the first anniversary of the storming of the Tuileries, displaying paintings and objects seized from the crown and from fleeing nobles.

The opening collection ran to a few hundred works, far smaller than what followed once Napoleon's armies began shipping art home from conquered Italy and Egypt, some of it later returned after his defeat. Open only three days a week at first and free to enter, it has been added to and rebuilt continuously since.

Lucan began his ten-book poem on the war that Caesar fought against Pompey around 61, while still on good terms with Nero. The friendship soured, Nero banned him from publishing or performing verse, and Lucan kept writing anyway, carrying the story through Pharsalus and into Caesar's campaign in Egypt.

He was twenty-five when he was named in the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero in 65 and ordered to take his own life; the tenth book breaks off mid-scene, unfinished. All ten survive regardless, choosing the losing republican side and its dead rather than the victors, which is unusual for an epic written under the regime that descended from that victory.

Ma Yuan painted at the Southern Song imperial academy in Hangzhou from around 1190 until his death in 1225. He pushed mountains, pines and small figures into one corner of the silk, leaving the rest of the surface as open mist or blank paper, a composition later named the one-corner style.

Xia Gui, active at the same court, used a similar asymmetry pushed to one side rather than one corner, and later cataloguers grouped the two under the joint name Ma-Xia. A surviving Ma Yuan album leaf, Watching the Deer by a Pine-Shaded Stream, is held today by the Cleveland Museum of Art.

The Seleucid king Antiochus IV had banned circumcision and Sabbath observance and ordered sacrifice to Zeus performed on the altar in the Jerusalem Temple. When a royal officer tried to enforce this in the village of Modiin, the priest Mattathias killed him and fled to the hills with his five sons, among them Judah, who took the name Maccabee, meaning hammer.

Judah's guerrilla forces won a string of battles against Seleucid garrisons and retook Jerusalem in 164 BCE, cleansing and rededicating the Temple, an event the books of Maccabees describe and which later gave rise to Hanukkah. Full independence took another two decades of fighting after Judah's death, and his brothers founded the Hasmonean dynasty that ruled Judea until the Romans arrived.

The Macedonian emperors, beginning with Basil I in 867, ruled Byzantium through a period when scribes copied and preserved far more ancient Greek texts than survive from earlier or later centuries. Much of what remains today of Homer, Plato and the Greek tragedians reached later readers only because copyists working under Macedonian patronage transcribed them from older, now-lost manuscripts.

Constantine VII commissioned encyclopedic compilations of history, agriculture and court protocol, while illuminated manuscripts such as the Paris Psalter revived classical figure poses and settings abandoned since late antiquity. The period ended with the dynasty's fall in 1056, after which Byzantine art and scholarship took different directions under new rulers.

Niccolo Machiavelli wrote his short handbook on ruling in 1513, the year after he lost his post in the Florentine government and was tortured and jailed on suspicion of conspiracy against the restored Medici. He dedicated it to Lorenzo de Medici, hoping for a way back into office. It did not work; he never held real power again.

The book argues that a ruler who wants to keep his state must sometimes lie, break faith and use cruelty efficiently rather than avoid it, breaking with advice literature that told princes to be virtuous. It was not printed until 1532, five years after his death, and was placed on the Catholic Church's list of banned books in 1559.

The vizier Nizam al-Mulk laid the foundations of a madrasa in Baghdad in 1065 and opened its doors two years later, one of a network of Nizamiyya schools he funded across Seljuk territory. State money paid teachers' salaries and student stipends directly, tying religious and legal training to the government rather than leaving it to private endowment alone.

By the time the theologian al-Ghazali left his teaching post there in the 1090s, the Baghdad school reportedly held around 3,000 students studying Islamic law and theology under a fixed curriculum. The model spread to other cities under Seljuk rule and gave the word madrasa its lasting sense of a formally endowed college rather than an informal study circle.

The Mahabharata grew over centuries from oral bardic tales of a war between two branches of a royal family into a text of roughly 100,000 couplets, absorbing philosophical and legal material including the Bhagavad Gita along the way. By this period scholarly tradition treats its Sanskrit text as settled into the form later scribes copied, though no single dated manuscript survives to fix the moment.

Tradition credits the sage Vyasa with composing it, dictating it to the elephant-headed god Ganesha, who agreed only if Vyasa never paused; the tale itself signals how far its compilers wanted authorship kept legendary rather than pinned to one hand. Twentieth-century critical editions, compiled from manuscripts across India, still disagree on which verses count as the core text.

Mamluk sultans and the officers who served under them built madrasas across Cairo that combined a mosque, a law school and a library under one roof, endowed by a waqf, a permanent charitable trust, so the institution could outlive its founder. Sultan Barquq and Sultan Qaytbay both left madrasa complexes that still stand in the city.

These libraries held Quranic commentary and law alongside Greek philosophy and medicine translated centuries earlier into Arabic, copied and recopied by scribes attached to each institution. Cairo's book trade also supported paper workshops and binderies whose output has partly survived in library and mosque collections, including illuminated Qurans commissioned by Mamluk patrons.

Painters working in Florence and Rome in the 1520s, among them Jacopo Pontormo and Parmigianino, began stretching figures beyond normal proportion and crowding compositions with poses that no single viewpoint could resolve. Pontormo's Deposition, painted for the Capponi chapel in Florence's church of Santa Felicita, replaces a cross and ladder with an unstable knot of pale, elongated bodies holding Christ.

Parmigianino's Madonna with the Long Neck, begun around 1534, stretches the Virgin's neck and fingers well past anatomical accuracy and sets an oddly small, distant column beside a crowd of full-sized angels. Critics at the time argued over whether such distortion showed skill or affectation, a dispute that later gave the style its name, from the Italian maniera, meaning manner or style.

Mali was not on any European map before this trip. The Catalan Atlas, drawn on Majorca fifty years later in 1375, put it there: a crowned Mansa Musa sits south of the Sahara holding a gold nugget, with a caption naming him the richest king in the region because of the gold mined in his territory.

Al-Umari, a Cairo official who gathered accounts of the visit about a decade later, wrote that Mansa Musa gave away so much gold in alms and trade that the metal did not regain its value in the city for years; later estimates of the slump range from about ten to twelve years. Chroniclers also say he tried to undo the damage on the way home by borrowing gold back from Cairo's merchants at interest, though how much he recovered is not recorded.

James Cook charted much of New Zealand's coastline aboard the Endeavour, and his crew's early contact with Maori communities included both trade in nails, cloth and tools and violent clashes when landing parties misread local protocol. Cook's naturalist Joseph Banks catalogued plants unknown in Europe during the stops ashore.

Maori quickly saw the value of European metal tools and muskets, trading dressed flax, food and timber for them at coastal harbours. Within decades the same contact brought whaling ships, missionaries and introduced disease, reshaping tribal politics and trade networks well before formal British settlement began.

The march was organised chiefly by Bayard Rustin, a veteran pacifist and openly gay strategist whose role other organisers played down for fear it would be used against the event, and by union leader A. Philip Randolph, who had planned a similar march for 1941 and called it off only when Roosevelt agreed to ban discrimination in defence industries.

On 28 August 1963, speakers stood on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial for hours before King spoke last. He departed from his prepared text partway through, following gospel singer Mahalia Jackson's shouted urging to tell them about the dream, a passage he had used in earlier speeches but not written into that day's draft.

Marco Polo travelled with his father Niccolo and uncle Maffeo, merchants who had already made one trip east, on a journey of roughly three and a half years by caravan route across Persia, the Pamir mountains and the Taklamakan desert. He was about twenty when the party reached Kublai Khan's summer court, and the Great Khan, according to Marco's later account, took an interest in him and sent him on missions across the empire.

Marco stayed in Mongol territory for around seventeen years before the family made their way home by sea. His account of it all, dictated to a writer named Rustichello da Pisa while Marco was a prisoner of war in Genoa, mixes firsthand description with secondhand and clearly exaggerated material, and historians still argue over which parts he actually saw.

Marcus Aurelius kept notes to himself while commanding troops against Germanic tribes along the Danube frontier in the 170s. One passage is signed off from Carnuntum, a legionary base near modern Vienna, and another from among the Quadi on the river Gran, placing the writing squarely in the middle of a war rather than in any study.

He never gave the notebook a title or intended it for readers; Meditations is the name later editors gave twelve books of short entries reminding himself to bear pain, ignore insults and expect death without complaint. It survived through Byzantine copying rather than wide circulation in his own lifetime, and the earliest complete manuscripts date from many centuries after his death in 180.

Maria Antonia, a fourteen-year-old Austrian archduchess, was married by proxy in Vienna on 19 April 1770, her brother Archduke Ferdinand standing in for the absent groom. She then travelled to France, was formally handed over to French officials at a pavilion built on the border, and met the future Louis XVI, also aged fifteen, for the first time only days before the Versailles ceremony on 16 May.

The marriage sealed an alliance between France and Austria, former enemies for generations, arranged by their mothers, the Empress Maria Theresa and the French court. It was not consummated for years, a delay that fed gossip and pamphlets long before either of them reached the throne in 1774.

The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015 that the Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment required every state to license and recognise same-sex marriages. The lead plaintiff, Jim Obergefell, had sued Ohio for refusing to list him as spouse on his husband John Arthur's death certificate after Arthur died of ALS in 2013.

Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, his fourth ruling favourable to gay rights in two decades on the court. Before the decision, thirty-seven states already permitted same-sex marriage through earlier court rulings or legislation; the remaining thirteen, mostly in the South, were required to comply immediately.

Masaccio was in his early twenties when the wool merchant Felice Brancacci hired him, alongside the older painter Masolino, to fill a chapel in the Florentine church of Santa Maria del Carmine with scenes from the life of Saint Peter. Masaccio died in Rome in 1428, likely still in his twenties, before the chapel was complete, and the work stood unfinished for decades.

In his scenes a single light source falls consistently across each figure, casting shadows that match from one panel to the next, and his crowds recede along Brunelleschi's new perspective rules rather than floating on a gold ground. Later painters including Michelangelo were sent to the chapel specifically to copy from it, and Filippino Lippi finally completed the missing scenes around 1485.

Around 750, cities such as Tikal, Calakmul and Caracol supported populations that some archaeologists put above 100,000 within their surrounding regions, sustained by raised-field agriculture and reservoirs built to store rainwater through the dry season. Each city was ruled by its own dynasty, recording wars, marriages and captures in stone inscriptions rather than forming a single Maya state.

Within a century many of these cities were largely abandoned, a decline debated among archaeologists and usually attributed to some mix of drought, overfarming and warfare between rival courts. Populations did not vanish everywhere at once: cities in the northern Yucatan, including Chichen Itza, continued to grow after the southern lowlands emptied.

Tikal and Palenque did not know each other as parts of one civilisation; each was an independent kingdom with its own dynasty, ruling through alliance and war with rivals such as Calakmul. Their scribes carved dated stelae recording accessions, marriages and battles, giving Maya history exact calendar dates that most contemporaneous societies elsewhere cannot match.

Palenque's ruler Pakal, who took the throne as a boy in 615, later commissioned the Temple of the Inscriptions, where his tomb was found sealed beneath the pyramid in 1952 with a carved sarcophagus lid and a jade mosaic mask. Tikal's twin pyramid complexes and causeways supported a population that peasant farming on the surrounding thin soil should not, by itself, have been able to feed.

Maya script combined logograms, whole signs standing for a word, with syllable signs that could spell a word out sound by sound, so a single term might be written either way or as a mix of both. Carved on stone stelae and painted in folded bark paper books, it recorded royal genealogies, war captures and calendar dates rather than everyday record keeping.

Only four of these bark paper books, called codices, are known to have survived the sixteenth century, when Spanish clergy burned most that they found on the grounds that they held pagan content. Decipherment took until the late twentieth century, when epigraphers established that the signs recorded spoken Mayan languages rather than abstract symbols, work that let historians read the stelae as history rather than as decoration.

Around 800, Maya cities from the Yucatan peninsula down into highland Guatemala were raising temple pyramids, carved stelae and ballcourts under dynasties that recorded their own histories in a hieroglyphic script only fully deciphered in the late twentieth century. Tikal's tallest temple, Temple IV, rises above 60 metres, among the highest pre-Columbian structures known.

Rulers commissioned stelae dated by a Long Count calendar that let them track dynastic events across centuries with precision. Within a few generations of this peak, southern lowland cities including Tikal and Copan stopped erecting new monuments altogether, a collapse whose causes are still debated among archaeologists working the region.

The Long Count fixed a single date, 11 August 3114 BC by the modern correlation, as the start of the current cycle of the world, and counted every day forward from it in units of twenty. A date carved on a stela gives a ruler's birth or accession against that count, sometimes to the day.

Alongside it ran the 260 day Calendar Round, made of a 20 day names cycle and a 13 number cycle that only realigned with the 365 day solar year once every 52 years. A person's birth date under both systems would not repeat in their lifetime, which made the combination useful for tracking descent and legitimacy.

The Senate held the Army-McCarthy hearings between April and June 1954 after McCarthy accused the army of harbouring communists and the army countered that he had pressured officers to favour a staff member. ABC and the fledgling DuMont network carried the sessions live, giving much of the country its first extended look at McCarthy in action.

Army counsel Joseph Welch's exchange with McCarthy over a young lawyer's past associations, asking whether he had no sense of decency left, drew audible applause in the hearing room. McCarthy's Senate colleagues censured him that December, and he lost most of his political standing before his death in 1957.

Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin told a Republican women's club in Wheeling, West Virginia, on 9 February 1950 that he held a list of State Department employees who were communists or communist sympathisers. The number he cited that night was later disputed even by people present, and he gave different figures in speeches over the following days.

The claim launched years of congressional investigations into government employees, universities, Hollywood and the army, during which accusation alone could cost a career even without evidence. McCarthy chaired his own Senate subcommittee from 1953, and the term coined for this style of unproven denunciation has outlasted the detail of any single list he claimed to hold.

Hitler dictated the book in Landsberg Prison in 1924 while serving a sentence for the failed Beer Hall Putsch, and the Nazi Party's own press, Franz Eher Nachfolger, issued the first volume, subtitled A Reckoning, on 18 July 1925. A second volume followed in December 1926. Early sales were modest: fewer than ten thousand copies of the first volume sold that year.

Sales rose sharply once Hitler became chancellor in 1933, when German municipalities began giving copies to newlyweds and it became compulsory reading in some schools. Germany's Bavarian state government, which held the copyright after the war, blocked new German editions until it expired in 2015, when an annotated academic edition appeared instead.

The phrase had already existed for over a decade, coined in 2006 by activist Tarana Burke to support survivors of sexual violence. It became a hashtag on 15 October 2017, when actress Alyssa Milano asked followers to reply metoo if they had experienced harassment or assault, days after reporting on producer Harvey Weinstein.

Within 24 hours the tag had been used hundreds of thousands of times on Twitter and over 12 million times on Facebook. Weinstein was expelled from the Academy and later convicted; other resignations and firings followed across film, media and politics as accusers named individual men rather than describing harassment in the abstract.

Song painters before him built mountains and rivers from outlines, the ink brush tracing edges the way a draughtsman traces a plan. Mi Fu, a calligrapher and collector working around Henan's misty lake country, instead loaded a wet brush and laid down clusters of overlapping dots, building a hillside out of shadow and damp air rather than contour.

The technique became known as Mi dots, and later painters, including his son Mi Youren, kept using it to paint the same clouded riverbanks. Very little of Mi Fu's own work survives; much of what is attributed to him is copied or reworked by followers, so his reputation as a painter rests almost as much on his writing about art as on the paintings themselves.

Epic released the album on 30 November 1982, produced by Quincy Jones from sessions that reportedly ran through much of that year at Westlake Recording Studios in Los Angeles. It yielded seven top-ten singles in the United States, including Billie Jean, Beat It and the title track, an unusually deep run of hits from a single record.

Jackson had asked for a fright-styled cover shoot and title change from the working name Starlight, and the finished record went on to top the Billboard 200 for 37 weeks. Its sales figures are disputed between sources and later re-tallies, but it is consistently cited among the handful of highest-selling albums ever released.

The marble block Michelangelo carved had already been quarried and roughed out decades earlier by another sculptor, who abandoned it after botching the legs; it sat outdoors in a cathedral workshop yard in Florence for so long that officials had nearly given up on using it. Michelangelo, then in his late twenties, took the commission in 1501 and worked mostly behind a screen for two years.

A committee that included Leonardo da Vinci was consulted on where to place the finished statue and chose the Piazza della Signoria, outside Florence's town hall, rather than the cathedral roofline originally intended, since the figure was judged too fine and too heavy to hoist up there. It stood exposed to weather and, in 1527, a thrown bench during a riot that broke its left arm, before being moved indoors in 1873.

Pope Julius II hired Michelangelo, who considered himself primarily a sculptor, to paint the chapel ceiling in 1508. Working from scaffolding of his own design rather than lying on his back, he covered over five hundred square metres with more than three hundred figures across four years, largely without the workshop of assistants typical of a fresco this size.

The nine central panels retell episodes from Genesis, running from the separation of light from darkness to the drunkenness of Noah, with the Creation of Adam, God's hand reaching toward Adam's, among the last painted. The ceiling was unveiled on 1 November 1512, All Saints' Day, and Michelangelo returned to the same chapel decades later to paint The Last Judgement on its altar wall.

Steamboat Willie was not Mickey's first cartoon; two earlier shorts, Plane Crazy and The Gallopin' Gaucho, had already been made but sat without a distributor because they were silent. Walt Disney and animator Ub Iwerks reworked the character with a synchronised soundtrack, timing gags such as an animal orchestra played on a cow's teeth to a recorded score, and released it once sound had proved itself with The Jazz Singer.

It opened at New York's Colony Theatre on 18 November 1928 and its tight sound timing, rather than the character design, is what drew attention from other studios. Disney kept the drawn design of that early Mickey largely intact for the rest of his own lifetime, resisting later pressure to remodel him as animation style shifted around him.

On 16 October 1995, Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan called Black men to Washington for a day of atonement and unity, urging them to register to vote and take responsibility for their families and communities. Farrakhan spoke for over two hours from the Capitol steps as the crowd filled the National Mall.

The US Park Police put the crowd at 400,000, a figure organisers rejected as far too low. Facing the threat of a lawsuit, the National Park Service later conceded the true number was likely higher, and researchers at Boston University estimated it at around 837,000, still short of the million the march was named for.

John Milton had gone completely blind by the late 1650s and composed Paradise Lost by dictation, reciting lines each morning for whichever family member or assistant was available to write them down. He sold the copyright in 1667 for ten pounds, plus further small payments tied to sales, an unglamorous transaction behind one of the longest poems in English.

Written in unrhymed blank verse across ten books, later expanded to twelve, the poem follows Satan's rebellion and fall alongside Adam and Eve's expulsion from Eden. Milton had backed the losing side in the civil war and lost his government post at the Restoration, and the poem's argument that suffering can be endured under a just but distant authority reads against that personal defeat.

The gospel of Luke places the start of this period after a baptism by John in the Jordan, and dates John's preaching to the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius, which scholars usually read as around 28 to 30 CE. None of the gospels was written by an eyewitness during this window; the earliest, Mark, is generally dated several decades later.

From a base in Galilee, an unusually mixed group gathered around him: fishermen, a tax collector, women who funded the travelling group from their own means. The gospels describe teaching delivered mostly in parables and disputes with religious authorities over how strictly the law should be kept, tensions that sharpened once the group moved toward Jerusalem.

German-speaking court poets of the later twelfth century adapted the love songs of French troubadours and trouveres into a lyric addressed to an idealised, usually unattainable, lady. No single figure founded the practice; Heinrich von Morungen, Reinmar von Hagenau and later Walther von der Vogelweide composed within it at different courts across the empire.

Almost none of the original melodies survive in twelfth century notation. What does survive is the Codex Manesse, copied in Zurich around 1300, a manuscript of over six thousand verses with painted portraits of a hundred and thirty-seven poets, the main reason the tradition's words can still be read at all.

Around 1600 BCE, plaster walls at Knossos on Crete and at Akrotiri on the island of Thera were painted while still wet, fixing the pigment into the surface. Surviving fragments show young men vaulting over the horns of a charging bull, dolphins arcing beside a ship, and processions of figures in profile with the narrow waists typical of the style.

Much of what visitors to Knossos see today is restoration work carried out under archaeologist Arthur Evans in the early twentieth century, using surviving fragments as a guide but filling large gaps with new paint. The Akrotiri paintings, buried by volcanic ash, needed far less reconstruction.

At Cahokia, on the floodplain across the river from what is now St Louis, labourers moved an estimated fifty five million cubic feet of earth basket by basket to raise more than one hundred and twenty mounds, the largest, Monks Mound, covering roughly fourteen acres at its base. No wheeled carts or draft animals did the carrying; it was done by hand over generations.

Archaeologists still debate how many people actually lived within the city itself rather than its farming hinterland, with estimates for the core commonly falling between ten and twenty thousand. A large plaza held a chunkey playing field and a ring of tall cedar posts whose postholes survive, aligned closely enough with solstice sunrises that they are usually read as a calendar marker.

Mixtec scribes painted their histories on long strips of deerskin or bark paper folded into screenfolds, using red and black outlines filled with flat colour rather than words in an alphabet. Figures are identified by name glyphs attached to their heads, and events are strung along the page in a path a reader follows by footprints or connecting lines rather than by lines of text.

The Codex Zouche Nuttall and the Codex Bodley trace the deeds of a ruler named Eight Deer Jaguar Claw across war, marriage and sacrifice in the Mixtec highlands of Oaxaca. Only a handful of these manuscripts escaped Spanish burnings after the conquest; most now survive in European libraries, far from the valleys whose ruling families they were made to record.

Around AD 400 the Moche controlled a string of valleys on Peru's arid north coast, irrigating desert land with canals fed from the Andes and building adobe brick platforms including the Huaca del Sol, one of the largest structures in pre Columbian South America. The bricks were made in workshops that stamped some of them with maker's marks, allowing archaeologists to trace which communities contributed labour to a single monument.

Metalworkers alloyed gold, silver and copper and used gilding techniques to make objects look like solid gold with far less metal, work recovered largely intact from the tomb of the Lord of Sipan, excavated in 1987. The Moche left no writing, so most of what is known about their rulers and rituals comes from these burials and from painted scenes on their pottery.

The Moche built without the wheel, draft animals or writing, using millions of sun dried adobe bricks stamped by different work gangs to raise the Huaca del Sol near modern Trujillo into one of the largest structures in the Americas. Their engineers cut irrigation canals across the coastal desert to farm maize and beans on land that received almost no rainfall.

Moche potters modelled stirrup spout vessels into portraits of individual faces and scenes of ritual combat, sacrifice and sexual acts, fired in single colour clay rather than painted. At Sipan, a royal tomb excavated in 1987 held a lord buried with gold and turquoise ornaments and attendants, giving archaeologists a rare intact record of Moche burial practice.

Moche potters on Peru's north coast made stirrup spout vessels moulded into human heads, with individual noses, scars, missing teeth and facial paint reproduced closely enough that archaeologists can match several vessels to the same sitter across different pots. No two portrait vessels found so far are identical, which argues against a stock set of generic types.

Who these portraits show is not recorded in writing, since Moche left no script, so identification rests entirely on comparing faces and the regalia painted or moulded onto each vessel, headdresses and ear ornaments that seem to mark rank. Many were found in elite burials, suggesting the portraits served a role in commemorating specific rulers or priests after death.

In the mountainous border country of what is now southern New Mexico and Arizona, communities began combining maize farming with a shrinking reliance on wild plants and game, settling into pit houses dug into ridge tops and terraces. Archaeologists name this culture Mogollon after the mountain range itself named for an eighteenth-century Spanish colonial governor, not for any people who lived there.

The rugged terrain kept these farming settlements smaller and more scattered than those of neighbouring valley cultures, but pottery and pit house remains show maize, beans and squash were established staples early on. Mogollon potters later became known for a distinctive black-on-white painted ware that spread through trade well beyond the mountains where it was made.

Moliere's company first performed Tartuffe for Louis XIV at Versailles in May 1664, presenting a pious fraud who fleeces a wealthy household by faking religious devotion. The Archbishop of Paris and a faction of devout courtiers judged the play an attack on the church itself, and pressed the king to ban public performances within days.

Moliere spent five years rewriting and lobbying before a revised version won permission for public staging in 1669, by which point pirated manuscripts had already circulated among readers curious about the banned play. The dispute made Tartuffe the most argued over comedy of his career, and one that outlasted the specific courtiers who had tried to suppress it.

The Mon, settled across what is now lower Myanmar and parts of Thailand, are credited by later chronicles with early adoption of Theravada Buddhism, brought by sea and overland trade routes from Sri Lanka and India rather than through any single missionary journey that can be dated precisely. Their kingdom of Dvaravati, centred in the Chao Phraya valley, left behind Buddhist sculpture and inscriptions in the Mon language and in Pali.

Mon script, adapted from a South Indian alphabet, was later borrowed to write Burmese and other regional languages, carrying Buddhist vocabulary with it. When the Burmese king Anawrahta conquered the Mon capital of Thaton in the eleventh century, Mon monks and texts helped establish Theravada Buddhism at the Burmese court in Pagan.

Mon speaking communities had settled the lowlands of what is now central Thailand and Myanmar centuries before Khmer power spread west from Angkor, and by the thirteenth century the two traditions overlapped across a shared frontier rather than in a single conquest or treaty. Temple inscriptions from the region mix Mon, Khmer and Pali script on the same stones, evidence of scribes working across more than one tradition at once.

Buddhist imagery drawn from Mon workshops appears in temples built under Khmer patronage, while Khmer administrative titles and court ritual spread into kingdoms, including early Sukhothai, that were Mon influenced. The blending left no single founding date or named ruler, only a layer of hybrid art and inscriptions archaeologists still use to trace which influence reached where first.

A scriptorium was a working room, often unheated, where monks sat at slanted desks copying text by hand, one letter at a time, for hours that the Benedictine Rule scheduled alongside prayer and manual labour. Vellum was scraped from calfskin, ink mixed from oak galls and iron, and a single large Bible could consume the hides of an entire herd.

Copying classical Latin authors alongside scripture was not incidental: monasteries such as Fulda, Corbie and Reichenau built libraries that preserved texts by Cicero, Virgil and others whose original manuscripts have since been lost entirely. Errors crept in with every copy, so surviving versions of ancient works are compared across manuscript families to catch where scribes miscopied or corrected each other.

Montaigne retired from public life to his family's chateau in the Dordogne in 1571 and spent much of the next decade writing short pieces he called essais, trials or attempts, on subjects from cannibals to thumbs to his own kidney stones. He printed the first two books in Bordeaux in 1580, and kept revising and adding to them for the rest of his life.

He wrote in the first person about his own doubts rather than arguing a fixed thesis, a method new enough that French had no settled word for it until he coined one from the verb essayer, to try. Later editions grew thicker with a third book and hundreds of added passages, some found in his own annotated copy only after his death in 1592.

Benedict of Nursia climbed a hilltop south of Rome around 529 and, according to his biographer Pope Gregory the Great, tore down a shrine to Apollo still kept by local farmers before building his monastery over it. He stayed there until his death, and it was for this community that he wrote his Rule.

That Rule balanced prayer, manual labour and communal reading under an elected abbot, plain enough that other houses across Europe adopted it wholesale. The abbey itself was destroyed and rebuilt more than once, sacked by Lombards around 580 and by Saracen raiders in 884, and rebuilt again each time.

Roughly 200,000 people gathered at the Monterey County fairgrounds over three days in June 1967 for a festival organised largely by producer Lou Adler and Mamas and the Papas singer John Phillips, who wrote the festival's theme song for Scott McKenzie in an afternoon. Performers were unpaid, and profits were pledged to a charitable foundation.

Jimi Hendrix, virtually unknown to American audiences after building his reputation in London, closed his set by setting his guitar alight on stage, an act he later said he had not planned until the moment itself. Janis Joplin's performance with Big Brother and the Holding Company drew enough attention that she was asked back for a second set, filmed for the festival's documentary.

Montesquieu spent roughly twenty years compiling examples from ancient Rome, Persia, England and China before publishing his conclusions in two volumes, anonymously at first, in Geneva rather than France. He argued that a country's laws should suit its climate, size and customs, and that liberty survived best where power was divided among separate bodies.

The Catholic Church placed the book on its list of forbidden texts within two years, but copies kept selling across Europe. Delegates drafting the American Constitution in Philadelphia decades later cited Montesquieu's account of separated powers more than any other single author.

Monteverdi wrote L'Orfeo for the Mantuan court of Duke Vincenzo Gonzaga, where it was staged during carnival in 1607 for an academy of noblemen who staged such entertainments among themselves. The story follows Orpheus into the underworld to reclaim his dead wife Eurydice, a myth already used by Peri and Rinuccini for their own Florentine attempt at the form only years earlier.

Monteverdi scored it for an unusually large and varied instrumental group for the period, shifting the accompaniment to match each scene's mood rather than repeating one texture throughout. Later, in Venice, he helped move opera out of court settings and into paid public theatres.

Hishikawa Moronobu began as a textile designer in his family's embroidery business before moving to Edo and turning to book illustration. Through the 1670s he produced illustrated volumes and standalone prints of the city's theatre districts and pleasure quarters, and he was among the first artists to sign such prints with his own name rather than leaving them anonymous.

Before Moronobu, woodblock printing mostly served text, with pictures as a minor accompaniment. His prints reversed that balance, treating the image as the main attraction and the caption as secondary, which gave later ukiyo-e artists a commercial template: single sheet prints of fashionable figures and city scenes, sold cheaply enough for ordinary Edo residents to buy.

Samuel Morse is credited with the code, but its working form was largely built with Alfred Vail, a machinist who helped fund and construct Morse's telegraph and who is thought to have devised the shortest signals for the most frequently used letters, such as a single dot for E. The two men refined the system through the early 1840s while building working telegraph lines in New Jersey.

On 24 May 1844, Morse sent the message What hath God wrought between Washington and Baltimore over a line Congress had funded with 30,000 dollars. The phrase had been chosen for him by a friend's daughter, Annie Ellsworth, who found it in the Book of Numbers. Morse code later became the basis for international telegraphy standards used across most of the world.

Mozart died in Vienna on the night of 5 December 1791, aged 35, after several days of fever, swelling and vomiting that his doctors could not identify; rheumatic fever and kidney failure are among the causes now suspected, and the poisoning rumours that later attached to his rival Antonio Salieri have no support in the medical record.

He left his final commission, a Requiem Mass, unfinished; his widow Constanze had his pupil Franz Xaver Sussmayr complete it so the fee already paid could be kept. He was buried in a common grave outside the city walls, standard practice in Vienna at the time rather than a mark of poverty, and its exact location was never recorded.

Mozart wrote this opera on commission from Prague's National Theatre, following the success there of The Marriage of Figaro the previous year, with a libretto by Lorenzo da Ponte based on the old legend of the libertine Don Juan. He conducted the first performance himself on 29 October 1787, reportedly finishing the overture only the night before.

The opera opens with its title character killing a woman's father in a duel and closes with him dragged to hell by the dead man's animated statue, a supernatural ending Mozart labelled a dramma giocoso, a mixed comic and serious drama. Vienna saw its own production the following year, with Mozart adding new arias to suit the local singers.

MTV signed on at 12:01am on 1 August 1981 from studios in New York, opening with footage of a rocket launch and the spoken line ladies and gentlemen, rock and roll, before playing the Buggles' Video Killed the Radio Star, chosen for its title rather than its chart success. It reached only a small patch of New Jersey cable subscribers on its first night, since most systems had not yet signed carriage deals.

Early hosts, called VJs, introduced videos supplied largely free by record labels keen for the exposure, a model that let the channel launch with almost no content budget. Within a few years it was reshaping how singles were marketed, giving heavy rotation to acts able to produce striking videos and drawing early criticism for showing few Black artists before pressure from Columbia Records helped change that.

Muhammad was around forty and had taken to retreating alone to a cave on Mount Hira, outside Mecca, when he reported being addressed by a voice commanding him to recite. The Quran calls this night, in the month of Ramadan, the Night of Power. Muslim tradition holds that the angel Gabriel delivered the words, and that Muhammad, frightened, ran home to his wife Khadija, who wrapped him in blankets and calmed him.

Khadija is described in early biographies as the first person to accept the message, followed by his cousin Ali and his friend Abu Bakr. Public preaching did not begin for several years; the revelations continued intermittently for over two decades and were eventually collected as the Quran's 114 chapters, arranged roughly by length rather than the order in which they arrived.

The school trained naval engineers in navigation, fortification and shipbuilding mathematics, subjects the Ottoman military had until then largely learned from hired European specialists. Instruction leaned on translated French and Dutch textbooks, and its early staff included French and Hungarian renegades who had converted to Ottoman service.

It grew out of the same push for technical reform as the empire's new printing press and revamped artillery corps, an attempt to close a widening gap with European armies after a run of lost wars. A parallel school for army engineers followed later in the century.

Muisca goldsmiths in the highlands around Bogota worked tumbaga, an alloy of gold and copper, into flat votive figures called tunjos, showing human and animal shapes meant to be offered to the gods rather than worn or displayed. Offerings were sunk into lakes and caves considered sacred, which is why so many survived undisturbed until archaeologists and treasure hunters later recovered them.

At Lake Guatavita a new Muisca chief was reportedly coated in gold dust and poled out on a raft to the lake's centre, where he dived in to wash the gold away while attendants threw gold objects and emeralds into the water as offerings. Spanish accounts of this ceremony, heard secondhand after the conquest, gave rise to the legend of El Dorado, the gilded man, which sent later expeditions searching for a city of gold.

A lady in waiting to Empress Shoshi kept a diary of court gossip and ceremony that happens to mention, in an entry from 1008, a work already circulating among the women of the palace: a long tale about a prince named Genji. That diary is the earliest evidence the story existed at all, since Murasaki Shikibu left no manuscript of her own hand.

The finished text runs to fifty four chapters and was probably not complete until over a decade later, copied and recopied by scribes long before printing reached Japan. No original survives; every version read since comes from later transcriptions, and scholars still argue over how much of the final chapters is hers rather than a continuation by another writer.

Four knights, Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy and Richard le Breton, crossed from Normandy after hearing Henry II curse Becket's name in a fit of temper, though the king later denied ordering the killing. They found the archbishop in Canterbury Cathedral on the evening of 29 December 1170 and demanded he absolve the bishops he had excommunicated in a dispute over church versus royal authority.

When Becket refused, the knights cut him down at the altar steps; one blow, by most accounts from le Breton, was hard enough to break his sword on the stone floor. Henry did penance at Canterbury in 1174, walking barefoot and allowing monks to whip him, and Becket was declared a saint within three years, making his shrine one of medieval England's busiest pilgrimage destinations.

Zen temples in and around Kyoto kept monk painters on their rolls, men trained first in religious practice who took up the brush partly as another form of discipline. Josetsu, active in the early fifteenth century, is credited with bringing Chinese Song and Yuan ink wash techniques fully into Japanese painting, though little of his work survives with certain attribution today.

His pupil Shubun continued the style at Kyoto's Shokokuji temple, training a generation of painters in landscapes built from washes of black ink graded from pale grey to near black rather than from colour. Among Shubun's students was Sesshu Toyo, who later travelled to Ming China and carried this ink painting tradition to its furthest development later in the fifteenth century.

The gold mask Heinrich Schliemann pulled from Grave Circle A at Mycenae in November 1876 is centuries older than the war it was named for. Schliemann was convinced he had found Agamemnon himself; the shaft graves he opened actually date to around the sixteenth century BC, three or four hundred years before any plausible Trojan War.

Alongside the mask, the same graves held bronze dagger blades inlaid with silver and niello scenes of lion hunts and men in boar's tusk helmets. Painted pottery from the same period shows warriors marching out in file, spears raised, on jars found as far off as Cyprus and the Levant, evidence of how widely Mycenaean workshops traded.

Before 710, Japan's court moved with each new emperor, since a ruler's death was thought to leave the palace polluted. Empress Genmei broke that pattern by building a fixed capital at Heijo-kyo, modern Nara, laid out on a grid copied from the Tang Chinese capital Chang'an, with government ministries, markets and temples set along broad avenues.

The move let the court accumulate records rather than start each reign from nothing, and Nara produced Japan's earliest surviving chronicles, the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Buddhism, imported centuries earlier, became state-sponsored on a large scale; the wooden hall at Todai-ji temple, rebuilt since but still on its original site, once housed a bronze Buddha statue cast in the 750s.

Cahuachi covers roughly 24 square kilometres of Peru's coastal desert and holds more than forty earthen mounds, several capped with truncated adobe pyramids; the largest, the Great Pyramid, rises about 28 metres over a base some 100 metres long. Excavation found few permanent houses for a site of that size, which is why archaeologists now read it as a gathering place rather than a city.

The current reading treats Cahuachi as a pilgrimage centre, its population swelling for ceremonies and shrinking again once they ended, rather than the capital of a Nazca state once assumed from its scale. The famous ground lines nearby, cut into the desert surface as the Nazca Lines, sit within the same river valley the mounds overlook.

Bill France Sr. called the founding meeting in the bar of the Streamline Hotel on Daytona Beach in December 1947, gathering promoters and drivers to settle a problem that had wrecked earlier stock car circuits: promoters skipping town with the gate money before a race finished. Papers were signed on 21 February 1948, and the organisation's first sanctioned race ran on the Daytona beach and road course days later.

That first race was won by Red Byron, driving a modified Ford, though the results were disputed for weeks over which car classes should count. France kept tight personal control of the organisation for decades, setting rules on cars and payouts himself rather than leaving them to individual track owners as before.

Workers on the arid Nazca plateau in southern Peru scraped away the dark, sun-oxidised surface stones to expose the pale ground beneath, cutting straight lines that run for kilometres and figures of hummingbirds, monkeys and a spider, some over a hundred metres across. The dry, windless climate and stony surface have kept most of the lines readable for close to two thousand years without rain to wash them out.

Because the shapes are legible only from height, later theories reached for astronomy or extraterrestrial visitors; most archaeologists now read them as ritual paths walked on the ground, connected to water and fertility ceremonies rather than built to be seen from above. Excavated pottery and radiocarbon dates from nearby settlements place the main construction period between roughly 200 BC and AD 200.

Nazca potters painted their designs before firing rather than after, using slips of mineral pigment mixed into clay so the colours, up to a dozen shades on one vessel, fused permanently into the surface. The same coastal valleys are famous for the Nazca lines, geoglyphs scraped into the desert floor, and some of the pottery's supernatural beings, part human, part bird or feline, echo figures traced across that ground.

Double spout and bridge bottles were shaped to be carried or poured for ritual use rather than everyday eating, and many were found in graves rather than settlements, buried with the dead alongside textiles. The pottery gives archaeologists a fuller record of Nazca belief than the desert lines do, since painted scenes name plants, animals and rituals that the geoglyphs leave silent.

Today went on air on 14 January 1952 from a street level studio in New York's Rockefeller Plaza, its window deliberately left open to passers by so the outside world could be seen behind the anchor desk. NBC executive Sylvester Weaver designed the format to let viewers dip in and out over breakfast rather than sit through a fixed narrative.

Dave Garroway hosted in horn rimmed glasses and a calm, unhurried manner that became the show's signature, closing broadcasts with an upraised palm and the word peace. A chimpanzee named J. Fred Muggs joined the cast in 1953 to lift ratings, and stayed on air for five years.

On 11 February 1990, Mandela walked out of Victor Verster Prison near Paarl holding the hand of his wife Winnie, and was driven to Cape Town's Grand Parade to address a crowd that had waited most of the day. President F.W. de Klerk had lifted the ban on the African National Congress days earlier and ordered the release without conditions.

Mandela had spent his last years of confinement in a warder's cottage rather than a cell, receiving visitors and holding early talks with government officials. Four years later he stood for president in South Africa's first election open to all races, and was inaugurated in Pretoria on 10 May 1994.

Christians of the Church of the East, later called Nestorian after a bishop condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431 for describing Christ's divine and human natures as loosely joined rather than fully united, kept spreading east along the same routes that carried Persian and Sogdian merchants. Communities took root in Persia under Sassanid rule and then further along the Silk Road into Central Asia.

By the seventh century missionaries from this church had reached the Tang capital, where a stone stele erected in 781 records an earlier arrival and describes the faith to a Chinese audience in terms borrowed from Buddhist and Daoist vocabulary. Congregations also appeared among Turkic and Mongol peoples of the steppe, long before the later, better known Mongol contact with Christian Europe.

Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, objected to calling Mary Theotokos, God-bearer, arguing the title blurred Christ's divine and human natures together and that Christotokos, Christ-bearer, kept them properly distinct. Cyril of Alexandria took the objection as an attack on Christ's unity and convened bishops at Ephesus in 431 to answer it before Nestorius's own allies could arrive to defend him.

The council opened on 22 June with Nestorius absent, and 197 bishops present condemned his teaching and deposed him that same day; more subscribed once outvoted latecomers accepted the result. Churches that rejected the ruling, largely across Persia and further east, kept a distinct communion afterwards, one still commonly called Nestorian though the label simplifies a dispute over wording as much as belief.

Nirvana recorded the album in three weeks at Sound City studios in Van Nuys with producer Butch Vig, on a modest budget after signing to Geffen's DGC label. The image of a swimming baby chasing a dollar bill on a fishhook came from a documentary Kurt Cobain had seen about underwater births.

Geffen initially pressed under fifty thousand copies, expecting sales in line with the band's small punk following. Radio picked up Smells Like Teen Spirit on its own, MTV followed, and by January 1992 the record had displaced Michael Jackson's Dangerous at the top of the Billboard chart.

Orwell wrote the book on the Scottish island of Jura while seriously ill with tuberculosis, typing the final manuscript himself in bed because no one else was available and finishing it in December 1948. It was published by Secker and Warburg on 8 June 1949, seven months before his death.

The novel supplied terms still used outside fiction: Big Brother, doublethink, Room 101, and the adjective Orwellian, coined from his own name by later critics. Orwell had drafted an earlier working title, The Last Man in Europe, before his publisher persuaded him toward the sharper number.

Alfred Nobel had died in 1896, leaving most of his fortune, made from dynamite and other explosives patents, to fund annual prizes. His will named physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace, and it took nearly five years for his executors to settle the estate and set up the foundation against objections from relatives and the Swedish crown.

The first prizes were handed out on 10 December 1900 in Stockholm, the anniversary of Nobel's death, though the ceremony is usually counted as marking 1901. Wilhelm Rontgen won for physics, and the peace prize, awarded separately in Oslo, went jointly to Henry Dunant, founder of the Red Cross, and the pacifist Frederic Passy.

Sarugaku troupes performed comic skits and acrobatics for temple crowds until Kan'ami's company caught the attention of the young shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu at a performance in Kyoto in 1374. Yoshimitsu took Kan'ami's twelve year old son Zeami into his court, and that patronage let the family reshape a popular entertainment into a slower, masked drama built around chant and restrained movement.

Zeami inherited leadership of the troupe when Kan'ami died in 1384 and went on to write dozens of the plays still performed and treatises setting out how an actor should train through each stage of life. His idea of yugen, a beauty felt rather than stated outright, became central to how later performers judged whether a Noh performance had succeeded.

Nok terracotta came to notice through tin mining, not excavation. In 1943 miners on the Jos Plateau in central Nigeria turned up a clay head that was propped in a field as a scarecrow before the mine's director brought it to the British archaeologist Bernard Fagg, who recognised it as something far older than the workings that had disturbed it.

The figures, often life-size heads and full bodies with elaborate hairstyles and pierced pupils, come from sites scattered across the plateau rather than one settlement, and radiocarbon dates put the tradition's span roughly from 1500 BC to the early centuries AD. Nok furnaces also produced iron early enough, and independently enough, that the culture is treated as one of the earliest ironworking traditions in sub-Saharan Africa.

Bishop Maurice de Sully ordered the old Merovingian basilica on the Ile de la Cite demolished to raise a cathedral in the newer pointed style already tried at Saint-Denis, and construction proceeded from the choir westward over nearly two centuries. Flying buttresses, added partway through the build once cracks appeared in the choir walls, let the nave carry taller windows than earlier Romanesque churches could support.

The building was not finished until around 1345, long after Sully's death, and it was altered repeatedly afterward, including the removal of medieval stained glass during the French Revolution. A 2019 fire, caused by an electrical fault during restoration work, brought down the spire and much of the roof; the cathedral reopened for services in December 2024.

Seventeen colossal Olmec heads have been found in Mexico's Gulf lowlands, ten of them at the site of San Lorenzo. Each was cut from a single basalt boulder quarried at the Cerro Cintepec flow in the Tuxtla Mountains, some 80 kilometres from where the finished heads were finally set upright.

Moving a boulder that size without wheels or draft animals meant floating it on rafts along rivers where possible and dragging it over log rollers on land. Every head wears a fitted helmet but shows an individual face, and archaeologists read the differences between them as portraits of specific rulers rather than one generic image.

Garcia Marquez wrote the novel in an 18-month stretch in Mexico City, reportedly selling his car and household goods to cover the family's bills while he finished it. The Buenos Aires publisher Sudamericana printed the first edition in 1967 and sold out its run within days, an unusual pace for a serious Spanish-language novel at the time.

The book traces seven generations of the Buendia family in the invented town of Macondo, mixing a plague of insomnia, a rain of yellow flowers and a levitating priest with real events from Colombia's civil wars and banana-company massacres. It has since been translated into dozens of languages and is credited with bringing Latin American fiction to a mass international readership.

Jacopo Peri set Ottavio Rinuccini's text for Dafne, staged privately at the Corsi family's Florence palace during the 1598 carnival season, with singers delivering the Greek myth in a speech-like melody rather than song built for its own sake. Almost none of the music survives; only fragments and later accounts describe it.

Peri and Rinuccini repeated the experiment with Euridice in 1600, for a Medici wedding, and that score does survive complete, which is why it is often named the oldest opera anyone can still perform. Dafne came first and set the method the later work refined.

Organum began simply, a second voice shadowing the chant melody a fourth or fifth below or above, moving in step with it throughout. A ninth century treatise called Musica enchiriadis is among the earliest surviving texts to set out rules for this parallel singing, treating the added voice as a fixed interval rather than an independent melodic line.

Over the following two centuries the added voice gained its own rhythm and rise and fall, no longer bound to move in lockstep with the chant beneath it. That shift, worked out further at Notre-Dame in Paris by composers such as Leonin and Perotin, turned a single melodic line sung by a congregation into music built from two or more parts moving against each other.

John Murray printed 1,250 copies of Charles Darwin's book in November 1859, and the entire run sold out to booksellers on the first day. Darwin had delayed publishing his theory for roughly twenty years, partly from caution about the reaction, and finished the book in a rush after receiving a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace outlining strikingly similar ideas.

The book itself avoided the word evolution, and it barely touched on human origins, a gap Darwin only addressed directly in a later book, The Descent of Man, in 1871. Its full title, On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, described a mechanism, variation acted on by survival and reproduction, rather than a single moment of discovery.

Suleiman kept a court workshop, the nakkashane, staffed with painters drawn from across his empire, including artists trained in Persian and Central Asian traditions who adapted their style to Ottoman taste. They worked in teams on single manuscripts, one hand for figures, another for landscape or architecture, bound together under a single director.

Their main subject was history rather than legend: illustrated chronicles recorded specific campaigns, sieges and court ceremonies with named participants, functioning almost as an official visual record of the sultan's reign. The Suleymanname, a chronicle of Suleiman's rule finished in 1558, contains hundreds of such scenes painted flat, without shadow, in a manner distinct from the Persian models it drew on.

Ovid finished the Metamorphoses around 8 CE, a poem of roughly 12,000 lines in dactylic hexameter running from the creation of the world to the deification of Julius Caesar, strung together through some 250 stories of change: gods turning into animals, humans into trees, rivers and stars. He claimed to have left it unrevised when a separate blow fell that same year.

Augustus exiled him to Tomis on the Black Sea in 8 CE, officially over an earlier poem, the Ars Amatoria, though Ovid's own later letters hint at a cause he never named outright. He died there around 17 CE without recall, and the Metamorphoses survived only because copies had already circulated in Rome before he left.

There was no single founding charter. Teaching at Oxford grew from clerics already lecturing near the town's churches, and it expanded sharply in 1167 when Henry II, in a dispute with the French crown, barred English students from studying at Paris, sending many of them home to Oxford instead. Halls of residence under a master, the ancestors of the college system, appear in records within a few decades.

Town and gown tension turned violent in 1209, after a student was hanged for a woman's death he probably did not cause; scholars fled and some founded what became Cambridge. Oxford's earliest surviving college, University College, traces its endowment to 1249, though its buildings are far later.

Teaching at Oxford is recorded from 1096, but it grew quickly after 1167, when Henry II, in a dispute with France, barred English students from studying at Paris and sent them home. Masters organised into faculties of arts, law, medicine and theology over the following decades.

The town was not always safe for scholars: a student's killing of a woman in 1209 provoked the hanging of two other students by townspeople, and a group of masters left Oxford rather than risk further reprisals, founding a rival teaching community at Cambridge that grew into its own university.

The University of Padua began with a walkout: in 1222 a large group of students and teachers, reportedly numbering in the hundreds, left Bologna over disputes with civic authorities there and reconstituted themselves in Padua under the city's protection. Further waves of Bologna migrants joined in 1306 and again in 1322, swelling the new institution.

Padua became known especially for law, medicine and later anatomy, and its motto, granting freedom to teach and to inquire, drew scholars uneasy with tighter church oversight elsewhere. Galileo taught mathematics there from 1592, and the university's anatomical theatre, built in 1594, is the oldest surviving purpose built dissection hall in the world.

Byzantine forces under Michael VIII Palaiologos retook Constantinople from its Latin Crusader rulers in 1261, ending a period in which a Venetian backed emperor had held the city since 1204. Michael's dynasty ruled a much reduced empire, hemmed in by Ottoman advances and Latin states in Greece, yet its capital kept producing scholars, painters and manuscript copyists.

Painters working under Palaiologan patrons moved away from the stiffer poses of earlier Byzantine icons toward figures with more weight and movement, a style visible in surviving churches in Mistra and Constantinople itself, and in mosaics such as those of the Kariye Camii. Scholars in this period also recopied classical Greek texts that would later reach Italy, some carried west by refugees after Constantinople's fall in 1453.

Boniface VIII issued Unam Sanctam in November 1302 during an escalating quarrel with Philip IV of France, who had taxed French clergy without papal consent and arrested a bishop for treason. The bull's image of two swords, spiritual and temporal, both ultimately under the church's authority, was the clearest written claim any pope had made that kings answered to Rome even in worldly matters.

Philip's minister Guillaume de Nogaret answered by having the pope arrested at his summer palace in Anagni the following year; Boniface died weeks later, reportedly never recovering from the shock. His successors backed away from the bull's claims in practice, and within a decade the papacy itself had relocated to French-controlled Avignon.

A Paris salon was a private drawing room, usually a woman's, opened on a fixed evening for conversation among writers, aristocrats and visiting foreigners. The hostess set the guest list and the tone; a badly chosen remark could end an invitation, and a well-turned one could make a career.

Madame Geoffrin and later Madame du Deffand ran two of the best known rooms, where a young philosopher without rank could sit beside a duke. Manuscripts too risky to print, including material Diderot was assembling, circulated first by being read aloud there.

Paul had persecuted the early church before a reported experience on the road to Damascus turned him into one of its travelling organisers. From around 47 he set out from Antioch by ship and on foot, working through Cyprus, Asia Minor and Greece, staying long enough in each city to leave behind a small congregation before moving on.

What survives is not a diary but letters, sent back to the churches he had planted, dealing with disputes over money, conduct and doctrine as they arose. Those letters, addressed to places such as Corinth, Philippi and Thessalonica, are the earliest written Christian documents to survive, older than any of the gospels.

Pelagius, a lay teacher from Britain working in Rome, taught that people could choose to do good through will alone and did not need divine grace to overcome sin. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, argued the opposite: that Adam's fall had corrupted every human being from birth, leaving no one capable of goodness without God's help, a position he had already set out in his own account of struggling against his will.

The Council of Carthage condemned Pelagius's teaching in 418, and Rome and the eastern churches confirmed the condemnation over the following years, including at the Council of Ephesus in 431. The label Pelagianism outlived the man, attached ever since to any Christian teaching accused of understating how much grace a person needs.

Shah Tahmasp I kept royal workshops producing carpets for his palaces and as diplomatic gifts, knotted from silk and wool with dye recipes the weavers guarded. The Ardabil carpet, made for a shrine and now split between two museums, carries a woven inscription naming a court official, Maqsud of Kashan, and the Islamic year 946, corresponding to 1539 or 1540.

Designs were drawn first by court artists rather than improvised by the weavers, medallion patterns radiating from a central point across a field of vines and animals, which is why carpet design and manuscript illustration under Tahmasp share the same visual vocabulary. Finished carpets travelled west as gifts to European courts and Ottoman rivals alike.

A page from this tradition is smaller than a hand and painted with brushes fine enough to render a horse's eyelashes. Ilkhanid courts in Tabriz and Baghdad paid for copies of the Shahnameh, the Persian book of kings, and the Jami al-Tawarikh, a world history commissioned by the vizier Rashid al-Din, filling their margins with battles, feasts and court audiences.

Chinese motifs entered through Mongol trade routes: clouds rendered as ribbons, dragons coiling beside Persian horsemen. Pigment was ground from lapis lazuli and gold leaf, then bound with egg white so the colour held its brightness for centuries. Later Timurid and Safavid workshops in Herat and Tabriz built directly on these Ilkhanid manuscripts, copying their compositions into new commissions.

Pope Sixtus IV had already seen Perugino's work in the old St Peter's Basilica when he commissioned him, around 1481, to help decorate the new chapel he had built beside the Vatican Palace. The resulting fresco, roughly three metres by five and a half, shows Christ handing a pair of keys to a kneeling Peter, with the other apostles ranged on either side.

Behind the figures stands an imagined Temple of Jerusalem, rendered as a domed octagonal building flanked by two arches copied from Rome's Arch of Constantine. Perugino led a workshop of assistants on the Sistine walls alongside Ghirlandaio and Botticelli; the fresco remained in place through the later work of Michelangelo above it, whose ceiling changed the room around it completely.

Peter travelled through the Netherlands and England in 1697 and 1698 disguised as a low-ranking member of his own delegation, working in Dutch shipyards to learn carpentry and rigging first-hand. He returned determined to rebuild Russian institutions on Western European models, taxing beards and ordering nobles into short Western coats rather than traditional robes.

In 1703 he founded St Petersburg on marshland taken from Sweden at the Baltic edge of his empire, using conscripted labour under harsh conditions to drain and build it. He moved the capital there from Moscow in 1712, giving landlocked Russia a functioning window onto the Baltic and European trade.

No surviving eyewitness account describes either death; the tradition rests on later writers such as Tertullian and Eusebius, plus Clement of Rome's first-century letter, which mentions both men's suffering without giving dates or method. Church tradition, first stated clearly a century afterward, holds that Peter was crucified upside down at his own request and that Paul, as a Roman citizen, was beheaded rather than crucified.

Both deaths are usually linked to Nero's blaming of Christians for the great fire of Rome in 64, an association Tacitus records for the fire but not for either apostle. Archaeological work beneath St Peter's Basilica uncovered a first-century Roman necropolis and bones the Vatican later announced as likely Peter's, a claim resting on tradition and location rather than any inscription.
