Petrarch searched monastic libraries for manuscripts of Roman writers that had gone unread for centuries, and in 1345 he found a set of Cicero's letters at Verona that let him picture Cicero as a private man rather than only a public orator. He wrote his own letters to long dead authors, addressing Cicero and Livy directly as though they might answer him back.

He climbed Mont Ventoux in southern France in 1336 and described the view in a letter, an act later writers have pointed to for its interest in the world for its own sake rather than as a religious symbol. Crowned poet laureate in Rome in 1341, he wrote chiefly in Latin, and the vernacular love poems to a woman he called Laura became his most read work only after his death.

Petrarch dated his obsession precisely: he says he first saw Laura in the church of Santa Chiara in Avignon on Good Friday, 6 April 1327, and never approached her. He wrote over three hundred sonnets and other short poems about her over the following decades, collected as the Canzoniere, most of them exploring his own unrequited longing rather than describing her directly.

Laura's identity remains unconfirmed; she is often identified with a married noblewoman named Laura de Noves, who died of plague in 1348, an event Petrarch mourned in later poems written as if still addressing her. His sonnet form, an octave and sestet with a fixed rhyme pattern, was later adapted into the English sonnet used by Shakespeare and others.

Phoenician traders used a script of twenty-two consonant signs, with no vowels marked, inherited from earlier Canaanite writing and standardised on inscriptions such as the Ahiram sarcophagus at Byblos. Because it was compact enough for merchants to learn quickly, it travelled with Phoenician trade across the Mediterranean rather than staying confined to scribal schools.

Greek scribes adapted it by around the ninth century BC, repurposing several consonant signs that had no equivalent sound in Greek to represent vowels instead, something the Phoenician script itself never did. That Greek alphabet was later carried into Etruscan and then Latin script, so the letters used to write most of Europe's languages descend from a Phoenician trading tool.

Thomas Edison sketched the phonograph in late 1877 and had it built within days by his machinist John Kruesi, who reportedly doubted it would work at all. A stylus traced grooves into a sheet of tinfoil wrapped around a rotating cylinder, cutting a physical record of sound rather than an electrical one.

Edison tested it by reciting a few lines of Mary Had a Little Lamb into the mouthpiece and then playing them back, to Kruesi's surprise. Tinfoil recordings wore out after only a handful of playbacks, and Edison set the invention aside for nearly a decade to focus on the electric light before returning to build a sturdier wax-cylinder version.

Picasso's friend Carlos Casagemas shot himself in a Paris restaurant in February 1901 after a failed love affair, and Picasso, then nineteen, began working almost entirely in blue and blue green tones soon after. He painted Casagemas dead in his coffin and later in a mock heaven surrounded by naked women, an image he revisited more than once.

Over the next few years Picasso, then splitting his time between Barcelona and Paris, painted beggars, blind men, prostitutes and destitute mothers in the same cold palette, often elongating their limbs. The pictures sold poorly at the time; dealers found the subject matter and the colour uninviting, and Picasso's money troubles did not ease until the warmer tones of his Rose Period after 1904.

Picasso worked on the canvas through the spring of 1907 in his Montmartre studio, originally sketching a scene with two men among the women, one holding a skull, before cutting both figures. The five women are prostitutes in a Barcelona brothel on Carrer d'Avinyo, their faces borrowed partly from Iberian sculpture and from African masks Picasso had seen at a Paris ethnographic museum.

Even close friends reacted badly at first: Georges Braque reportedly said it looked as if Picasso wanted them to eat rope, and Matisse was said to be angered by it. Picasso kept the painting in his studio for years rather than showing it publicly, and it did not go on public display until 1916, under a different, less blunt title than the one he had first used.

Philipp Jakob Spener, a Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt, published Pia Desideria in 1675 as a preface to an older devotional collection, then let it circulate on its own once readers responded to it. He argued that Lutheran churches had grown correct in doctrine but cold in practice, and proposed small home gatherings where laypeople would study scripture and pray together outside the formal Sunday service.

Spener's home groups, and the personal conversion experience he expected of a genuine believer, spread through German universities and courts over the following decades, most notably at Halle, where his followers trained missionaries and ran an orphanage. Lutheran clergy who resented the movement's implied criticism of ordinary church life labelled its followers Pietists, intending it as an insult.

Disney's studio pushed multiplane camera work and character animation further than Snow White had, giving Pinocchio's puppet body a weighted, wooden feel distinct from the humans around him, and spent more per minute of film than any animated feature before it. It opened on 7 February 1940 in New York, adapted loosely from Carlo Collodi's darker 1883 Italian children's book, with much of the original's harsher punishments softened for the screen.

The film lost money on its initial release, partly because European markets closed off by the war in 1939 had been expected to cover part of its cost. Jiminy Cricket's song about wishing on a star won the Academy Award for best original song and became a recurring theme in the Disney studio's own branding for decades afterward.

Plato set up his school around 387 BC on ground outside Athens's walls named for a minor local hero, Academus, where a sacred olive grove and a gymnasium already stood. Students paid no formal fee, and the school owned no permanent building at first; teaching happened in the grove itself, in the manner of the philosophical walks Plato describes in his dialogues.

Aristotle studied there for about twenty years before founding his own school elsewhere in Athens, and the Academy kept operating under a succession of heads long after Plato's death in 347 BC, drifting through different philosophical positions over the centuries. The emperor Justinian finally closed it, along with other pagan schools, in AD 529.

The dialogue is framed as a conversation at a private house in Piraeus, Athens's port, where Socrates and several younger men debate a single question raised almost in passing: what is justice. Scholars place its composition around 380 BCE, though Plato never dated his own work and the text shows signs of having been assembled over years rather than written in one sitting.

Its most quoted passage describes prisoners chained in a cave, mistaking shadows on a wall for reality until one is dragged into daylight. Plato used the image to argue that most people never see the world as it truly is. The city he proposes to fix that problem, ruled by philosopher-kings and stripped of private families for its guardian class, was never attempted anywhere.

Benedict XVI announced his resignation in Latin before a consistory of cardinals on 11 February 2013, telling them his strength was no longer adequate to the office. He stepped down on 28 February, the first pope to resign since Gregory XII in 1415, and took the title Pope Emeritus rather than reverting to his given name, Joseph Ratzinger.

He moved into a converted monastery inside the Vatican walls, where he lived for nearly a decade under his successor Francis, elected on 13 March 2013. Benedict died there on 31 December 2022, and Francis presided over his funeral, an arrangement without precedent since no living pope had ever buried a predecessor who had voluntarily left office.

By 452 Attila's forces had already sacked Aquileia, Padua and Milan and were advancing on Rome itself, which had no army left capable of stopping them. Leo led a delegation out to meet Attila near the Mincio river, close to Mantua, rather than wait behind Rome's walls. No transcript of their conversation survives.

Attila withdrew from Italy afterward, though contemporaries also credited plague and food shortages among his own troops rather than the meeting alone. Later legend, painted by Raphael a thousand years on, added the apostles Peter and Paul appearing over Leo's shoulder with drawn swords. Whatever the cause, the retreat let Leo claim papal authority had done what Rome's soldiers could not.

The Cistercian convent of Port-Royal, reformed under its young abbess Angelique Arnauld earlier in the century, moved part of its community to Port-Royal-des-Champs outside Paris, where it drew laymen and scholars who lived nearby as solitaries rather than monastics. The convent became known for austere theology emphasising human dependence on divine grace over free will.

Blaise Pascal's sister Jacqueline was a nun there, and Pascal himself wrote in its defence after the community came under attack from Jesuit critics and, later, the crown. Louis XIV eventually had the buildings at Port-Royal-des-Champs demolished in 1709 and 1710 and the site ploughed over.

Alexander Dubcek became First Secretary of the Czechoslovak Communist Party on 5 January 1968, replacing the hardline Antonin Novotny. He loosened censorship, allowed independent clubs and reformist newspapers to operate, and floated market reforms under the slogan socialism with a human face, alarming the Soviet leadership within weeks.

On the night of 20 to 21 August 1968, roughly 200,000 Warsaw Pact troops and 2,000 tanks crossed into Czechoslovakia. Dubcek was arrested and flown to Moscow, and by April 1969 he had been removed from office. Soviet-aligned officials spent the following two decades purging reformers in a process the new leadership called normalisation.

Jane Austen's title page in 1813 gave no author, only the words By a Lady, following the same anonymity she had used for Sense and Sensibility the year before. She had sold the copyright outright to publisher Thomas Egerton for 110 pounds, so the book's early success brought her little further money however many copies sold.

Austen had drafted an earlier version called First Impressions in the 1790s, and her father had once tried to place it with a publisher who turned it down unread. She revised it over a decade before Egerton accepted it, and only close family and a few friends knew who had written the novel that opens with Mrs Bennet plotting her daughters' marriages.

Johannes Gutenberg was a goldsmith by training, working in Mainz when he adapted a wine or olive screw press to hold individually cast metal letters that could be arranged, inked and reused. He kept the process secret for years while running up debts to a financier named Johann Fust, who eventually sued him and took over the workshop and its equipment around 1455.

Gutenberg's Bible, printed in that workshop, ran to roughly 180 copies on paper and vellum, each requiring six presses working for months. Fewer than fifty copies survive today. Within decades presses using his method were operating in cities across Germany, Italy and France, cutting the cost of a book by a factor that hand copying could never match.

Wittenberg's printers turned Luther's short tracts into a mass product: his 1520 pamphlet To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation sold out its first print run of around four thousand copies within days, and further editions followed quickly. Pamphlets were cheap, short and often illustrated with woodcuts, letting readers who could not follow a Latin sermon grasp an argument from the cover alone.

Printers in other cities reprinted Luther's texts without paying him anything, spreading the same words through the German lands faster than any single press could manage alone. Church and imperial authorities tried licensing and burning offending books, but the trade was too dispersed among small workshops for either measure to choke it off.

Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar teaching theology at Wittenberg, drafted 95 propositions attacking the sale of indulgences, certificates that shortened a soul's time in purgatory. He sent them to the local archbishop and, by his later account, posted a copy on the door of Wittenberg's castle church on 31 October 1517. No copy from that day survives.

The theses were written in Latin for churchmen, but printers translated and reprinted them across German towns within weeks, helped by presses that had barely existed a century earlier. Luther was summoned to defend his views, refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, and was declared an outlaw. The split within Western Christianity that followed never healed.

Miramax paid eight million dollars for the script Quentin Tarantino wrote with Roger Avary, splitting the film into interlocking segments that play out of order, so a character shot dead midway reappears alive in a later scene set earlier. John Travolta, whose career had stalled through the 1980s, was cast as hitman Vincent Vega for a fraction of his old fee.

The film won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in May 1994, the festival's top prize, and went on to seven Academy Award nominations, winning only for its screenplay. Its soundtrack of surf rock and soul cuts, chosen largely by Tarantino from his own record collection, sold over two million copies.

The Ramones began playing CBGB, a small club on New York's Bowery, in 1974, stripping songs down to short bursts built on three chords and a fast, steady beat. Malcolm McLaren, who had managed a New York Dolls tour, took the attitude back to London and assembled the Sex Pistols around singer Johnny Rotten in 1975.

The Sex Pistols released Anarchy in the UK that November and were dropped by two record labels within months over the swearing and walkouts their television appearances provoked. Independent labels such as Stiff Records and cheap, self-financed singles let bands bypass the major studios entirely, a model that fed directly into the DIY fanzine and independent-label scenes of the following decade.

Pythagoras left Samos for the Greek colony of Croton in southern Italy, where he gathered a community that pooled property and lived under strict rules: no eating beans, no wearing wool, silence for new members for a set period before they could speak in his presence. Membership was open to women as well as men.

The group treated numbers as the hidden structure of reality, tied to music, the movements of the stars and the shape of the physical world, and it kept its findings secret from outsiders. A local uprising against Croton's ruling class eventually turned on the Pythagoreans, and Pythagoras fled to Metapontum, where he died.

The order followed a court debate over whether the Qin should be governed by ancient precedent or by the emperor's new law. His chancellor Li Si argued that scholars quoting old texts against current policy undermined the state, and the emperor agreed: officials were told to hand in the Book of Songs, the Book of Documents and the rival states' records for burning, keeping only Qin's chronicles and technical manuals on farming and medicine.

Sima Qian's later history adds that several hundred scholars were buried alive the following year, though the two episodes are recorded separately and some historians doubt the second happened as described. Copies survived in private hands and in the imperial library itself, which is why most of the condemned works were recovered once the Han replaced the Qin a few years later.

George Fox, a shoemaker's apprentice turned itinerant preacher, spent the late 1640s walking through the English Midlands arguing that anyone could receive divine guidance directly, without a priest or a church building. In 1652 he climbed Pendle Hill in Lancashire and, by his own later account, saw a vision of people gathering to this teaching, which he took as confirmation to keep preaching.

The group that formed around him refused hat honours and oaths, addressed everyone as equals, and met largely in silence waiting for someone to speak. Opponents mocked their trembling under conviction as quaking, and the nickname stuck even after the movement organised into regular meetings and began sending missionaries to Ireland, the American colonies and the Caribbean within a decade.

Elizabeth II died at Balmoral Castle on 8 September 2022, aged 96, two days after appointing Liz Truss as her fifteenth prime minister in a photograph that showed her visibly frail and leaning on a cane. Her son acceded immediately as Charles III, though his coronation did not take place until the following May.

Operation London Bridge, the plan drawn up for her death years in advance, moved her coffin from Balmoral to Edinburgh, then to London, where it lay in state in Westminster Hall. Queues to view it stretched for miles along the Thames, and her state funeral on 19 September drew heads of state and royalty from across the world to Westminster Abbey.

Victoria died at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight on 22 January 1901, with her grandson Kaiser Wilhelm II at her bedside among other family. She had worn mourning black for four decades after the death of her husband, Prince Albert, in 1861, and by 1901 she had outlived most of the politicians who had served her at the start of her reign.

Her funeral procession ran through London before her body was taken to Windsor for burial beside Albert at Frogmore. Her son Edward VII succeeded her, and the change of monarch is the usual marker historians use to close the period named after her and open the shorter Edwardian one.

By the time Uthman became caliph, Islam had spread far beyond Arabia, and reports reached him of soldiers in different garrisons reciting the Quran with different wordings. He ordered a single authoritative text drawn up from written fragments and the memories of those who had heard Muhammad recite, and had copies sent to Kufa, Basra, Damascus and Medina, with variant versions ordered destroyed.

One copy, kept in Medina, is traditionally said to be the one Uthman was reading when he was killed by mutinous soldiers in 656; a bloodstained Quran attributed to him is preserved in Tashkent, though its exact history is disputed. The Uthmanic text fixed the consonantal skeleton of the Quran; vowel marks and diacritics were added centuries later to guide pronunciation.

A doctor in Lyon writing under the anagram Alcofribas Nasier put out a sequel about a giant's son the year after his first giant book sold well at the fair. The Sorbonne's censors condemned the work for obscenity, and Rabelais kept publishing anyway, later admitting his authorship openly under his own name.

The books mix invented words, drinking songs and a fictional abbey, Theleme, whose one rule left each member to do as they wished, with real anatomy lectures and legal argument, since Rabelais had trained and practised as a physician. Later editions were repeatedly revised to answer the censors without dropping the jokes that had drawn them.

Jean Racine's Andromaque opened in Paris in 1667, telling of the Trojan widow forced to choose between her son's death and her own remarriage to the Greek king holding her captive. The play broke with the swashbuckling heroics of earlier French tragedy, keeping its violence offstage and its focus on characters trapped by desires they cannot act on directly.

Racine wrote in strict alexandrine couplets and observed the classical unities of time, place and action inherited from Aristotle, compressing whole crises into a single day and a single room. That discipline, tested first in Andromaque, became the model for the tragedies he wrote through the 1670s, including Phedre a decade later.

Tradition credits the sage Valmiki with composing the Ramayana's core story in Sanskrit verse: the exile of prince Rama, the abduction of his wife Sita by the demon king Ravana, and the war fought to recover her. By this period the poem's roughly 24,000 couplets, in seven books, had settled into the form later commentators treated as authoritative, one of the two epics that shaped Hindu literature.

The first and last books, framing Rama as a god incarnate rather than only a wronged king, are generally judged later additions to an older core narrative, traced through differences in language and style between sections. The story travelled well beyond India, producing distinct retellings in Southeast Asia including Thailand's Ramakien and Indonesia's Kakawin Ramayana.

Pope Julius II had Raphael decorate his private library, the Stanza della Segnatura, and the fresco filled one wall between 1509 and 1511. Plato and Aristotle stand at the centre beneath a coffered barrel vault, Plato pointing upward and Aristotle gesturing toward the ground, surrounded by more than fifty figures identified with ancient philosophers and mathematicians.

Raphael gave several of those figures the faces of his contemporaries: Plato is thought to resemble Leonardo, a brooding Heraclitus in the foreground resembles Michelangelo, who was at that time painting the Sistine ceiling in an adjoining part of the same palace, and Raphael placed his own face among a group at the right edge of the scene.

On 21 January 1525 a small group meeting in Zurich, including Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz, rebaptised each other as adults, rejecting infant baptism as lacking any basis in scripture. The city council, backed by the reformer Huldrych Zwingli, banned the practice within weeks and made rebaptism a capital offence.

Manz was drowned in the Limmat river in 1527 on the council's order, the first Anabaptist executed by a Protestant authority rather than a Catholic one. Persecution scattered the movement into Moravia, the Netherlands and beyond, where descendant groups including the Mennonites and Hutterites kept adult baptism and refusal of civil oaths as founding practices.

Gaius, nicknamed Caligula, little boots, for the miniature soldier's uniform he wore as a child among his father Germanicus's troops, succeeded Tiberius in March 37 to general relief; his early months brought tax cuts and the recall of exiled relatives. The surviving accounts, written decades later by Suetonius and Tacitus, describe a severe illness that same year after which his behaviour changed sharply.

What followed in those accounts includes forcing senators to run alongside his chariot, demanding worship as a living god and reportedly threatening to make his horse Incitatus a consul, though no source says the horse held the office. His guards, the Praetorians, stabbed him to death in a palace corridor in January 41, four years into a reign that had begun with the Senate voting him every honour available.

Rembrandt finished this group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company in 1642, commissioned by its captain Frans Banninck Cocq and paid for by the eighteen or so guardsmen shown in it, each contributing according to how prominent his own likeness turned out to be. Some grumbled that men who paid the same amount were pushed to the back or half hidden.

Its true subject is a company marching out by daylight; the dark varnish that built up over the following centuries gave it the nickname by which it is now known. Cut down on one side to fit a new wall in 1715, it survived a slashing attack in 1975 and hangs, restored, in the Rijksmuseum.

On 20 March 1854, around fifty-four of Ripon, Wisconsin's roughly hundred voters crowded into a small wooden schoolhouse to organise a new party opposed to the Kansas-Nebraska Act, which had just opened northern territories to slavery by popular vote. The building, built the year before, still stands and is kept as a museum.

The name Republican spread through similar meetings across the North that year, and the party held its first national convention in Pittsburgh in February 1856. Its second presidential candidate, Abraham Lincoln, won the White House in 1860, a result that several Southern states treated as grounds for secession.

Bandleader Paul Whiteman needed a headline piece for a concert billed as an experiment in modern music at New York's Aeolian Hall, and George Gershwin, reading about the plan in a newspaper, learned only then that he had apparently agreed to write it. He composed the piano part in about three weeks in January 1924, leaving the orchestration to Whiteman's arranger Ferde Grofe because there was no time left to do both.

The clarinet's opening glissando, now the piece's signature, began as a joke by clarinettist Ross Gorman during rehearsal, a slide Gershwin liked enough to keep. The 12 February 1924 concert ran long and the hall grew stuffy, but Rhapsody in Blue, placed near the end, drew the loudest response of the afternoon and Gershwin himself played the piano part.

No manuscript of the Rigveda survives from anywhere near its composition. Its 1,028 hymns, addressed to gods such as Indra and Agni, were preserved by memorisation and recitation across generations of Brahmin families, using techniques designed to catch a single dropped syllable, before they were ever written down.

The oldest surviving manuscripts date only to around the eleventh century CE, more than two thousand years after the hymns were composed. Scholars reconstruct the earlier text by comparing regional recitation traditions against each other, since a copying error in one lineage rarely matches an error in another.

Delegates from 172 governments met in Rio de Janeiro in June 1992 for the United Nations conference on environment and development, alongside a parallel gathering of non-governmental groups. It opened for signature the Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity, and adopted Agenda 21, a lengthy non-binding plan for sustainable development that member states were left to implement individually.

Neither convention set binding emissions targets; those came later, through the 1997 Kyoto Protocol negotiated under the climate treaty's own follow-up process. The United States signed the biodiversity convention but did not ratify it, a split that has persisted through subsequent American administrations of both parties.

The Ballets Russes opened the piece at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees on 29 May 1913, with choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky built around deliberately turned-in feet and stamping steps that broke every convention of classical ballet. Stravinsky's score opened with a bassoon pushed to the top of its range, and dissonant chords hit early enough to unsettle an audience expecting something closer to Tchaikovsky.

Laughter, jeering and counter-shouts from Stravinsky's supporters drowned out much of the orchestra within minutes, and the conductor Pierre Monteux kept the musicians playing through the noise. Police reportedly attended later performances, though accounts of that first night, written years afterward by people involved, disagree on how much of the chaos was theatre in itself.

Wartime factory jobs and rationing gave way to consumer spending on cars, radios and ready made clothes, while Prohibition, which banned the sale of alcohol in the United States from 1920, pushed drinking into speakeasies rather than stopping it. Women who had gained the vote in 1920 cut their hair short and wore looser dresses, a look the press labelled the flapper.

Jazz spread out of New Orleans and Chicago into dance halls and recordings heard across the Atlantic, and radio broadcasting reached ordinary households for the first time. The decade's borrowing and speculation ended abruptly with the stock market collapse of October 1929.

The figure was cast small in 1880 as one piece of a much larger commission, a bronze doorway called The Gates of Hell for a Paris museum that was never built. Rodin called the seated man The Poet and meant him for Dante, bent forward above carved circles of the damned, brooding on the poem that described them.

Foundry workers casting an early bronze started calling the figure Le Penseur, and the nickname stuck. Rodin exhibited it alone in 1888, and an enlarged version cast in 1904 stands roughly 1.8 metres tall. Dozens of authorised bronze casts exist in museums, since Rodin never treated a single cast as the unique original.

The case began as a lawsuit filed under the pseudonym Jane Roe by Norma McCorvey against Dallas County district attorney Henry Wade, challenging a Texas law that banned abortion except to save the mother's life. The Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 on 22 January 1973, finding a right to privacy under the Fourteenth Amendment that covered a woman's decision, subject to limits tied to pregnancy trimesters.

Justice Harry Blackmun wrote the majority opinion; Byron White and William Rehnquist dissented. The framework it set stood for nearly fifty years, reshaped and narrowed by later rulings such as Planned Parenthood v. Casey in 1992, until the Supreme Court overturned it outright in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization in June 2022.

Roman wall painters worked fast, laying pigment onto wet lime plaster so the colour bonded as it dried, in houses across Italy from the late Republic onward. By the first century the technique had settled into recognisable styles, from painted marble panelling to illusionistic gardens and mythological scenes filling whole rooms, in the villas of Pompeii, Herculaneum and Rome itself.

The eruption of Vesuvius in 79 buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and mud, sealing houses and their painted walls in place rather than destroying them. That accident of burial is why so much ordinary domestic painting from this period survives at all, rooms decorated for private dining and reception rather than public display.

Under the old Byzantine reckoning Russians counted years from a supposed creation of the world, and by that count it was 7208 as December 1699 ended. Peter the Great, home from touring western Europe and eager to align Russia with it, decreed on 19 December that the new year would be counted from the birth of Christ instead, and would begin on 1 January rather than 1 September.

Russians went to bed in year 7208 and woke on 1 January 1700. Peter kept the Julian calendar itself rather than switching to the Gregorian one already used in Catholic Europe, which by then ran eleven days ahead, so Russia's dates stayed out of step with the rest of Europe until the Bolsheviks changed it in 1918.

Shah Abbas I moved his capital from Qazvin to Isfahan in 1598 and rebuilt its centre around a vast new square, the Naqsh-e Jahan, ringed by a mosque, a palace and a bazaar entrance rather than left as the old city's random streets. Foreign visitors, including English and Dutch merchants seeking silk trade deals, recorded the square as one of the largest public spaces they had seen anywhere.

Abbas brought Armenian merchants from Jolfa to a new suburb of Isfahan to run the silk export trade, and craftsmen he resettled or commissioned produced the tile work, carpets and blue-domed mosques that filled the rebuilt city over the following decades. Isfahan remained the Safavid capital until the dynasty's collapse in the 1720s.

Riza Abbasi, the leading painter attached to Shah Abbas I's court, worked in Isfahan producing single-page portraits and album drawings alongside the larger workshops still illustrating manuscripts such as the Shahnameh, the Persian book of kings. Tabriz had been the earlier centre of this painting tradition before the court's move south.

Painters used fine brushwork and mineral pigments on paper to render courtiers, lovers and dervishes in profile, often with a single plant or fold of drapery carrying most of the composition's colour. European engravings reaching Persia through trade left a visible mark on later poses and shading in this school.

Shah Abbas I moved the Safavid capital to Isfahan in 1598 and built royal workshops there that wove silk, velvet and brocade for the court and for export along routes reaching Ottoman lands, India and Europe. Weavers combined figures from Persian poetry, hunting scenes and floral scrollwork into patterns run in continuous repeat across the loom.

Carpet production expanded alongside it, with knotted wool and silk pieces commissioned for mosques, palaces and foreign gifts. Silk sold abroad became a major source of state revenue under Abbas, who also granted merchants trading privileges to move Persian silk past Ottoman middlemen toward European buyers.

Patrick's own account, the Confessio, says Irish raiders seized him from Britain at sixteen and held him as a slave for six years, herding sheep on the slopes of Slemish in what is now County Antrim before he escaped and reached home. He returned to Ireland afterwards not as a captive but as a bishop, a decision he presents in his own writing as an answer to visions rather than a plan of his own devising.

Almost everything told about Patrick beyond his two surviving letters, driving snakes from Ireland, explaining the Trinity with a shamrock, comes from biographies written centuries later and cannot be checked against anything he wrote himself. The Confessio and the Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus remain the only text from his own hand, and neither mentions a snake.

Alfonso IX of Leon issued the charter for a studium generale at Salamanca in 1218, but the institution he founded taught few subjects and left little documentary trace for its first decades. Its real expansion came under his grandson Alfonso X, who around 1254 endowed named chairs in canon law, grammar, arts and medicine, the point from which continuous teaching records survive.

That same year Pope Alexander IV placed Salamanca alongside Paris, Bologna and Oxford as one of four institutions holding the status of a general school, meaning a degree earned there was recognised across Latin Christendom. The university still occupies its old quarter of the city, and its plateresque facade, carved later, remains a landmark in Salamanca.

William and Catherine Booth began preaching to the poor of London's East End in July 1865 under the name East London Christian Mission, offering soup and shelter alongside sermons in tents and rented halls. Booth had left the Methodist ministry two years earlier, unwilling to be posted away from the itinerant street preaching he preferred.

The mission became the Salvation Army only in 1878, and the name arrived almost by accident: a secretary drafting an annual report described the group as a volunteer army, and Booth crossed out volunteer and wrote in Salvation. He restructured it on military lines afterwards, taking the title of General and issuing ranks and uniforms to his preachers.

By 1200 Samarkand stood on the branch of the Silk Road linking Persia to China, and its madrasas taught grammar, law and the Quran alongside astronomy and mathematics, subjects that in this period were not separated from religious study. Students boarded in cells built around a central courtyard, a layout that let one endowed institution house teaching, prayer and lodging together.

The city's schools drew scholars from across Transoxiana and further afield, supported by waqf endowments, property set aside permanently to fund teachers' salaries and student stipends. Much of what stood in 1200 was later destroyed when Genghis Khan's army took the city in 1220, and the madrasas visible in Samarkand today were rebuilt afterward under Timurid patronage.

Timur rebuilt Samarkand as his capital using craftsmen and materials brought back from conquered cities in Persia, Syria and India, so that the buildings going up combined techniques from lands his armies had passed through. Construction of the Bibi Khanym mosque began after his 1399 campaign in India and was nearly complete by 1404, when he returned from another campaign to see it.

Timur is buried in the Gur e Amir mausoleum, its ribbed turquoise dome one of the few structures from his reign to survive largely intact. Craftsmen he settled in Samarkand trained successors who carried the same tile work and brickwork techniques into Timurid building projects across Iran and Central Asia over the following century.

Timur brought captured architects, astronomers and craftsmen back to Samarkand from campaigns in Persia, Syria and India, and it was this forced concentration of skilled people, more than any single decree, that filled the city's new madrasas with teachers. His grandson Ulugh Beg, who governed Samarkand and later ruled as sultan, built an observatory there in the 1420s and compiled a star catalogue used by astronomers well beyond Central Asia.

Ulugh Beg's own madrasa on the Registan square, built between 1417 and 1420, taught mathematics and astronomy alongside religious law, an unusual pairing for the time. His most famous pupil there, the astronomer Ali Qushchi, carried that training on to the Ottoman court in Istanbul after Ulugh Beg's death.

Sogdian Samarkand sat on the trade route linking Persia to China, and its merchants carried Zoroastrian worship east along with their goods, building fire temples where a permanently tended flame stood at the centre of ritual rather than an image of a god. Excavated foundations at Samarkand show a raised platform for the fire, kept apart from the outer walls to protect it from wind.

Sogdian Zoroastrianism absorbed local ancestor cults and outside influences, so the temples of Samarkand were not identical to those of Persia itself. Arab armies took the city in the early eighth century, and Sogdian religious practice faded over the following generations as Islam spread through Central Asia.

San Lorenzo sits on an artificial plateau raised above the Coatzacoalcos river floodplain in what is now Veracruz, Mexico. Its builders carved at least ten colossal basalt heads, each several tonnes, from stone quarried in the Tuxtla mountains some 60 kilometres away and moved without wheels or draft animals, almost certainly by raft along the river system.

Excavations have also uncovered stone drains built to carry water away from the plateau's summit, among the earliest engineered drainage known in the Americas. San Lorenzo's dominance ended around 900 BC, when the site was abandoned and many of its monuments were deliberately defaced and buried, for reasons archaeologists still debate.

Sappho's poems were written to be sung to a lyre on Lesbos, addressed to named women and to the goddess Aphrodite, in a metre later generations called sapphic after her. Ancient critics ranked her among the greatest lyric poets, and her portrait appeared on coins from Lesbos centuries after her death.

Almost none of it survives whole. Alexandrian librarians catalogued nine papyrus rolls of her verse, but only one complete poem and a few hundred fragmentary lines reached the modern era, quoted by later grammarians or recovered from torn papyrus scraps found in Egypt. New fragments have surfaced as recently as the last decade, pieced together from previously unpublished papyrus.

Schiller wrote his first play while still a medical officer bound to a Wurttemberg regiment, and had it printed anonymously and at his own expense because he expected trouble. Its story of two feuding brothers, one an outlaw leading a robber band, was staged in Mannheim with the action moved earlier in time to soften its politics.

Duke Karl Eugen, unhappy that a serving officer had written something so inflammatory, forbade Schiller from publishing further and threatened him with arrest. Schiller fled the dukedom on foot at night, and the play that got him into trouble became the founding text of Sturm und Drang theatre.

Peter Abelard taught in Paris by setting apparently contradictory statements from scripture and the church fathers side by side and forcing students to reconcile them through logical argument, a method he collected in a book whose title translates as Yes and No. Crowds of students followed him from teacher to teacher before he began lecturing independently near Notre Dame.

His affair with his student Heloise ended in his castration by her uncle's men and both entering religious life separately, a scandal that did not end his teaching career. Their surviving letters, alongside his logical method, kept his name current among later scholastics even after church councils twice condemned specific propositions from his theological writing as heretical.

In 1822 Franz Schubert wrote out a full first movement and a second movement of a symphony in B minor, sketched a few bars of a scherzo, and then stopped. He gave the manuscript to a friend, Anselm Huttenbrenner, apparently as thanks for an honorary diploma from a music society in Graz, and never returned to finish the piece.

The manuscript sat unplayed for over forty years. Huttenbrenner did not show it to anyone until 1865, when a conductor named Johann Herbeck finally persuaded him to hand it over, and it was performed in Vienna that December, decades after Schubert's death in 1828. No later movements or sketches have ever surfaced to explain why he abandoned it.

John Knox returned to Scotland in 1559 after years of exile in Geneva under John Calvin, and preached to crowds that broke into open rioting against friaries and church images. The Scottish Parliament met in August 1560 and voted to abolish papal authority in Scotland and forbid the Catholic mass, without waiting for the young queen, Mary, then still in France, to agree.

Knox and five colleagues drafted the Scots Confession and a Book of Discipline setting out a Presbyterian church run by ministers and elected elders rather than bishops. Mary returned the following year to a country already legally Protestant, and the settlement Knox had pushed through survived her own eventual deposition.

Herodotus describes Scythian kings buried with a strangled concubine, a cupbearer, a cook and horses, all placed in a deep pit before earth was piled over them, and he adds that every subject rode past afterwards to cut off a piece of his own ear in mourning. Excavated kurgans across the steppe from the Black Sea to the Altai confirm the horse burials and the gold ornament, if not every detail of his account.

Permafrost preserved what soil elsewhere destroys. At Pazyryk in the Altai mountains, kurgans excavated by Sergei Rudenko in the late 1940s held felt saddle covers, carved wooden ornaments, textiles and tattooed human skin frozen intact for over two thousand years, giving Scythian burial practice a level of physical detail Herodotus could only describe in words.

Sei Shonagon served Empress Teishi at the Heian court and finished her book around 1002, mixing diary entries, character sketches of courtiers and blunt opinion pieces with numbered lists titled things like elegant things or things that give an unpleasant feeling. Nothing in it was written for eyes beyond the court, which is part of why its tone stays so unguarded.

She kept a running rivalry, on the page at least, with Murasaki Shikibu, author of The Tale of Genji, who accused her in her own diary of showing off her Chinese learning. The book survives in several manuscript lines that disagree on the order and even the wording of individual entries, since no autograph copy has come down to the present.

Korean scholars had written their spoken language using borrowed Chinese characters, a system that fit Korean grammar poorly and took years to master. King Sejong's court finished a new script around 1443 or early 1444, but rather than issue it at once he had it tested and explained for three more years before making it public.

The explanatory document, Hunminjeongeum, was published in 1446 and gave each letter a shape meant to mirror the mouth or tongue position used to say it. Yangban officials who had spent years learning Chinese characters resisted a script they thought beneath serious writing, and Hangul was pushed to the margins of Korean literacy for centuries before its twentieth century revival.

Seljuk potters in Anatolia and Iran developed a turquoise glaze fired onto star- and cross-shaped tiles that locked together edge to edge to cover a wall or dome without a single continuous painted surface. Only the visible face carried glaze, over a cheap unglazed backing cut to shape, which kept material and cost down.

The clearest surviving example is the tilework from the Seljuk summer palace at Kubadabad on Lake Beysehir, built in the 1220s and excavated in the twentieth century, where figural tiles of animals and courtly riders sit alongside the plain geometric star tiles that lined mosques and madrasas from Konya to Isfahan.

Around 300 people crowded into the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, over two days in July 1848, most of them women who had travelled from nearby towns after seeing a five-day notice in the local paper. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott had organised it partly out of frustration at being barred from speaking on the floor of an anti-slavery convention in London eight years earlier.

Stanton read out a Declaration of Sentiments modelled on the Declaration of Independence, listing grievances against laws that gave husbands control of a wife's property, wages and children. Of the resolutions put to a vote, only the call for women's suffrage passed by a narrow margin, and it did so mainly because Frederick Douglass, one of the few men present, spoke in its favour.

Work on the grotto began under Kim Daeseong, a chief minister of the Silla kingdom, and was completed by the court in 774, shortly after his death, as part of the same building programme that produced the nearby Bulguksa temple. It is not a natural cave: the chamber is built from cut granite blocks assembled to form a domed ceiling, then covered over with earth.

At its centre sits a granite Buddha 3.45 metres high, seated with one hand touching the earth in the gesture associated with his enlightenment, facing an entrance aligned toward the sea. Smaller carved figures, bodhisattvas and disciples, line the surrounding walls. The site suffered damp and looting attempts under Japanese colonial rule before later restoration work sealed the dome.

Seoul hosted the Summer Games from 17 September to 2 October 1988, the first Olympics with no major boycott since 1972, drawing 159 nations after Cuba and a small group of allied states stayed away over North Korea being denied a co-hosting role. Ben Johnson's 100 metres win was stripped days later after he tested positive for stanozolol, handing the gold to Carl Lewis.

South Korea had been under military-backed rule for much of the preceding decade, and preparing the Games coincided with mass pro-democracy protests through 1987 that forced direct presidential elections that December. The government used the Olympics to present a rebuilt, industrialised capital to a global television audience, a deliberate contrast with the war-damaged city of the 1950s.

Villages on the Sepik River in northern Papua New Guinea carved wooden ancestor and spirit figures, shields and canoe prows, finished with white lime, red ochre and black soot rather than imported paint. Large ceremonial spirit houses, called haus tambaran, held carvings used in male initiation rites and stored a village's ritual objects between ceremonies.

Because the river and its swamps kept villages isolated from one another, carving styles differ sharply within short distances, a variety that drew early twentieth century collectors and museums, including Germany's Linden Museum, which acquired large Sepik holdings before the First World War disrupted colonial trade routes.

The Children's Television Workshop, founded by Joan Ganz Cooney and Lloyd Morrisett, aired the first episode on National Educational Television on 10 November 1969. Researchers had tested early footage on groups of preschoolers, timing how long their attention held on each segment, and cut or reworked whatever failed to hold it.

Jim Henson's puppets, including Big Bird, Oscar the Grouch and Bert and Ernie, shared the fictional New York street with human cast members, letting the show teach letters, numbers and social lessons inside something closer to a sitcom than a classroom film. The format spread to dozens of countries, each producing its own local version with new characters alongside familiar ones.

No birth certificate survives for William Shakespeare. What exists is a parish register entry at Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon recording his baptism on 26 April 1564, and tradition, not record, puts his birth three days earlier on 23 April, which also became the date of his death in 1616.

His father John was a glover and local alderman; his mother Mary Arden came from a landowning family nearby. Stratford's grammar school, which took the sons of burgesses free of charge, is the likeliest place he learned the Latin that runs through his later plays, though no school record naming him has ever turned up.

By 1592 a dying rival playwright, Robert Greene, was warning fellow university-educated writers about an actor turned author, calling him an upstart crow dressed in borrowed feathers. It is the earliest surviving mention of Shakespeare in print, and it confirms he was already writing for London stages by his late twenties.

The Comedy of Errors, built on mistaken identity between two sets of twins, and the three parts of Henry VI belong to this early stretch, before the London theatres closed for roughly two years when plague deaths in the city climbed sharply from 1592.

Shakespeare based Hamlet on an old Danish revenge story already known on the London stage in an earlier, now-lost play scholars call the Ur-Hamlet. He wrote his version around 1600 for the Lord Chamberlain's Men, the company he had shares in, to perform at the Globe on the south bank of the Thames.

Three early printed texts of the play survive, and they disagree with each other: a short, garbled 1603 quarto, a longer 1604 quarto, and the version in the 1623 First Folio, assembled by his fellow actors after his death. Editors still argue over which cuts and additions were his and which were the printer's or the players'.

Hamlet reworked an older revenge play, now lost, that scholars call the Ur-Hamlet, turning a straightforward plot of murder and vengeance into a prince who delays and doubts at every turn. Richard Burbage, the leading actor of Shakespeare's company, is thought to have taken the role at the Globe on the south bank of the Thames.

Othello, staged at court before King James in 1604, cast a Venetian general as the outsider destroyed by a subordinate's manufactured evidence of his wife's infidelity. Across this run of plays Shakespeare kept returning to a hero brought down less by an outside enemy than by his own judgement.

The publisher Thomas Thorpe brought out the 1609 quarto with a dedication to a mysterious Mr. W.H., whom he called the only begetter of these ensuing sonnets, a phrase that has never been settled to anyone's satisfaction. It is not known whether Shakespeare approved the printing or whether Thorpe worked from a manuscript that had circulated without him.

Most of the sequence addresses a young man, urging him toward marriage and children and later working through jealousy and betrayal, before a smaller final group turns to a woman later readers nicknamed the Dark Lady. Scholars still argue over whether any of it describes real people or events.

What survives is not a foundation charter but a pit of cracked bones. Diviners at the Shang capital near modern Anyang scorched ox scapulae and turtle shells, then scratched questions and answers into the cracks about harvests, illness and royal ancestors, giving the earliest confirmed Chinese writing.

Bronze foundries cast ritual vessels heavy enough that some exceed 800 kilograms, made in sectioned clay moulds rather than by lost wax casting. Because the oracle bones name kings who match later chronicles, the Shang became China's first dynasty for which archaeology, rather than tradition alone, supports the record.

Nanak was born in 1469 in the village of Talwandi, in Punjab, to a Hindu family of the merchant caste, and worked for years as a village storekeeper. Tradition holds that around 1499, after bathing in a local river, he emerged with a message that there was no Hindu and no Muslim, only one God, and began travelling to preach it.

He is said to have journeyed for two decades before settling at Kartarpur, where a community gathered to farm, sing hymns and eat together at a shared kitchen regardless of caste. Those hymns, later collected with those of his successors, became the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture that Sikhs treat as their living Guru.

Rachel Carson, a former US Fish and Wildlife Service biologist, spent four years compiling scientific studies on DDT and other pesticides before the book appeared in September 1962, after serialisation in the New Yorker that summer drew attacks from chemical manufacturers. She opened with a fictional town whose birds had died silent, then spent the rest of the book building the case with documented studies.

Velsicol Chemical Company threatened her publisher with a lawsuit before release, and several scientists funded by the chemical industry publicly dismissed her work. President Kennedy ordered his Science Advisory Committee to review her claims; its 1963 report largely supported them, and DDT was banned for most US uses in 1972.

Chinese silk moved west along overland caravan routes through Central Asia, changing hands at oasis markets in Kushan and Parthian territory before reaching Roman buyers, who paid such high prices for it that Pliny the Elder complained the trade drained the empire's gold. No single merchant travelled the whole route from China to Rome; goods and techniques passed through a chain of regional traders, each covering one stretch.

Along the same roads travelled dyeing methods, weaving patterns and eventually the silkworm's cultivation itself, which China guarded closely for centuries before the knowledge spread west. Wool and linen textiles moved the other direction into Central Asia, so the exchange carried craft knowledge in both directions rather than silk flowing only one way.

Simone Martini painted his Annunciation with his brother in law Lippo Memmi for the chapel of Saint Ansanus in Siena Cathedral, signing and dating it on the frame itself. The angel Gabriel's words to Mary are picked out in raised gold letters running from his mouth across the panel, a device that lets the viewer read the greeting rather than simply see it delivered.

Mary draws back from the angel, her body curving away in a posture painters after Martini kept copying for their own Annunciation scenes. Gold leaf covers the background instead of any landscape, and the drapery folds in sharp curling lines rather than the rounded volumes Giotto had been giving his figures in Florence and Padua only a few years earlier.

The Slavery Abolition Act received royal assent in August 1833 and took effect the following year, but it did not free anyone outright. Most enslaved people over six were reclassified as apprentices bound to their former owners for years more, a term set at six years for field labourers and shortened after protests to four.

Parliament voted 20 million pounds in compensation, paid not to the enslaved but to the roughly 46,000 British slave owners for the loss of their property. The debt raised to fund it was so large that the British government did not finish repaying it until 2015. The Act also excluded India and territories held by the East India Company.

The 13th Amendment passed Congress in January 1865 after Lincoln pushed hard for a House vote he had previously seen fail, and it was ratified by the required three-quarters of states by December, months after his assassination. His own Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 had freed enslaved people only in Confederate territory, leaving slavery legal in border states that stayed in the Union.

Mississippi did not ratify the amendment at all until 1995, and even then a clerical error meant the ratification was not formally sent to the federal register until 2013. The amendment's second clause, barring slavery except as punishment for crime, has since been cited in debates over prison labour.

Zhou Dunyi, an eleventh century Song official, wrote a short diagram-based text explaining how the cosmos unfolded from a single ultimate principle through the interaction of yin and yang, language closer to Daoist cosmology than to the older Confucian classics. He held minor provincial posts rather than high office, and his influence spread mainly through students who taught after him.

Later Song thinkers, particularly Zhu Xi in the twelfth century, built on this cosmological framework while insisting their ideas simply restored the original meaning of Confucius and Mencius against centuries of Buddhist and Daoist influence. Zhu Xi's commentaries on the Confucian classics became the fixed syllabus for China's civil service examinations from the fourteenth century onward.

Sunni Ali took the Songhai throne in 1464 from a base at Gao on the Niger River and spent much of his thirty-year reign at war, seizing Timbuktu from Tuareg control in 1468 and taking the trading city of Djenne after a long siege. Both had been centres of Mali's fading empire.

He governed with a fleet of war canoes on the Niger to move troops and supplies between the two flood plains bordering his territory, an approach suited to a state stretched thinly along a river rather than a compact heartland. Songhai outgrew Mali within his lifetime, though the ruling line he founded did not survive his own son's usurpation in 1493.

Askia Muhammad, who seized the Songhai throne in 1493, made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496 with 500 horsemen and 1000 infantry, and returned with the titles of al-hajj and khalifa, using that new prestige to patronise judges and teachers back in his own territory. Grants of land and tax exemption drew jurists and copyists to settle around Timbuktu's mosques.

Under his rule and that of his successors, qadis were appointed to apply Islamic law in the empire's cities while older customary practice continued in the countryside, a split authority that generated decades of correspondence and legal opinion. Much of that record survives only because families in Timbuktu kept private manuscript collections rather than a single royal archive.

The Sankore mosque had stood in Timbuktu for close to two centuries before Songhai rule turned its quarter into a centre of study. There was no single chartered body: independent scholars taught law, theology, mathematics and astronomy in their own houses and courtyards, and students travelled from as far as Cairo and Fez to sit with them.

What survives is the paper trail. Tens of thousands of manuscripts, in Arabic and in Songhai written in Arabic script, were copied, bought and passed down through Timbuktu's private libraries, covering contracts and correspondence as much as scripture. Many were later hidden in family collections to keep them out of reach of raiders and colonial seizure.

No record fixes the date Oedipus Rex was first staged; scholars place it around 429 BC from internal clues, including a plague scene that may echo the epidemic then striking Athens during the Peloponnesian War. The play opens with that plague already ravaging Thebes, sent, an oracle says, because the city harbours its own king's father's killer unpunished.

Sophocles builds the whole plot from information the audience already has: everyone watching knew Oedipus had killed his father and married his mother before the play began. The suspense sits entirely in watching Oedipus piece together, testimony by testimony, what the audience was told at the door, ending in his self-blinding rather than his death.

Calderon took up the leading position in Spanish theatre after Lope de Vega's death in 1635, the same year he published Life Is a Dream, in which a prince raised in a tower is briefly freed to test whether he can rule himself before being returned to captivity. The play turns repeatedly on how a person can trust what they perceive as real.

Calderon also wrote autos sacramentales, short allegorical plays performed on wagons through city streets for the feast of Corpus Christi, work he kept producing after he was ordained a priest in 1651 and largely left the commercial stage behind.

Pope Sixtus IV issued the bull authorising the tribunal in November 1478, but Ferdinand and Isabella controlled its appointments, not Rome. That put the inquisitors under the crown rather than the church, a break from earlier medieval inquisitions run by bishops and friars answering upward to the papacy.

Its earliest targets were conversos, Jews who had converted to Christianity, suspected of secretly keeping their old faith. Seville's tribunal opened in 1481 and burned dozens within its first year. The institution outlasted the monarchs who founded it by centuries, and was not formally abolished until 1834.

Tribunals across Spain in the mid sixteenth century widened their attention from converted Jews and Muslims to include Protestants and anyone owning banned books. Suspects could be denounced anonymously, and confiscation of a convicted person's property funded the tribunal that convicted them, a standing incentive that inquisitors themselves were occasionally accused of abusing.

An auto de fe, a public sentencing ceremony, could involve hundreds of onlookers and end in penance, imprisonment, or death by burning for those who refused to recant. Valladolid held a large auto de fe in 1559 against a Protestant cell that had included members of the court, and the Inquisition kept written records of confessions that historians still use to study the period.

Edmund Spenser brought the first three books of his poem to London in 1590 and had them printed with a dedication to the Queen, who granted him a modest yearly pension for it. Each book follows a knight, such as the Redcrosse Knight or Britomart, on a quest that doubles as a moral lesson about a single virtue.

Spenser wrote most of it in Ireland, where he held land confiscated after English suppression of rebellion, and the poem was left unfinished at six of a planned twelve books when he died in 1599. Its stanza form, nine lines ending in an alexandrine, still carries his name.

Baruch Spinoza finished the Ethics by 1675 but held it back after friends warned that its arguments, which identified God with nature itself and denied a personal creator who intervenes in the world, would bring prosecution. Friends published it in Latin within months of his death in 1677, alongside his unfinished political writings.

The book is written as a sequence of geometric proofs, borrowing the format of Euclid, with definitions and axioms leading step by step to propositions about the mind and the passions. Dutch Reformed authorities banned it soon after publication, and it circulated for decades chiefly among a small circle of readers willing to risk the label of atheist.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, recognised by Twelver Shia as the twelfth imam, was said to have been born around 870 and to have vanished from public view soon after his father's death in 874. Twelver tradition holds he did not die but entered a state of concealment, guided at first through a line of deputies in what is called the Lesser Occultation.

That period ended in 941, when the last deputy died without naming a successor, opening the Greater Occultation that Twelver Shia hold continues still. The belief left no visible imam to obey, so religious authority passed instead to scholars interpreting his guidance, a structure that still separates Twelver practice from Sunni Islam's reliance on caliphs and consensus.

Mecca surrendered to Muhammad in January 630 with almost no fighting, after the Quraysh's ten-year truce with Medina broke down. He entered the Kaaba and had its idols removed, then let most of the city's Meccans keep their property and status rather than punishing them as a conquered population.

Word of the surrender brought delegations from tribes across Arabia to Medina to submit and accept Islam over the following two years, a process later Muslim sources call the Year of Deputations. By the time Muhammad died in 632, most of the peninsula's tribes had aligned with Medina, though several broke away again immediately afterward and had to be brought back by force.

Stalin collapsed at his dacha outside Moscow on 1 March 1953 and lay untreated for hours because his guards were afraid to enter his room uninvited. He died four days later, on 5 March, with members of the Politburo, including Khrushchev and Beria, gathered at his bedside.

His funeral drew crowds so large that a crush on Moscow's streets killed an unknown number of people, estimated in the hundreds. Within three years his successor Khrushchev denounced his purges and cult of personality in a closed speech to the party congress, opening a limited political thaw.

Twentieth Century Fox opened the film on just 32 screens in the United States on 25 May 1977 after several studios had turned it down as an unmarketable science-fiction script. Industrial Light and Magic, a special-effects house George Lucas set up specifically for the production, built its motion-control camera rigs largely from scratch to shoot the model spacecraft.

Lines stretched around city blocks within days, and the film held the domestic box-office record for over two decades until Titanic passed it in the late 1990s. Lucas had negotiated to keep merchandising and sequel rights, an arrangement Fox agreed to as a minor concession that later made the Star Wars toy and licensing business worth far more than the ticket sales.

Police raided the Stonewall Inn on Christopher Street in Greenwich Village shortly after 1am on 28 June 1969, a routine tactic against unlicensed gay bars. This time patrons and bystanders refused to disperse quietly, throwing coins, bottles and a parking meter as officers barricaded themselves inside the bar awaiting reinforcements.

Crowds returned to the street on several of the following nights, and the confrontations drew in activists including Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera, both later credited as early organisers of gay liberation groups. The following June, marches in New York, Los Angeles and Chicago marked the first anniversary, a pattern that grew into the annual Pride marches held in cities worldwide.

Su Shi held government posts, was exiled more than once for his politics, and still found time to argue that a painting by a scholar was worth more for what it revealed of his character than for how closely it copied nature. He compared painting to poetry, saying a work judged only on likeness showed the judgement of a child.

Around his circle in the 1080s, scholar officials traded ink bamboo and rock paintings as informal gifts rather than commissioned works, signing and inscribing them with poems the way they signed letters. That habit of amateur, personal painting among the educated class became the model later critics called literati painting, distinct from the professional court workshops.

Kilns around Sukhothai and the nearby town of Si Satchanalai fired grey stoneware under a pale celadon glaze, decorated with fish, chrysanthemums and scrollwork painted in iron black under the glaze rather than carved into it. Archaeologists have identified hundreds of kiln sites clustered along the Yom river, suggesting production on a scale meant for export as much as local use.

Divers and archaeologists have recovered Sukhothai wares from shipwrecks scattered across the South China Sea and as far as the Philippines and Indonesia, evidence that the pottery travelled the same maritime routes as spices and cloth. The kilns' output declined as Vietnamese and Chinese ceramics came to dominate those same export markets in later centuries.

A stone stele found at Sukhothai and dated by its own text to 1283 claims that King Ramkhamhaeng devised the Thai script that year, adapting Khmer letterforms and adding marks for tones that Khmer did not need. The stone carries 124 lines across four faces and was not rediscovered until 1833, when the future King Mongkut found it among the ruins.

Scholars have argued for decades over whether the stele is genuinely from Ramkhamhaeng's reign or a later composition, and electron microscopy of the stone's surface has not settled the dispute completely. Whatever its exact date, the script it records, built on consonant and vowel signs derived from Khmer and ultimately from Indian Brahmi writing, is the direct ancestor of the Thai alphabet used today.

England's 1363 statute set out, rank by rank, who could wear what: labourers were limited to cloth costing no more than a set price per yard, while knights and merchants above a certain income were allowed furs and silks denied to those below them. The stated aim was to stop people dressing above their station, but the laws also tried to keep money from leaving the country on imported cloth.

The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 had killed a large share of Europe's population and left survivors, particularly labourers, with more bargaining power and often more money than before, since fewer people now held the same land and jobs. Rulers in England, France and Italian cities responded with rules on dress precisely because clothing had become one of the few visible ways a labourer could now look like his social better.

Andre Breton had trained as a medical orderly treating shell-shocked soldiers, and it was there he first tried automatic writing, letting a pen move without conscious control. His 1924 manifesto turned that wartime technique into a programme, defining surrealism as pure psychic automatism meant to bypass reason and release material Breton believed reason kept locked away.

The text split a circle of poets Breton had gathered around the earlier, short-lived Dada journal Litterature, and several, including Louis Aragon and Philippe Soupault, signed on to the new movement while others walked away from Breton's increasingly strict rulings on who counted as a true surrealist. He kept revising and expelling members from the group for decades afterward, treating the label almost like a party membership card.

Basil Brown, a local excavator without formal training, opened the mound at Sutton Hoo in 1939 and found the rotted outline of an oak ship over 27 metres long, its shape preserved only as a stain in the sand and a pattern of iron rivets. No body was ever recovered; acidic soil had dissolved it entirely, leaving archaeologists to work out the burial from grave goods alone.

Those goods included a helmet with a face mask, a shield, gold buckles inlaid with garnet, silver bowls from the Byzantine world and coins that helped date the burial to the early seventh century. Historians debate who lay in the ship, most often naming Raedwald, a king of East Anglia known to Bede as a ruler who kept both Christian and pagan altars in his household.

King Oswiu of Northumbria called the meeting because his own household kept two calendars: he observed Easter by the Celtic reckoning brought from Iona, his queen by the Roman one, so the royal court sometimes feasted and fasted on different days in the same year. Bishop Wilfrid argued Rome's case at the abbey Hild had built at Whitby; the Celtic side was led by Bishop Colman of Lindisfarne.

Oswiu ruled for Rome after Wilfrid argued that Saint Peter held the keys to heaven, reasoning that offending the gatekeeper seemed unwise. Colman resigned his see and withdrew to Iona and then Ireland rather than accept the ruling, taking a group of monks with him, while Northumbria's church realigned its calendar and practice with the rest of Latin Christendom.

Tacitus began the Histories after holding a consulship under Nerva, drawing on his own memory of the year 69, when four men in succession claimed the imperial throne, and on the accounts of officials he had known personally. He planned the work to run from Galba's accession up to the death of Domitian, the reign under which Tacitus himself had served in the Senate.

Only the first four books and part of a fifth survive, covering roughly a year and a half out of the decades he intended; the rest was lost sometime in the manuscript tradition of late antiquity. What remains is blunt about the emperors it covers, treating the throne as a prize seized by whichever army paid its soldiers first.

Taino communities across the Caribbean inhaled a snuff called cohoba, ground from the seeds of a Anadenanthera tree, through carved wooden or bone tubes shaped like forked animal snouts. Spanish chroniclers who watched the ritual in the decades after 1492 described caciques and shamans, called behiques, snorting the powder until they fell into trances they took as visits from spirit beings called cemis.

Surviving cemi figures are carved from wood, stone, shell and cotton, some with hollowed backs meant to hold the cohoba powder itself before it was inhaled. The behique who led a ceremony was expected to report what the cemi had said, on matters from illness to whether a coming harvest or raid would go well, and his standing depended on being believed.

Takshashila, near modern Rawalpindi, drew students from across northern India to study under individual named teachers rather than a single enrolled institution with a shared curriculum; subjects taught there are said to have ranged from medicine and law to archery and the interpretation of omens. Buddhist texts describe monks travelling there for advanced study alongside students preparing for secular careers.

Later tradition links the city to the grammarian Panini and to Chanakya, adviser to the first Mauryan emperor, though neither connection rests on a document contemporary with either man. Alexander's campaign reached Takshashila in 326 BC, and the Greek and Indian accounts of that encounter are among the earliest outside references to the city's standing as a place of learning.

By the mid eighth century Chang'an's population is estimated near a million inside its walls, with a comparable number in the surrounding metropolitan region, making it among the largest cities anywhere in the world at the time. Its western market drew Sogdian caravan traders, Persian merchants and Nestorian Christian clergy alongside Buddhist monks and Confucian officials.

The city's grid, 108 walled wards south of an imperial palace complex, was copied directly for the layout of Heian-kyo, the new Japanese capital founded in 794. Chang'an's peak did not last: the An Lushan rebellion beginning in 755 emptied much of the city and the dynasty never fully recovered its earlier reach.

Chang'an was laid out on a grid nearly ten kilometres across, with the palace at the north and 108 walled wards fanning south, each closed by gates at dusk. A foreign merchant needed a travel permit to move between wards after dark, and the western market held Sogdian traders, Persian silversmiths and a Zoroastrian fire temple among its stalls.

Population estimates for the eighth century run close to a million within the walls, with a similar number in the surrounding region, figures that made the city a byword for scale among later Chinese and Japanese planners, who copied its grid for Heian-kyo. Little of the Tang city survives above ground; modern Xi'an occupies part of the same site.

The Complete Tang Poems, compiled centuries later under the Qing, gathers roughly 48,900 poems from over 2,200 named poets. Most worked as officials first, since the Tang civil examinations tested verse composition, so a magistrate posted to a remote province might send poems home describing the road, the weather, and a friend left behind.

Li Bai wrote of wine and wandering and drowned, by one late story, trying to embrace the moon's reflection in a river. Du Fu, less celebrated in his own lifetime, catalogued famine, conscription and exile in plain language that later readers valued for its detail. Fewer than half the era's poems are thought to survive.

The Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow staged Swan Lake in March 1877 with choreography by Julius Reisinger, who was working from a score most of the dancers and musicians found unusually difficult and symphonic for a ballet of the period. Tchaikovsky had been paid a flat fee for the commission and had no say over how it was staged.

Reviewers criticised the choreography, a worn set and a corps de ballet that struggled with the music, and the production closed after only a handful of performances. Tchaikovsky did not live to see the ballet succeed, since the version now performed everywhere, with revised choreography by Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov, was not staged in St Petersburg until 1895, two years after his death.

Sen no Rikyu was tea master to two successive warlords, Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi, advising on the design of tea rooms deliberately built small and plain, sometimes with a low crawling entrance that forced even a lord to stoop before entering. He favoured rough, irregular Raku ware bowls over imported Chinese porcelain that earlier tea gatherings had prized.

Rikyu's approach to tea, later called wabi, valued a worn or asymmetrical object over a costly one, and his written instructions and stories about him were passed down by his pupils as the basis for later schools of practice. Hideyoshi ordered him to commit suicide in 1591, for reasons contemporaries disputed, and Rikyu did so by ritual seppuku.

Tepeyac is a low hill north of what was Tenochtitlan, on the causeway route into the Aztec capital. Spanish friars writing after the conquest recorded a shrine there to a maternal deity called Tonantzin, meaning Our Revered Mother, a title applied to more than one Aztec goddess rather than the name of a single figure.

In December 1531, according to church accounts written decades later, a Nahua man named Juan Diego reported an apparition of the Virgin Mary on the same hill, an event now venerated as Our Lady of Guadalupe. Many Nahuatl speakers continued and still continue to call the Virgin Tonantzin, a name the Catholic church came to treat with unease as evidence the old cult had never fully gone.

On 27 February 380, Theodosius, together with his co emperors Gratian and Valentinian II, issued an edict at Thessalonica ordering all subjects of the empire to hold the faith taught by the bishops of Rome and Alexandria, the Nicene formula that named Father, Son and Holy Spirit as one substance. Other Christian creeds, Arianism among them, were now branded heresy under imperial law rather than simply argued against in council.

Theodosius had fallen seriously ill at Thessalonica and been baptised there shortly before the edict, which named the local bishop Acholius alongside the bishops of Rome and Alexandria as the standard of orthodoxy. He followed the edict with further laws closing pagan temples and stripping Arian clergy of their churches, work that took most of the rest of his reign.

On 24 October 1795 Russia, Prussia and Austria signed the final division of what had been the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
