Russia took roughly half the remaining territory; Austria and Prussia split most of the rest. King Stanislaw August Poniatowski abdicated the following month and died in Saint Petersburg in 1798.

The partition followed the failed Kosciuszko Uprising of 1794, an armed rising against the earlier two partitions that the three powers crushed within a year. No Polish state appeared on maps of Europe again until 1918, though Polish language and institutions survived under each occupying administration in different forms.

No first-century document places Thomas in India; the story comes from the third-century Acts of Thomas, which has him sold as a carpenter-slave to an Indian king's envoy and later martyred near Mylapore. Communities on India's Malabar coast, the Saint Thomas Christians, trace their founding to his arrival by sea around the middle of the first century.

What can be checked is older trade, not the apostle himself: Roman coin hoards and pepper routes linking the Malabar coast to the Mediterranean by this period show the sea crossing he is said to have made was already a working shipping lane. Later Portuguese and Syriac writers built cathedrals and liturgies on the tradition without adding to the evidence for it.

Aquinas worked on his Summa Theologica for roughly a decade before stopping abruptly in December 1273, after what he described to a companion as an experience during Mass that made further writing feel pointless; he died a few months later in 1274 with the Summa unfinished. Later editors completed the final section from his earlier writings.

The work is organised as a long series of questions, each stating objections before Aquinas answers them, a format built for classroom debate rather than continuous reading. It drew on Aristotle's logic and natural philosophy, recently retranslated into Latin from Arabic commentaries, to argue that reason and Christian doctrine could support rather than contradict each other.

John Landis directed the video, released on 2 December 1983, on a budget reported around 500,000 dollars, roughly ten times what a typical clip then cost. Epic's own contribution covered only a fraction of that, so Jackson and Landis pre-sold a behind-the-scenes documentary, Making Michael Jackson's Thriller, to MTV and Showtime for 250,000 dollars each to close the gap.

Choreographer Michael Peters designed the zombie dance sequence, and makeup artist Rick Baker built the werewolf and ghoul prostheses. Because it ran nearly fourteen minutes, well past the format of any single, MTV and cable channels aired it as a stand-alone programme rather than in normal video rotation, and the documentary alone reportedly sold over a million copies on video cassette.

The Djinguereber mosque, commissioned in the city and completed around 1330, and the nearby Sankore mosque anchored a cluster of Islamic scholarship that grew alongside Timbuktu's trade in salt, gold and books. Sankore was a loose federation of independent teachers rather than a single chartered university.

Private households built up libraries of manuscripts on law, astronomy, medicine and theology, copied by hand in Arabic and in Songhai and Bambara written in Arabic script. Many of those family collections survived centuries of Saharan heat and later conflict and are still catalogued in Timbuktu today, giving historians a written record of West African scholarship that oral tradition alone could not.

Timbuktu grew up as a trading post on the edge of the Sahara, where camel caravans carrying salt and gold met boats on the Niger river. The Sankore mosque there, expanded under Mansa Musa's patronage after his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, grew into a loose federation of independent teachers rather than a single chartered institution, each running classes in law, grammar or theology out of his own house.

Students travelled from across West Africa to study under these teachers and to copy texts by hand, and private family libraries in the city still hold manuscripts, some running to hundreds of thousands of pages across Timbuktu as a whole, on subjects from astronomy to medicine as well as Islamic law. Most were never printed and survive only as these handwritten copies.

Sankore grew up around a mosque rather than as a single chartered institution. Scholars taught in its courtyard and in private houses nearby, and students paid them directly, often in salt, cloth or grain, rather than through fees to any central body. A student who finished a course of study with a particular teacher received a turban rather than a diploma.

Manuscripts on law, astronomy and medicine, many in Arabic and some in Songhay written in Arabic script, were copied, bought and traded in Timbuktu's markets, and merchant families built private libraries alongside the mosque schools. Thousands of these manuscripts survived in family hands into the twenty first century, when looting during the 2012 occupation of the city prompted a rescue effort that smuggled many of them south to Bamako.

After Timur's death in 1405, his son Shah Rukh moved the dynasty's capital from Samarkand to Herat and gave up his father's campaigning for building and collecting. His own son, Baysunghur, ran a workshop of calligraphers, painters and bookbinders inside the palace, commissioning an illustrated Shahnameh that took craftsmen from 1426 to January 1430 to complete.

Herat's workshops paired Persian verse with paintings using flattened space and mineral pigments ground from lapis lazuli, standards later copied across Safavid Iran and Mughal India. Baysunghur died in 1433, before his own project of compiling a critical edition of the Shahnameh text was finished, but the Herat school he had built kept working under later Timurid patrons for decades.

Titian ran the busiest workshop in Venice from a house on the Grand Canal, taking commissions from the doge, the pope and the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who made him a count palatine in 1533. He worked directly onto canvas with pigment rather than finishing every detail in underdrawing first, building up colour in layers he adjusted as the painting progressed.

That method let him rework a figure's pose or a sky's tone late, something fresco and tempera painters could not do. Venetian merchants supplied pigments, including costly ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli, and Titian's late paintings grew looser and more visibly brushed as his eyesight and hand steadied less with age.

By 1700, the Tokugawa shogunate's policy of confining lords to alternating residence between their home domains and Edo had swollen the city to roughly a million people, among the largest in the world at the time. Feeding, clothing and entertaining that population created a commercial economy that ran alongside, and increasingly around, the formal samurai hierarchy above it.

Bookshops rented out illustrated fiction, kabuki and puppet theatres ran daily programmes, and licensed pleasure districts operated under shogunate oversight rather than outright ban. None of this culture challenged the political order directly, since merchants remained legally beneath samurai, farmers and artisans, but it gave commoners a public life and set of shared references the earlier warrior centred decades had not offered them.

Tokyo had been awarded the 1940 Olympics before Japan's own government cancelled them over the war in China, so the October 1964 games, the first held in Asia, closed a twenty four year gap. The final torchbearer, Yoshinori Sakai, had been born near Hiroshima on the day the atomic bomb was dropped there, a choice organisers made deliberately.

The games introduced satellite television transmission, letting pictures reach the United States within hours rather than days by film, and debuted judo and women's volleyball as Olympic sports, the volleyball final watched by television audiences that reportedly exceeded 80 percent of Japanese households with a set.

After Toledo fell to Christian Castile in 1085, its libraries held Arabic manuscripts of Greek philosophy and science with no Latin equivalent. Archbishop Raymond, in office from 1126, sponsored translators who often worked in relay: a Jewish or Mozarab scholar turning the Arabic into Castilian, then a cleric turning that into Latin.

Gerard of Cremona, working in the city until his death in 1187, is credited with translating around eighty-seven works, including Ptolemy's Almagest and treatises by Avicenna and al-Razi. Copies travelled to Paris and Bologna, giving European scholars their first Latin access to texts previously known there only by title.

In the highlands of Sulawesi, Toraja communities built tongkonan houses with peaked roofs sweeping upward at each end, raised on piles and carved with buffalo motifs marking a family's standing. A death was not treated as final until a funeral was held, sometimes delayed for years while relatives gathered enough buffalo to sacrifice.

Bodies were kept at home, wrapped and treated as sick rather than dead, until the family could afford the ceremony. Some were then placed in tombs cut into cliff faces, guarded by carved wooden effigies called tau tau, while infants who died before teething were set inside a hollow cut into a living tree.

The Norman court in Palermo kept Greek, Arabic and Latin speaking scribes side by side, a legacy of Sicily's earlier Byzantine and Islamic rule. Under this trilingual administration, a scholar translated Ptolemy's Almagest directly from a Greek manuscript around 1160, independently of the Arabic route being used at the same time in Toledo.

Henricus Aristippus, an archdeacon at the court, translated Plato's Meno and Phaedo into Latin, the first versions of those dialogues available anywhere in western Europe. The court official Eugenius of Palermo translated Arabic and Greek astronomical texts, working in a chancery that issued official documents in three languages at once.

Homer's Iliad, composed centuries after any siege it describes, gives the war a cast of gods intervening on the battlefield and a quarrel over a woman as its cause. Excavations at Hisarlik in northwest Turkey, the site identified as Troy since Heinrich Schliemann's digs in the 1870s, show a fortified city there was burned and possibly attacked around the time ancient chronographers dated the war.

Later Greek writers fixed the fall of Troy at specific years, one tradition settling on 1184 BC, though nothing in the archaeology confirms a ten-year siege, a wooden horse or Helen. What survives is a city that existed, was destroyed by fire in the late Bronze Age, and was rebuilt into the legend that outlasted the physical evidence for it.

Guilhem de Peiteus, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, is the earliest troubadour whose poems survive under his own name, composing in Occitan rather than Latin or French. His verses treat a noblewoman as an unattainable object of service, a stance later poets systematised into the conventions of fin'amor.

The tradition spread through courts in Provence, Aquitaine and Toulouse, carried by trobairitz, women poets, as well as men, and by jongleurs who performed the songs to melodies that mostly do not survive in notation. The Albigensian Crusade against Cathar heretics in the thirteenth century broke up many of the southern courts that had supported troubadour poets, scattering the tradition northward into other languages.

Sultan Ahmed III's grand vizier, Ibrahim Pasha, staged tulip festivals at night in the palace gardens, with candles fixed to the backs of tortoises to light the flowerbeds. A single rare bulb could sell for the price of a house, and regulations were issued to control speculation in tulip prices.

The period also brought Istanbul its first printing press, run by a Hungarian convert named Ibrahim Muteferrika, and embassies sent to Paris that came back describing French gardens and architecture. It ended in 1730 when a janissary revolt forced Ahmed III to abdicate, and the mob killed Ibrahim Pasha in the street after the sultan handed him over.

Jack Dorsey, Biz Stone, Evan Williams and Noah Glass built Twitter out of a side project at the podcasting company Odeo, sending the first public post from Dorsey's account on 21 March 2006. The 140-character limit was set to fit inside a single SMS text message, the medium the founders first imagined it running on.

Growth stayed slow until South by Southwest in March 2007, where organisers put screens showing the feed in hallways and attendance on the service jumped from around 20,000 to 60,000 tweets a day over the festival. The @ symbol for replies and the hashtag were both conventions users invented themselves, adopted by the company only afterwards.

John Locke published Two Treatises of Government anonymously in 1689, the year after the parliament that installed William and Mary as joint monarchs. The first treatise attacks Robert Filmer's argument that kings inherit absolute authority from Adam; the second sets out Locke's own case that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed and exists to protect life, liberty and property.

Locke had drafted much of the work earlier, in the 1680s, while political tension over royal succession was already running high, and he did not publicly admit authorship until near the end of his life. The argument that a government breaking that trust could be lawfully resisted fed directly into later debates in America over the following century.

Edo's licensed pleasure quarters and kabuki theatres gave woodblock printers a ready subject and a ready market: patrons wanted portable, cheap images of the actors and courtesans they had seen or wished to see. Publishers commissioned an artist's design, then handed it to separate block carvers and printers, so a single popular image could be run off in large numbers.

Early prints around 1670 were sold as plain black outlines, sometimes hand coloured afterward with an orange or red wash, since multi block colour printing had not yet been developed. The genre's name, pictures of the floating world, borrowed a Buddhist phrase for life's transience and turned it toward the opposite meaning, celebrating fleeting pleasure rather than warning against it.

Before Suzuki Harunobu, woodblock prints were mostly hand coloured or limited to two or three printed pigments. Harunobu worked with Edo publishers and carvers to register ten or more colour blocks accurately onto a single sheet, producing what were called brocade pictures for their resemblance to woven cloth.

The new technique suited the calendar prints wealthy patrons commissioned as New Year gifts, which hid the year's lucky and unlucky days within a picture rather than printing them plainly. Harunobu's delicate figures of young women and lovers set the look that later ukiyo-e print makers built on.

No mainstream printer in Britain or the United States would touch it, so Sylvia Beach, the American owner of the Paris bookshop Shakespeare and Company, published it herself on 2 February 1922, Joyce's fortieth birthday. Chapters had already appeared in the American magazine The Little Review, where an obscenity prosecution over a passage describing masturbation halted serialisation before the book was finished.

United States customs seized and burned copies for over a decade until a 1933 federal ruling, United States v. One Book Called Ulysses, found the novel not obscene and let it be sold there. Joyce compressed the whole story into a single day in Dublin, 16 June 1904, tracking the advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom, which Joyceans now mark every year as Bloomsday.

The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem was completed around 692, its inner walls covered in gold and glass mosaics of vine scrolls, vases and jewelled crowns rather than figures of people or animals, which Umayyad patrons avoided in religious buildings. The Great Mosque of Damascus followed a few years later, its courtyard walls covered in mosaics showing rivers, trees and empty palaces without any human figure at all.

Making the Damascus mosaics used roughly two hundred tonnes of glass and gold foil beaten from more than two thousand coins, according to estimates by conservators who studied the surviving tesserae. Byzantine craftsmen working in the techniques of Ravenna and Constantinople were brought in alongside local artisans, so the empire the Umayyads had displaced supplied the skill behind their new monuments.

The UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181 on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions including Britain, which held the mandate over Palestine and had asked the UN to decide its future. The plan divided the territory into separate Jewish and Arab states with Jerusalem placed under international administration.

Jewish leaders accepted the plan; the Arab League and Palestinian Arab leadership rejected it, and fighting between Jewish and Arab militias began within days of the vote. Britain ended its mandate on 14 May 1948, the day Israel declared independence, and neighbouring Arab states sent troops across the borders the plan had drawn.

Harriet Beecher Stowe first ran the story in weekly instalments in the abolitionist paper the National Era through 1851, then published it as a two-volume book in March 1852. She wrote it partly in response to the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which made it a federal crime to help an escaped enslaved person even in free states.

The book sold around 300,000 copies in the United States within its first year and far more abroad, and it was quickly adapted into touring stage shows that outlived interest in the novel itself. Southern writers responded with a wave of pro-slavery novels answering it, none of which matched its readership.

Before 1200, advanced teaching in Europe was largely a cathedral or monastery affair, run by a bishop's school or an abbey for a handful of clerics. Over the following decades masters and students in several cities organised themselves into guilds, unions that could bargain collectively with local authorities over rent, food prices and legal protection from secular courts.

These guilds won charters granting them the right to set their own curricula and examinations and, crucially, exemption from ordinary town justice. The result was a new kind of institution, neither church school nor royal academy, that could outlast any single teacher or patron and kept awarding degrees recognised well beyond the city where they were earned.

Masters and students at Paris had organised themselves informally from the mid twelfth century, but it was King Philip II's charter of 1200, granted after students clashed with the city watch, that first recognised them as a single legal body exempt from ordinary civic justice.

Fifteen years later the papal legate Robert de Courcon issued the university's first written statutes, fixing the length of study and the qualifications required for a licence to teach. Faculties of arts, law, medicine and theology, and the practice of granting degrees, spread outward from Paris to new universities across thirteenth century Europe.

Robert de Sorbon, a theologian who had risen from a poor family near Rethel to become confessor to King Louis IX, bought property in Paris in 1257 to house students too poor to otherwise study theology. Louis IX supported the purchase, and the resulting college took Sorbon's own name, the Maison de Sorbonne.

Pope Alexander IV confirmed the college in 1259, and it grew into the theological heart of the wider University of Paris, which had already existed informally for decades before Sorbon's foundation gave it a lasting institutional home. The name Sorbonne later came to stand for the university itself, long after the original almshouse for poor scholars had been absorbed into a much larger institution.

The earliest Upanishads were composed as prose and verse appendices to the older Vedic ritual texts, often as dialogues between a teacher and a pupil seated close together, which the word itself suggests. They shifted the centre of religious attention from fire sacrifice toward a single underlying reality, brahman, identified with the innermost self, atman.

There is no single author or founding date; the oldest layer, including the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya, took shape over centuries and later Upanishads kept being added for another thousand years. More than 200 texts eventually carried the name, though only a dozen or so are treated as the principal ones.

Thomas More wrote Utopia in Latin and had it printed at Louvain in 1516, framing it as a traveller's account told to him by a fictional sailor, Raphael Hythloday, who describes an island where property is held in common and gold is used to make chamber pots. The word itself is a pun More coined from Greek, meaning both a good place and no place.

An English translation did not appear until 1551, sixteen years after More was executed for refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the church. The book's island has no private ownership and religious tolerance, features More's own devout Catholicism did not extend to endorsing outright in the England he lived in.

Van Gogh painted it in June 1889 at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum near Saint-Remy, where he had admitted himself after cutting off part of his own ear in Arles. He worked from memory and imagination rather than directly from the view, adding a village and a cypress tree that were not visible from his barred window.

He wrote to his brother Theo that he thought the picture a failure next to his daytime wheat fields, and it stayed rolled up, unsold, through the rest of his life. The Museum of Modern Art in New York bought it in 1941 for less than 1,500 dollars, decades after Van Gogh had died penniless in 1890.

The Vedas were composed and transmitted orally in early Sanskrit for generations before being written down at all, memorised syllable by syllable through techniques designed to prevent even a single sound from drifting across centuries of recitation. Brahmin priests specialised in performing the fire sacrifices these texts prescribe, correct performance mattering as much as correct belief.

Later Vedic texts describe society divided into four varnas, with Brahmins as priests and scholars at the top, a framework that hardened over time into hereditary caste distinctions extending well beyond ritual roles. How closely this textual scheme matched everyday social organisation in the period is debated, since the surviving texts were composed and preserved by the priestly class describing its own position.

The Rigveda, the oldest of the four Vedas, took shape as an oral composition among Indo-Aryan communities in the Punjab region, with most scholars dating its core hymns to between roughly 1500 and 1200 BCE. It was composed and preserved through memorised recitation rather than writing.

Its 1,028 hymns, addressed to gods such as Indra and Agni, were passed down through strict rules of pronunciation and metre for centuries before being written down. Comparison of the recitation traditions preserved in different regions of India shows only minor variation between them, evidence of how tightly that oral transmission was controlled.

No inscription or manuscript survives from this period; the dating rests on the language of the hymns themselves and on cross reference to later, datable texts. Scholars generally place the composition of the Rigveda's oldest hymns somewhere in the second millennium BCE, in the Punjab region, among cattle herding communities speaking an early form of Sanskrit.

The hymns were preserved by memorisation and recitation from teacher to pupil for well over a thousand years before being written down, using techniques designed to guard against any change in a single syllable. They address gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna, and describe rivers, tribes and rituals that later Indian religious tradition drew on directly.

Venetian nuns and lay workshops built up needle lace from a technique called punto in aria, air stitch, in which thread was worked over a paper pattern with no woven base cloth at all, unlike the bobbin lace made elsewhere in Europe. Pattern books printed in Venice from the 1550s let buyers and workshops as far away as France copy the designs.

A single collar could take a skilled worker months, since every loop was stitched by hand rather than woven, and the finished lace was sold by weight of thread as much as by size. French demand grew so large that Louis XIV's minister Colbert later set up a rival state workshop at Alençon specifically to stop French money from paying Venetian workers for it.

Krishnadevaraya was crowned at Vijayanagara on 26 July 1509 and ruled for two decades from the capital at Hampi, on the Tungabhadra river. He commissioned the Vitthala temple complex, with its carved stone pillars said to ring like musical notes when struck, and the Hazara Rama temple, its walls carved with scenes from the Ramayana for the court alone to view.

A Portuguese horse trader named Domingo Paes visited the city during his reign and described markets selling diamonds and pearls beside street after street of houses, a rare outside account of a capital that later Deccan sultanates would sack and largely empty within a generation of Krishnadevaraya's death.

Andrea Amati worked in Cremona from around 1540, fixing a body shape, arching and f-hole placement that later makers largely kept. His earliest surviving instruments date from the 1560s, including a violin made for the French court of Charles IX, decorated with the king's monogram and motto in gold on a dark ground.

Amati's workshop passed to his sons and then his grandson Nicolo, whose own pupils included Andrea Guarneri and, by most accounts, Antonio Stradivari. Cremona kept its reputation for violin making across three more generations of the same families, working from the proportions Amati had settled on in the sixteenth century.

Virgil spent roughly a decade on the Aeneid, from about 29 BCE until his death in 19 BCE, following the Trojan survivor Aeneas from the fall of Troy to a landing in Italy, where his descendants would found Rome. Augustus, whose own lineage the poem flatters through Aeneas's son, took a personal interest and reportedly asked to hear passages read aloud as they were drafted.

Virgil left the poem unfinished and asked in his will for the manuscript to be burned rather than published incomplete. Augustus overruled that instruction, and the poets Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca edited the text for release, making only light corrections rather than completing any of its unfinished lines.

Vivaldi published the four concertos as part of a larger set of twelve called Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione, dedicated to a Bohemian count. Each season concerto came printed with a sonnet describing the scene it followed, a barking dog in Spring, a drunken dance in Autumn, teeth chattering in the cold in Winter.

Vivaldi worked for decades at the Ospedale della Pieta, a Venice orphanage for girls, training its choir and orchestra and writing much of his output for them to perform. He died in Vienna in 1741 in modest circumstances, and his music went largely unplayed for nearly two centuries afterward.

Voltaire wrote Candide in a matter of weeks, provoked partly by the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 and by his long dispute with the philosopher Gottfried Leibniz's followers, who held that this was, on balance, the best of all possible worlds. Its hero survives war, shipwreck, the Inquisition and an earthquake modelled on Lisbon's while his tutor Pangloss insists each disaster proves the world's underlying goodness.

Published simultaneously in several cities in January 1759 to dodge censors, it sold out fast enough that Geneva's authorities burned it and Paris banned it within weeks, which did nothing to stop pirated editions spreading across France. Its closing advice, to tend one's own garden rather than argue metaphysics, became the line most readers remembered.

Voltaire wrote the Letters after nearly three years in England, where he had gone following a duel-related scandal in Paris. The 24 letters praised English religious toleration, Newton's science and a parliament that could check a king, framed as friendly reports to a French audience.

The French government judged the comparison an insult to its own institutions and ordered the book burned; a warrant was issued for Voltaire's arrest, and he fled Paris for his mistress's chateau at Cirey. The letters circulated anyway, copied and reprinted outside French jurisdiction.

Peter Waldo, a wealthy merchant of Lyon, gave away his property around 1173 after commissioning a vernacular translation of the Gospels. His followers, known as the Poor of Lyon, preached voluntary poverty in the streets and read scripture aloud in French rather than the Latin used by ordained clergy.

The local archbishop banned their unlicensed preaching, and Pope Lucius III excommunicated the group at the Council of Verona in 1184. Driven into the Alpine valleys of France and Italy, Waldensian communities survived there for centuries and later joined the Protestant Reformation in the sixteenth century.

Sony launched the TPS-L2 in Japan on 1 July 1979 at a price of 33,000 yen, built by engineer Kozo Ohsone's team from an existing dictation recorder with the playback speaker stripped out and the recording circuit removed to save weight. Company chairman Akio Morita reportedly pushed the project through over doubts from Sony's own sales division, which questioned whether a tape player with no speaker or record function would sell at all.

It shipped with two headphone jacks so a pair of listeners could share one unit, a feature dropped from later models once solo listening turned out to be the point. Sony sold roughly 30,000 units in Japan within the first two months, and the device spread internationally under different names before the Walkman brand was adopted worldwide.

At a spring gathering on Mount Kuaiji in 353, forty two guests composed poems and Wang Xizhi wrote a short preface to the collection in running script, correcting several characters as he went. Tradition holds that the emperor Taizong of Tang loved the piece so much that it was buried with him two and a half centuries later, taking the original out of circulation for good.

What survives are copies made before or soon after that burial, traced stroke for stroke onto silk or paper by court scribes, and it is these copies, not Wang's own hand, that later calligraphers studied and imitated for over a thousand years. Scholars still argue over which surviving copy comes closest to the lost original.

Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre on the Air adapted H.G. Wells's novel for CBS radio on 30 October 1938, staging it as a dance programme interrupted by fake news bulletins about a Martian landing near Grovers Mill, New Jersey. A spoken disclaimer opened and closed the hour, and another ran at the midpoint.

The following day's newspapers reported nationwide panic, but a ratings service found only about two percent of the national audience had even tuned in. Print papers, which had been losing advertising revenue to radio through the Depression, had reason to play up radio's irresponsibility, and later research found little evidence of the mass flight the headlines described.

Irving Blum hung thirty two small canvases in a single row at his Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles in July 1962, one for each variety of Campbell's soup then sold, painted by hand and stencil from a photograph rather than mass printed. He priced them at 100 dollars each and sold five before deciding the set belonged together, buying back the sold ones on instalments to keep it whole.

A nearby gallery mocked the show by stacking real soup cans in its window with a sign offering the genuine article cheaper. Warhol had spent the previous decade as a commercial illustrator drawing shoe advertisements, and brought that trade's flat colour and repetition straight into the paintings.

Adam Smith spent roughly a decade writing the book, drawing on lectures he had given in Glasgow and on a tour of France where he met economists arguing that land, not trade, was the true source of wealth. He published it in March 1776, the same year as the American Declaration of Independence, in two quarto volumes priced at one pound sixteen shillings, well beyond most readers' budgets.

Smith argued that a nation grows richer through the division of labour and free exchange rather than through hoarding gold or restricting trade, and he attacked the tariffs and monopolies granted to merchant companies. Government ministers, including William Pitt the Younger, cited it within years, and it went through five editions in Smith's own lifetime.

The show opened at the Winter Garden Theatre on 26 September 1957 after a development that took Arthur Laurents, Leonard Bernstein and Jerome Robbins nearly a decade, during which the warring families first conceived as Jewish and Catholic became the Puerto Rican Sharks and the white Jets. A twenty seven year old lyricist named Stephen Sondheim, hired late, wrote his first Broadway words for it.

Robbins choreographed the gang confrontations as dance rather than mime, and rehearsed the two casts separately so real tension carried into the finger snapping opening. Reviews were respectful rather than rapturous, and the show lost that year's Tony for best musical to The Music Man, though its film version later won ten Academy Awards.

Urban VI's election in Rome in 1378 was contested within months by the same cardinals who had chosen him, who claimed mob pressure from a Roman crowd demanding an Italian pope had made the vote invalid. Those cardinals withdrew to Fondi and elected Robert of Geneva instead, who took the name Clement VII and set up a rival court back in Avignon.

France, Scotland and Castile backed the Avignon line while England, most of Italy and the German princes backed Rome, splitting Western Christendom's obedience along political lines rather than doctrine. A church council at Pisa in 1409 tried to end the split by electing a third pope instead of resolving it, and the schism was not fully closed until the Council of Constance in 1417.

Ockham was a Franciscan friar who studied at Oxford and completed every requirement for a master's degree in theology, yet was never named regent master, so admirers nicknamed him the Venerable Beginner. In 1324 Pope John XXII summoned him to the papal court at Avignon over heretical passages found in his commentary on the Sentences, an inquiry that produced critical reports but was never concluded.

His nominalism denied that general categories exist outside the mind; only individual objects are real, and general terms are words for groups of similar things. He never wrote the phrase now attached to his name; his own version held that plurality should not be assumed without necessity. Franciscan poverty disputes cost him standing with the church, and he spent his final years in Munich under the protection of Louis IV.

MGM shot the Kansas scenes in sepia-toned black and white and switched to three-strip Technicolor the moment Dorothy opens the farmhouse door onto Oz, a contrast built into the production rather than a later restoration effect. Margaret Hamilton, playing the Wicked Witch, suffered burns during a filmed exit through a trapdoor when the flame effect ignited early, and refused to return for the scene's reshoot.

The film cost around three million dollars, an unusually large budget for 1939, and did not turn a profit on its first theatrical run once promotion costs were counted against modest box office. Repeated television broadcasts from the late 1950s onward, rather than its original release, built the audience and reputation it is now known for.

Wolof-speaking communities along the Senegal river valley lived under the Jolof empire, a confederation that had pulled together smaller Wolof states by the fourteenth century and taxed trade passing between the Sahara and the Atlantic coast. Millet, salt, cloth and enslaved captives moved along these routes, carried by caravans that answered to Jolof's ruling lineage.

Teranga, the obligation to feed and shelter a guest without being asked, is first described in later written accounts, but the practice long predates any of them and was bound up with a household's standing. A family's reputation rested on how a stranger was received at its threshold, a measure that outlasted Jolof's own fragmentation into smaller Wolof kingdoms in the sixteenth century.

The Representation of the People Act received royal assent on 6 February 1918, giving the vote to women aged 30 and over who also met a property qualification, either owning land or being married to someone who did. That excluded most working class women under 30, including many who had taken factory jobs during the war just ended.

The same act removed property qualifications for men and lowered the male voting age to 21, so it added roughly 8.4 million women to the register alongside about 5.6 million newly enfranchised men. Full equal suffrage, at 21 for both sexes, did not arrive until the Representation of the People Act of 1928.

Kate Sheppard led a campaign built on petitions rather than protest, and the final one presented to parliament in 1893 ran to over five hundred sheets of paper glued end to end, carrying more than 31,000 signatures. Premier John Ballance had supported the bill; it passed under his successor after two members of the upper house switched their votes at the last moment.

The Electoral Act received royal assent on 19 September 1893, and women voted for the first time that November, twelve days after the law allowed enough time to register. Married women could vote alongside unmarried ones, though Maori women, like Maori men, voted through separate seats rather than the general roll.

Roughly 400,000 people gathered on Max Yasgur's dairy farm near Bethel, New York, from 15 to 18 August 1969, far more than the organisers had planned or ticketed for. Traffic backed up for miles on the surrounding roads, the fences came down early, and the promoters eventually declared it a free concert rather than turn people away.

Thirty-two acts performed over the four days, including Richie Havens, who opened, Janis Joplin, The Who and Jimi Hendrix, whose Star-Spangled Banner closed the festival on Monday morning to a crowd reduced to a few tens of thousands. Rain turned much of the site to mud, food and water ran short, and two attendees died, one from a heroin overdose and one run over by a tractor.

FIFA split hosting between South Korea and Japan after both countries lodged competing bids, a compromise that produced two separate organising committees, two mascots and matches split almost evenly across twenty stadiums in both nations. Ten new or rebuilt stadiums were completed for the tournament, including Yokohama's International Stadium for the final.

South Korea, coached by Guus Hiddink, reached the semi-finals as the lowest-ranked team ever to do so, beating Italy and Spain along the way amid disputed refereeing decisions. Brazil won a record fifth title, beating Germany 2-0 in the final on goals from Ronaldo, who finished the tournament as top scorer with eight.

The translation carrying John Wycliffe's name was probably not his own work. Historians now think it was produced by a group of his Oxford associates, including Nicholas of Hereford and possibly John Purvey, translating directly from the Latin Vulgate rather than the Greek or Hebrew originals, which were not yet widely available to English scholars.

The Church banned unlicensed English translations in 1409, partly because Wycliffe's followers, the Lollards, used the text to argue for reform without clergy as intermediaries. Copies kept circulating in secret regardless; around 250 manuscripts survive, an unusually high number for a banned book, and it stayed the main English Bible until William Tyndale's translation from the original languages in the 1520s.

The scare traced back to a coding shortcut from the 1960s and 1970s, when programmers stored years as two digits to save scarce memory, so 1999 rolling to 2000 risked machines reading the date as 1900. Governments and firms spent an estimated 300 to 600 billion dollars worldwide checking and rewriting code in the final years of the decade.

At midnight on 1 January 2000, power grids, banks and air traffic systems kept running in every time zone as the date changed, with only scattered minor glitches reported, including a few slot machines in Delaware and a handful of hospital equipment logs. Critics later argued the spending had been wildly disproportionate to the risk, while remediation advocates credited the quiet outcome to the work already done.

Paul VI died on 6 August 1978 after a fifteen year papacy. The conclave that followed elected Cardinal Albino Luciani of Venice, who took the name John Paul I to honour his two predecessors. He served only 33 days, found dead in his bed on 29 September, and the Vatican's shifting account of the discovery, including who found him and at what hour, fed persistent rumour rather than any established finding of foul play.

A second conclave in October elected Karol Wojtyla, archbishop of Krakow, who took the name John Paul II. He was the first non-Italian pope in 455 years, since the Dutch-born Adrian VI, and the choice of a Polish cardinal surprised observers expecting another Italian. His papacy ran almost twenty seven years, ending with his death in April 2005.

George Williams, a 22-year-old draper's assistant, called together a dozen other young men working in London's textile trade in June 1844 to found the Young Men's Christian Association. Many clerks and shop assistants at the time lodged above the shops where they worked, with long hours and few places to meet outside pubs or brothels.

The Association offered Bible study, reading rooms and eventually the gymnasiums and residential halls that became its trademark, spreading to Boston within a decade and then across the world. Williams, later knighted for the work, ran his own drapery business alongside it for much of his life and lived to see the YMCA established on every inhabited continent.

A German ethnographer named Leo Frobenius first drew outside attention to Ife's sculpture in 1910, but the copper and brass heads he found were cast by local artisans centuries earlier, most dated between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. The metal was worked so thin that some heads weigh only a few kilograms despite standing life size.

Beaded crowns on several heads point to royal subjects, likely past holders of the title ooni, and Yoruba oral tradition credits king Obalufon II with introducing brass casting and later becoming the craft's patron deity. Terracotta heads and fragments from the Iwinrin Grove, modelled with the same close attention to individual faces, stood on shrines within the palace compound.

Three former PayPal employees, Chad Hurley, Steve Chen and Jawed Karim, registered the domain on 14 February 2005 from an office above a pizzeria in San Mateo, California. Karim's own 19-second clip filmed at the San Diego Zoo, titled Me at the zoo, went up on 23 April and remains the site's earliest surviving video.

Adobe Flash video let clips play instantly in a browser without a separate download, which set YouTube apart from earlier sharing sites. Google bought the eighteen-month-old company for 1.65 billion dollars in stock in October 2006, by which point it was already serving tens of millions of views a day.

King Lalibela, who ruled Ethiopia's Zagwe dynasty from around 1181 to 1221, is credited with the eleven churches at Lalibela, each cut downward out of solid volcanic rock rather than built up from quarried blocks. Tradition holds he intended a new Jerusalem after Muslim control of the Holy Land cut off pilgrim routes.

Each church was isolated by trenches cut around a block of stone from the top down, then hollowed from inside to form windows, doors and columns, with tunnels connecting the buildings below ground level. The churches remain active places of worship, and pilgrims gather there each January for Ethiopian Christmas.

Zeami Motokiyo learned Noh as a boy performing for the shogun Yoshimitsu, who kept him close at court in Kyoto. Between roughly 1400 and 1402 he set down what he had absorbed from his father Kannami in a treatise called Fushikaden, written for his own troupe's eyes only and passed down as a secret transmission rather than a public text.

The treatise describes yugen, a quality of restrained, suggestive beauty, and yohaku, the unfilled space an actor leaves for the audience's imagination. Zeami went on writing further treatises into old age, after a shogunate succession he had not backed sent him into exile on Sado Island. His plays are still performed on Noh stages using the conventions he wrote down.

The monk Eisai returned to Japan in 1191 trained in the Linji tradition of Chan Buddhism from China and began teaching it as Rinzai Zen. Opposition from established Kyoto sects kept him at temples in Kyushu until 1202, when he became abbot of the newly built Kennin-ji in the capital itself.

Eisai also brought back tea seeds, planting them near the border of Fukuoka and Saga, and later wrote a treatise praising tea's medicinal benefits. Rinzai's emphasis on sudden insight through koan riddles, and its adoption by the samurai class, shaped garden design, ink painting and the tea ceremony in the centuries after his death in 1215.

Almost nothing about Zoroaster is fixed with confidence, including his century; estimates for his life have ranged from roughly 1500 to 500 BCE, with many historians now favouring somewhere near the second millennium BCE in what is now eastern Iran or Central Asia. His own words survive in the Gathas, seventeen hymns in an archaic form of Avestan.

The Gathas describe a single wise lord, Ahura Mazda, locked in struggle with a hostile spirit, and a final judgement weighing each soul's thoughts, words and deeds. The faith later became the state religion of the Achaemenid and Sasanian empires, and its Parsi descendants still keep fire temples in India today.

Zoroastrian priests had preserved their scripture by memory and recitation for over a thousand years before it was written down, probably beginning under the Sassanid king Shapur II in the fourth century. Committing the sacred hymns to writing required inventing a new alphabet, adapted from Aramaic script, precise enough to fix the exact pronunciation of ritual chant.

The resulting Avesta gathers older Avestan language texts, including hymns attributed to Zoroaster himself, alongside younger Middle Persian commentary explaining passages that priests could no longer fully parse. Much of the older material had already been lost by the time of this compilation, and later invasions destroyed more, so the surviving Avesta is a fraction of what priests once recited.

After Ardashir I overthrew the last Parthian king in 224 and founded the Sassanid dynasty, he and his son Shapur I backed Zoroastrian worship, with its fire temples and priestly hierarchy, as the empire's official faith. A chief priest named Kartir, serving successive kings, pushed the fire cult into a position rivals could not easily challenge, and left inscriptions boasting of suppressing other faiths.

Zoroastrian scripture, the Avesta, had circulated for centuries mostly through memorised recitation rather than as a fixed written book, and the Sassanid court began compiling and standardising it during this period. State backing gave the priesthood land and legal authority over marriage and inheritance, tying administration to the temple in ways later rulers had to dismantle.
